effects.log: You sit. The hunt flows round you both. The wolf glances at you, as at an equal.

choices.text: Leave the loop alone

effects.log: You watch. Some centres are to be passed, not entered.

events.text: Horang appears at dawn out of the snow, huge, in a cloak of pelts, and asks how it was. You say you cannot say. A nod: that is the right answer. Then Horang pours you a cup of hot broth, and the beasts lie down around you in a ring.
events.arc: The Hunt of the Wild Lord

choices.text: Drink the broth, and say thank you

effects.log: It tastes of woodsmoke and snow. The ring of beasts sighs, one after another.

choices.text: Ask to be invited again

effects.log: Horang laughs, a huge dry cough. Every year, comes the answer. Every year.

events.text: The Silent Hall has a hunt that makes no noise. Its quarry is a rumour: a whisper that has been going round the courts for a century, getting worse. The hunt follows it from mouth to mouth to find where it began. You have been asked to join, because you are quiet.

choices.text: Join, and listen

effects.log: You are given a notebook and a silence. The hunt begins at a feast, with a servant's sidelong glance.

choices.text: Ask what the rumour says

effects.log: It says that the Hall's oldest ledger has a page missing. That is all it says.

choices.text: Decline politely

effects.log: The Hall nods. A quiet no is the best kind.

events.text: The rumour passes through eleven mouths. At the eleventh you find the origin: a young clerk who made an error in a ledger, hid the page, and told a friend in a panic. The friend told another. The clerk has not slept in a month.

choices.text: Find the clerk, and offer help

effects.log: The clerk, thin and red-eyed, weeps with relief. The page is found behind a bookcase.

choices.text: Report the clerk to the Hall

effects.log: The Hall is stern but fair. The clerk is reassigned, but kept. You feel the weight of the word you said.

events.text: The missing page is real. The Hall's oldest ledger has a gap, and the gap is exactly the size of one name. The rumour is not false; it is only unfinished. Someone in the Hall knows whose name.

choices.text: Go to the oldest archivist and ask

effects.log: The archivist is silent for a long time. Then: it was the name of a god who asked to be forgotten. We kept the promise.

choices.text: Let the gap be

effects.log: A name left blank at someone's request. You respect it.

events.text: The rumour dies in a week. The Hall, with ceremony, burns the page in a small blue flame. The clerk bows to you at the hall door and says, in a whisper, thank you. The Hall, you realise, has never been so quiet, or so kind.

choices.text: Accept the thanks in silence

effects.log: You nod. The clerk is lighter by a hundred pounds.

choices.text: Invite the clerk to tea

effects.log: They come, shy as a deer. You talk of nothing for an hour. It is the finest tea the Hall has had in an age.

events.text: The Hall thanks you coolly, and the clerk is transferred to a posting at the world's far edge. You hear that they like it. You also hear that the rumour, in a smaller form, still goes round: the quiet god who tells.

choices.text: Own the choice, and let the rumour run

effects.log: You are the quiet god who tells. It is not a bad name, in its way.

choices.text: Write the clerk a letter of apology

effects.log: You send it. A reply comes years later: all is well.

events.text: {npc}, a young god of a small cold hearth, stops you in the lane outside the Hearth court and asks, shyly, for a bit of fire. Their own has gone out. They have heard that the ember from the First Hearth, if borne with care, will light any fire in the world.
events.arc: An Ember of the First Hearth

choices.text: Take {him} to the First Hearth

effects.log: The Hearth court is warm as a loaf. Hwarin's attendants look them up and down, and lead you to a small side-door.

choices.text: Give {him} a coal from your own shrine

effects.log: It is small, but it is warm, and {npc} cups it in both hands as if it were a bird.

choices.text: Direct {him} to the Hearth steward

effects.log: {He} bows and goes. You hope the steward is kind.

events.text: Hwarin looks at the shy god across the hearth for a long moment. Then the tongs are lifted, and from the First Fire comes a single, tiny, perfect ember, no larger than a bean. It is lit from within. It goes into a clay cup, and the cup into the hands of {npc}.
events.arc: An Ember of the First Hearth

choices.text: Carry the cup for {him} through the cold

effects.log: The ember is heavier than it looks. You walk it through the dark, a procession of two.

choices.text: Let {him} carry it alone

effects.log: {He} goes, back straight, cup held like a candle. The world makes way.

events.text: The coal from your shrine is not enough. The cold hearth swallows it, and goes out again. {npc} sits down in the ashes and says nothing. {He} is not crying, quite. You have a long moment to decide.
events.arc: An Ember of the First Hearth

choices.text: Take {him} to the First Hearth after all

effects.log: It is a long walk. You go anyway. {npc} does not speak, but walks closer to you.

choices.text: Sit with {him} until dawn

effects.log: You sit. At dawn, a stray cat arrives and sleeps in the ash. A start.

events.text: The ember takes at the cold hearth with a puff, and the room fills with a gold, low light. {npc} laughs, high and surprised, and the hearth-cat sneezes. Over the next month, a line of cold-hearthed gods forms at the door. {He} lights each from the ember and never lets it dim.
events.arc: An Ember of the First Hearth

choices.text: Stay a season to help tend the new fire

effects.log: You stay, learning the art of the small hearth: kindling, patience and a kind of listening. It is a good season.

choices.text: Praise {him} before the Hearth court

effects.log: Hwarin's court applauds, a little startled. {npc} blushes to the roots.

events.text: In the vault of a god of kings lies a crown, cracked from brow to nape. It is guarded by a warden who looks quite relieved to see you. The crown, the warden says, has opinions. It dislikes being left alone, and it dislikes being worn, and it is not quiet about either.

choices.text: Pick it up

effects.log: It is warm, and surprisingly light. It begins, softly, to mutter in an old grammar.

choices.text: Listen from a distance

effects.log: You stand back and listen. The mutter is a list of names, thousands of them, recited in a flat tone.

choices.text: Leave it with the warden

effects.log: The warden sighs. The crown mutters on.

events.text: The muttering shifts: the crown has chosen you. It slips onto your brow of its own accord, and for a moment you see through the eyes of every god who ever wore it: weary, proud, afraid. The crack in the crown aches like an old wound.

choices.text: Hold your own mind against the crown's

ok.log: You hold. The crown shivers, quiets, and sits on your head like a hat.

fail.log: The crown's voices wash over you. You lose a day, wandering the vault in a stranger's coat.

choices.text: Take the crown off at once

effects.log: It comes away with a small sigh. You set it down, shaking. It has the grace not to mutter.

events.text: The names the crown recites are the names of every worshipper who ever knelt to a king-god. It has not forgotten one. It is, the warden says, the longest prayer-list in the world, and it is going slowly mad with the weight.

choices.text: Offer to share the load, with a half-hour a day

effects.log: You sit with it and learn names. It is a lonely vow, and a worthy one.

choices.text: Suggest the warden read to it

effects.log: The warden does. The crown quiets by degrees.

events.text: The crown is not a weapon or a throne. It is a memory. You take it to the highest hill of your domain and set it on a stone, and read the names aloud, one by one, for a day and a night. By dawn the crack in the crown has closed.

choices.text: Leave the crown on the hill as a monument

effects.log: Pilgrims come. They read their own names on the air. It is a quiet, odd kind of faith.

choices.text: Return the crown to the vault, whole

effects.log: The warden weeps with joy. The crown, content, mutters no more.

events.text: You lose a day in the vault, and when you find yourself again the crown is on its shelf, and the warden is holding a cup of cold tea. You have been walking the halls and saying names. The warden, kindly, writes down two of them for you. You have the names of people who were once loved.

choices.text: Find where those two lived, and visit

effects.log: You find a hill and a stream. You leave a small stone in each. It is all you can do.

choices.text: Keep the names in your pocket

effects.log: You carry them. They are warm. They remind you of something you cannot name.

events.text: The kennels of the Wild Lord are full of hounds who have retired from the hunt. They lie in the straw and discuss, in low grumbles, whether the young hounds of today can run. One of them looks at you and says, quite clearly: you could use some training.

choices.text: Take the advice and train a season

effects.log: The old hounds put you through drills. You end the season thinner, quicker and humbler.

choices.text: Thank them and bring a bone

effects.log: They accept the bone and the courtesy. You are a friend of the kennels now.

events.text: A hunting horn sounds in the dusk, from a direction with no hunters. The horn is the wrong colour of sound. Beasts in the wood lift their heads. Whoever sounds it, you feel, expects you to answer.

choices.text: Answer on your own horn

effects.log: The first horn pauses, then sounds again, delighted. A call-and-answer begins that lasts till moonrise.

choices.text: Stay silent and listen

effects.log: The horn dies, patient. Some calls are not for you, tonight.

events.text: A crowned stag of the Wild stands in a clearing, looking at you. Its antlers hold a nest, a lantern and a small bell. A hunter-god drops their bow and weeps: it is the beast their pantheon has sought for a thousand years.

choices.text: Lower your own bow and bow

effects.log: The stag dips its antlers, graciously. The hunter-god thanks you for the example.

choices.text: Ask the hunter-god why they seek it

effects.log: They have forgotten. The question sits in them, strange and quiet.

events.text: A wolf pack holds a mountain pass in the Wild, and gods who wish to cross must bring a gift. The wolves are polite, a little bored. They name their fee: a story. It must be true, it must be short, and it must be new.

choices.text: Tell them about a small kindness you did

effects.log: They listen, ears up. The leader nods. Pass granted. A cub follows you to the end of the pass.

choices.text: Tell them a joke

effects.log: The wolves howl with laughter. The leader wipes an eye with a paw. Pass granted.

events.text: The net-makers of the Storm Throne sell nets woven of wind itself. A hunter god tries one on a gull, and the gull flies off with the net, bemused. A net-maker bows to you and says: for the right hunter, the net will wait.

choices.text: Buy a small net with faith

effects.log: You pay a small tithe. The net is light, shy, and as sure as a sigh.

choices.text: Learn to weave one

effects.log: It takes all afternoon. Your net holds a thought, which is as much as a net should.

events.text: A bear of the Wild is sleeping through winter in a cave under your shrine, and the rumble of its snoring shakes the incense off the altar. The shrine-keeper is nervous. You are, politely, asked to deal with it.

choices.text: Hang a quilt over the cave mouth

effects.log: The snoring muffles. The bear, in its dream, thanks you with a long sleepy sigh.

choices.text: Wait for spring and trade favours

effects.log: In spring the bear wakes, ambles out, and leaves a lump of honeycomb on the step.

events.text: A golden hare crosses your path at dawn and stops, twitching, as if daring you. Gods say whoever catches a golden hare is granted a harvest. Nobody has caught one in a thousand years. You are, as it happens, quite fast.

choices.text: Give chase

effects.log: You chase it over three ridges. It vanishes into a burrow with a flick of white. You laugh until you cry.

choices.text: Leave it a carrot and a bow

effects.log: The hare takes the carrot with great dignity. Your harvest, that year, is quietly good.

events.text: A boar in the hills has a grudge against a particular god, and the god has a grudge against the boar. They have been chasing each other for four hundred years in a long, tedious circle. Both would like to stop.

choices.text: Broker a truce over a bowl of acorns

effects.log: The boar and the god eye each other across the bowl. Slowly, both begin to eat.

choices.text: Let them keep chasing

effects.log: They are, in their way, content. Some feuds are a form of companionship.

events.text: A wooden spoon in a fallen god's kitchen is said to season any dish to the diner's heart. A cook-god offers to let you stir one pot. The stew comes out tasting of a particular afternoon in a particular kitchen that is no longer there.

choices.text: Eat the stew in silence

effects.log: You eat slowly. It is the best meal you have had in an age, and you did not want it to end.

choices.text: Share the stew with the cook-god

effects.log: The cook-god weeps over their bowl. It is a good thing you have done.

events.text: A lantern of a fallen god of travellers lights only for those who are lost. At the moment it is bright as noon. You had thought you knew where you were going.

choices.text: Follow the lantern a little way

effects.log: It leads you through three hedges and a very small door into a garden you have not seen. You rest there a while.

choices.text: Hang the lantern in your shrine porch

effects.log: It dims. It lights only for lost visitors. Many come, and some stay.

events.text: A jar of seeds from a fallen god of orchards sits in a vault, labelled in a clear hand: do not plant in anger. A warden says three gods have tried and got three very bitter pears. You are in an excellent mood.

choices.text: Plant one seed gently

effects.log: It grows into a pear tree in a week. The fruit is sweet and slightly smug.

choices.text: Plant it in a friend's garden as a gift

effects.log: The friend is moved. The pears are shared with the whole street.

events.text: A scroll from a fallen god's vault is blank, but when you breathe on it, words appear for a moment and fade. Three words, then six, then a line. It seems to be a love poem. It seems to be addressed to you.

choices.text: Read it fast

effects.log: You get half the poem before it fades. It is the second half. You must supply the first yourself.

choices.text: Breathe on it again, and slowly

effects.log: The words stay longer. By the end the poem is written, in your own hand, on a scroll that will never fade again.

events.text: A ring of grey iron lies on a table in a fallen god's vault. A note says that it holds a promise made by two gods who fell out. If one places it on a finger, one hears a little of the quarrel, and a little of the making-up.

choices.text: Put it on

effects.log: You hear a long argument about a boat, and then a laugh. The ring is warm. You take it off carefully.

choices.text: Leave it for the two to find

effects.log: It might help them, one day. Or it might not. You leave it be.

events.text: A kite hangs in the roof of a fallen god's vault: huge, patched, with a tail of a hundred ribbons. A note: for the day I get out. The string is long enough to reach the roof of the world.

choices.text: Take it out and fly it

effects.log: It rises, shy at first, then bold. For an hour you hold the string of a god's wish.

choices.text: Add a ribbon with your name

effects.log: The tail now has a hundred and one ribbons. The kite is pleased.

events.text: A map from a fallen god's vault shows only the realm's edge, with a small pencilled cross and a note: here. The cross is somewhere you pass on your way home most days.

choices.text: Dig under the cross

effects.log: You find a small tin box. In it is a pressed flower and a note: you took your time.

choices.text: Leave the cross unexplored

effects.log: Some places are best left a promise. You pass on, wondering.

events.text: A gong of green bronze hangs in a vault. A tag says it was struck once to announce a death, and has been silent since. It is slightly warm and trembles when anyone speaks of grief.

choices.text: Strike it softly for those unmourned

effects.log: The gong rings low and long. Somewhere, the unmourned feel it. A small lamp glows brighter in the vault.

choices.text: Place a hand on it and feel it hum

effects.log: It hums. You hum with it, and feel unaccountably better.

events.text: An hourglass in a vault of a fallen god of time is full of fine silver sand that does not move. When a visitor looks away, a single grain falls. It is keeping track of a very slow event.

choices.text: Stay and watch for an hour

effects.log: One grain falls while you blink. The vault chuckles. You have no idea what you missed.

choices.text: Turn the glass over

effects.log: The sand runs in a quiet river for a heartbeat. Then it stops, and the vault sighs, relieved to be moving, however briefly.

events.text: A comb of black horn in the vault of a god of the Sky is said to part the clouds of anyone who uses it. A cloud-keeper sells it for a modest tithe. The comb tugs a little: there is a tangle in the weather over your domain.

choices.text: Comb the clouds over your domain

effects.log: The sky unsnarls. A rainbow appears, rather self-satisfied.

choices.text: Pass the comb to a bald god

effects.log: They are touched, then amused. The cloud-keeper bursts out laughing.

events.text: You put on a plain brown coat and walk into your own domain by the road, with nothing to mark you. At the first inn, {npc} the innkeeper looks you over and says business is poor lately, and blames the god of the place. Nobody has seen the god in a year.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Your Own Domain

choices.text: Agree sympathetically and ask for details

effects.log: {npc} complains for an hour: the rain came late, the harvest was thin, the shrine bell cracked. It is a long list, and some of it is fair.

choices.text: Defend the god, mildly

effects.log: {npc} narrows {his} eyes. What would a stranger know? {He} serves you cold soup.

choices.text: Eat in silence and leave a good tip

effects.log: You eat and leave. The innkeeper pockets the coin, warming a little.

events.text: {npc} shows you the cracked shrine bell, hung from a post at the inn door. The hamlet used to ring it for rain. It has not rung true in a year. {He} says, if the god cared, the god would fix it.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Your Own Domain

choices.text: Offer to fix the bell

effects.log: You mend it by hand, with a smith's hammer and your own breath. When it rings true, the hamlet hears. {npc} stands with {his} mouth open.

choices.text: Ring the cracked bell and pray

effects.log: It clangs badly. A few hamlet folk come out of curiosity. You pray for them aloud, and the god, you hope, is listening.

events.text: The innkeeper warms by the end of the week and tells you the real grievance: a daughter who went to the high court and never wrote. {He} has been praying for a letter and getting only silence. {He} thinks the god does not hear small prayers.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Your Own Domain

choices.text: Say that you will find out

effects.log: You promise. {npc} snorts, but writes the daughter's name on a scrap of cloth and gives it to you.

choices.text: Tell {him} the god does hear

effects.log: {He} does not believe you. {He} also does not stop praying.

events.text: You go back to your shrine, find the daughter's name in a stack of unopened prayers, and answer it. A week later a letter arrives at the inn from the high court, with a pressed flower inside. {npc} reads it standing in the door, and then reads it again.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Your Own Domain

choices.text: Come back masked, to see the face

effects.log: You come back in the coat. {npc} is radiant, pours you the best tea, and tells you: the god finally heard.

choices.text: Leave it a miracle

effects.log: You stay away. The hamlet talks about the letter for years, and the shrine bell is rung true on the daughter's name-day.

events.text: You pray at the cracked bell until midnight. In the morning a few of the hamlet drift to the shrine, shy, and light a lamp. It is not a miracle. It is a start, and you see it from the road, in a brown coat, with a strange full heart.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Your Own Domain

choices.text: Keep the coat and visit each season

effects.log: You come back each season, unknown. The hamlet grows warmer, and the god, as far as they know, has been a long time reforming.

choices.text: Return openly and take up the work

effects.log: You come back in your own face. They are stunned, then wary, then glad.

events.text: You walk into the Storm Throne's hills in a plain coat, as a traveller. Nobody knows you. At a hill-farm a family feeds you without a question, and the youngest asks whether you have seen the Throne. Of course, you say. Is it big? Very, you say. The child nods, awed.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Another God's Domain

choices.text: Tell them honest stories of the Throne

effects.log: You tell them what you know. The family listens until the fire is embers. The child falls asleep on your knee.

choices.text: Ask what they ask of the Throne

effects.log: They answer shyly: rain in spring, the dog back, a daughter married well. Nothing grand.

choices.text: Thank them and go

effects.log: You walk on, warm. The child waves from the gate.

events.text: On the second night a storm breaks over the farm: a real one, a Throne-sent storm, heavy with hail. The family huddles. The father says the Throne is angry. You can see that it is not: the storm is a tantrum from a young storm-god, and it is about to flatten the barn.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Another God's Domain

choices.text: Calm the young storm-god from the doorway

ok.log: You call out in the old tongue. The storm sags, abashed, and withdraws. The barn is untouched.

fail.log: You shout and the storm only sulks. The barn loses its roof, but nobody is hurt.

choices.text: Hold up the barn roof yourself

effects.log: You brace the beams until the hail passes. Your hands bleed a little. The family never sees.

events.text: The family prays at dusk, to a Throne they have never seen, for the smallest things. You listen in the dark, a stranger by the fire, and for the first time you hear a prayer not as a claim on a god but as a gift from a friend.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Another God's Domain

choices.text: Add your own prayer to theirs, silently

effects.log: It rises with theirs. Somewhere in the rafters of the world, a Throne tilts an ear.

choices.text: Pray nothing, and just listen

effects.log: You listen. It is enough. You carry the sound away with you.

events.text: In the morning the family finds a small gift at their door: a bundle of dry kindling and a ribbon of lightning. They think it a gift of the Throne. The child, solemn, ties the ribbon to the gate, and says to nobody: thank you, big one.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Another God's Domain

choices.text: Smile from the road, and walk on

effects.log: You are a traveller still, with a coat and a secret and a full heart.

choices.text: Return to the Throne and tell the story

effects.log: The Throne listens, huge and still. Then: the child is to have a place in my feasts, whenever they come.

events.text: The barn loses its roof, but the farm survives. The family rebuilds, and you stay a week to help, still unknown. At the end the father shakes your hand and says: you were sent, I think. You say: no. All the same, comes the answer.
events.arc: A God Goes Masked: Another God's Domain

choices.text: Accept the handshake and the thanks

effects.log: It is a warm, calloused hand. You walk away feeling that you were paid in advance.

choices.text: Leave before sunrise, without goodbyes

effects.log: You go, light of foot. The farm will tell the tale in its own way.

events.text: Gods rarely walk the market towns in the human seasons, but you do, in a hat. At a stall of charms you meet {npc}, a seller of luck-knots, whose price is a story and a coin. {He} says business has never been better; people want something to tie to.

choices.text: Buy a luck-knot with a story

effects.log: You tell {him} a small, true story of a lost mule. {npc} grins and gives you a knot of red thread.

choices.text: Watch {him} work for an afternoon

effects.log: You watch {npc} sell to six customers. Each leaves feeling better than they came, which is a trick you did not expect.

choices.text: Browse and move on

effects.log: The stalls are bright with ribbons and bells. You eat a skewer and walk on.

events.text: The red knot warms in your pocket, and by dusk three small good things have happened: a coin in the road, an old friend's greeting, a sudden meal. {npc} says the knots have no power. {He} says the story is the power. You are not sure.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you to tie one

effects.log: {He} shows you the loop, the pull, the pause. Your first knot is lopsided, and it works.

choices.text: Tell {him} that you are a god

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard {he} has to sit down. Then {he} looks at you, and stops. {He} does not say anything for a while.

events.text: {npc} lets you try the sale. You stand at the stall and sell a knot to a worried mother by promising nothing, only listening. It works. The mother goes away lighter. You have a feeling that you have done your job as a god better in that minute than in a year.

choices.text: Keep working the stall for a week

effects.log: You sell forty knots and give away twenty. The customers like you. You like them.

choices.text: Hand the stall back with thanks

effects.log: {npc} nods approvingly. {He} says you have the knack.

events.text: {npc} keeps your lopsided knot in the stall window, with a card: made by a customer. It sells, in the end, for a high price. {He} sends you the coin with a note: the best stories are the ones that end in a knot.

choices.text: Spend the coin on lamps for the market shrine

effects.log: The market shrine glows. The sellers bring you pastries.

choices.text: Frame the note

effects.log: It hangs by your door. It has the dignity of an honest small thing.

events.text: {npc} is quiet for a while, and then {he} bows low and says: I have been selling luck-knots for forty years and I did not know I was selling them to a god. {He} gives you a knot for free. It is the most beautiful one you have ever seen.

choices.text: Accept it and say nothing more

effects.log: It sits on your wrist for the rest of your life, warm and small.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep selling, and promise to come back

effects.log: You come back every year for the festival. {npc} saves you the best stall.

events.text: A bell in a shrine of no particular fame has begun to ring a number, over and over: seventeen strokes, a pause, seventeen strokes. The shrine-keeper does not know who started it. The number is not a festival day or a prayer-hour. It is a mystery.

choices.text: Count with the bell for a night

effects.log: Seventeen strokes, again and again, until dawn. In the grey light you hear a faint eighteenth, from far away.

choices.text: Examine the bell

effects.log: The clapper is wound with a strip of cloth. Under it, scratched in the bronze, is a tally of marks: seventeen rows of seventeen.

choices.text: Ask the keeper to stop it

effects.log: The keeper tries. The bell rings on, by itself.

events.text: The eighteenth stroke comes from a second bell, in a second shrine, three valleys away. You walk there. It is ringing seventeen, too, in a different key. Between the two bells there is a line of faint light on the ground.

choices.text: Follow the line to the next bell

effects.log: It leads to a third, then a fourth. Seventeen bells, in seventeen shrines, all ringing seventeen. They form a ring on the map.

choices.text: Ask the nearest keeper who rang first

effects.log: The keeper says no one rang first. They simply began, together, on a certain morning.

events.text: The tally in the bronze is a calendar: seventeen years of seventeen days, each marked. The last row is nearly full. Whatever the bell is counting down to, it is soon.

choices.text: Count the days left

effects.log: There are eleven. You note them down. The date is not a feast or a death, but a dawn.

choices.text: Show the calendar to the Silent Hall

effects.log: The Hall is intrigued, and files it under the heading: pending.

events.text: Seventeen bells, in a ring round a quiet valley. At the centre of the ring, a hill. At the top of the hill, a cradle of stone, empty, with a blanket. The ringing is a call; the whole ring is a lullaby. It is waiting for a child.

choices.text: Wait at the hill until the day

effects.log: You wait. The eleven days pass. At dawn on the last, a mist rises, and something small and warm is in the cradle.

choices.text: Send word to the Green Assembly and the Hall

effects.log: Both send observers. The ring becomes a fixed point of interest, and your name is on the report.

events.text: The cradle holds a newborn god, no bigger than a loaf, with eyes the colour of the bell-bronze. The seventeen bells fall silent together. A lullaby, long rehearsed, has done its work: a new god is born into a world that rang for them.

choices.text: Carry the child down to the Assembly yourself

effects.log: They arrive wrapped in your coat. The Assembly names them with ceremony. You are asked to be the child's sponsor, and you accept.

choices.text: Stay on the hill and keep the child warm

effects.log: You sit by the cradle for three nights. The child sleeps. On the fourth, a pair of shrine-keepers arrive to take over.

events.text: The report becomes a legend: the Seventeen Bells, a miracle observed. The Hall and the Assembly argue for a decade over who should raise the child. In the end the child chooses, at age three, by walking into the lap of a shrine-keeper no one had heard of.

choices.text: Support the choice before the court

effects.log: You speak plainly. The court gives way. The shrine-keeper weeps, and the child laughs.

choices.text: Stay out of the quarrel

effects.log: The matter resolves itself, as most do.

events.text: A letter arrives at your shrine, addressed in a hand you do not know, to the god of this place. It is from {npc}, who writes from a sealed heaven and says the post is slow. {He} would like to know if the world is still there, and whether anyone remembers the old pantheon.

choices.text: Write back with the news

effects.log: You write three pages: the domains, the courts, a few gossips. You post it at the seal with a stamp of wax.

choices.text: Ask the wardens how a letter got out

effects.log: They are astonished. There is no post from the sealed heavens. The letter is genuine, and no one can say how.

choices.text: Keep the letter, unanswered, for now

effects.log: It sits on your shelf. It feels as if it is watching you.

events.text: A reply comes, in a week. {npc} is delighted, and shy. {He} writes of a garden in the sealed heaven, of a cat, of a long dull sleep. {He} asks, almost casually, if you would be so kind as to find out what happened to a god named Jiho.

choices.text: Search the court records for Jiho

effects.log: You find the name in an old register: Jiho, god of the evening star, who vanished the day the heavens were sealed. No cause is given.

choices.text: Say you will ask around, and mean it

effects.log: You ask in six shrines. Nobody has heard the name, but one old priest lowers their eyes.

events.text: The wardens are baffled, then frightened, then curious. They carry the letter into the archives and spend a week reading the paper. They find it is a type of paper not made since the pantheon fell. It is old, and it is fresh.

choices.text: Offer to write back on their behalf

effects.log: The wardens agree. You write a respectful letter and post it at the seal.

choices.text: Leave the matter to the wardens

effects.log: They hold a meeting. It goes on a long time.

events.text: The register, and the priest, between them tell the story: Jiho was the god of the evening star, and the pantheon sealed away as one. Jiho refused to go in. Jiho stayed outside, alone, and was forgotten. {npc} has been writing, you realise, to be told the friend lived.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth, gently

effects.log: You write: Jiho stayed out, and was forgotten, but not by me. I will keep the star.

choices.text: Soften it, and say Jiho is well

effects.log: You write that Jiho is well, in a far place. It is a kindness, and not entirely a lie, and it does not sit easily.

events.text: {npc} writes back, just once more: thank you for the truth. {He} says that the garden has been quiet since, but not sad. {He} asks that you light a lamp for the evening star every night, and promises to look for it from the other side.

choices.text: Light the lamp every night

effects.log: You do, for the rest of your life. On clear evenings a second light answers, faintly, from a seal in the distance.

choices.text: Light it on the first of each season

effects.log: It is what you can manage. The answering light comes four times a year.

events.text: {npc} thanks you for the kindness and does not write again for a year. When a letter comes, it is short: I know, it says. I have known for a long time. But thank you for the lie. It was a good one.

choices.text: Write back and apologise

effects.log: You apologise. The reply is one line: there is nothing to forgive.

choices.text: Keep the letter, and be humbler

effects.log: You keep it in your sleeve. It stings, and it is right.

events.text: Gods whisper in the courts that there are not twelve domains but thirteen, and that the thirteenth was cut out of the map by agreement. A pilgrim in a plain coat says as much to you at a roadside shrine, and then looks as if they regret it. They are not lying.
events.arc: The Rumour of the Thirteenth Domain

choices.text: Press them for the details

effects.log: They know little: a name, a direction, a feeling. The name is Mu. The direction is down.

choices.text: Reassure them and move on

effects.log: They are grateful. You keep the whisper in your pocket.

choices.text: Laugh it off

effects.log: The pilgrim blushes and changes the subject.

events.text: A folding map in the pilgrim's pack shows twelve domains in a ring and, at the centre, a dot labelled with a single stroke of ink. The stroke is a character no one has used in an age. It means, roughly: the one we did not name.
events.arc: The Rumour of the Thirteenth Domain

choices.text: Copy the map

effects.log: You trace it carefully. It will keep.

choices.text: Burn the map in a lamp

effects.log: You think better of passing it on. The pilgrim sighs, relieved.

events.text: Weeks later, you find the pilgrim dead on a hillside, peaceful and unmarked, with the pack beside them. In the pack, a note for you: please finish what I could not. The note is unsigned.
events.arc: The Rumour of the Thirteenth Domain

choices.text: Bury the pilgrim with ceremony

effects.log: You give the pilgrim a decent burial on the hill. The pack is yours.

choices.text: Leave the pack, and walk away

effects.log: It is not your quarrel. You feel the weight of that for a long while.

events.text: Beneath the Mountain domain, the map says, is an old stair. You find it behind a waterfall. It goes down for a long time. At the bottom, a door, with a lintel carved in a language that you can almost read. A single word, repeated: rest.
events.arc: The Rumour of the Thirteenth Domain

choices.text: Pick the lock of the door

ok.log: The lock turns. Beyond it, a warm, dim room with an empty throne and a window that looks out on nothing.

fail.log: The lock stings your fingers. You retreat, thinking.

choices.text: Knock, and wait

effects.log: You knock three times. After a long pause, a voice answers from within: come in, if you are the one.

events.text: The room is the thirteenth domain: the domain of Rest. It was cut away by the first gods, because the first gods could not bear to sleep. The throne is empty because Rest asked to be unseated. Rest says it is happy there, and lonely, and would like a visitor now and then.
events.arc: The Rumour of the Thirteenth Domain

choices.text: Promise to visit and keep the secret

effects.log: You promise. You do not know if you can keep it, but you will try.

choices.text: Tell Rest the courts would welcome it

effects.log: Rest thinks for a long time and says: not yet. You nod, and stay for tea.

events.text: The lock holds you off. You return to the surface and decide that some doors are meant to be stung at. Years later you hear of a god who found the room, and brought back only a sleeping-cat and a long, long rest. You smile.
events.arc: The Rumour of the Thirteenth Domain

choices.text: Wish the god well from afar

effects.log: You do. The cat, in a distant shrine, sneezes.

choices.text: Try the door again, some day

effects.log: Some day. Not today.

events.text: A masterless god gets no seat at the courts, and so you have learned to go masked. At a feast of the Will of Heaven you come in a plain coat as a servant's helper, carrying plates. Nobody looks at you. You hear everything.
events.arc: The Plain Coat at the Court Feast

choices.text: Listen for the court's plans

effects.log: You hear that the Will is quietly buying up the shrines of three small gods, and will not say why.

choices.text: Help a harried cook in the kitchen

effects.log: The cook is grateful, and gives you a secret pie. You eat it in the pantry, delighted.

choices.text: Carry plates, and do not interfere

effects.log: You carry plates all evening. Your arms ache and your mind is full.

events.text: The three small gods are being quietly absorbed, because they have offended no one but have no pantheon. They are, like you, masterless. You see one of them at the lower table, smiling, not knowing.
events.arc: The Plain Coat at the Court Feast

choices.text: Warn the small god in a note on a plate

effects.log: You slip a note under the dish. The god reads it, goes pale, and slips away.

choices.text: Say nothing, but follow the Will's agent

effects.log: You trail them through the halls and learn where the deeds are kept.

events.text: The cook is a small god of the third kitchen, a masterless one like you, and quietly furious at the court. The pie is a gift; the cook has a request. There is a ledger that must be read, and the cook cannot read it.
events.arc: The Plain Coat at the Court Feast

choices.text: Read the ledger for the cook

effects.log: It lists the shrines to be taken. The cook's own is on it.

choices.text: Decline, and keep the pie

effects.log: You eat the pie and leave the ledger. The cook sighs.

events.text: The three small gods band together in a back room of a tavern, with you, and make a plan: they will form their own small pantheon, with a name nobody can take away. You are asked to be the fourth. It is not a court, but it is a roof.
events.arc: The Plain Coat at the Court Feast

choices.text: Join the new pantheon

effects.log: The Small Hearth Assembly is born, in a back room, with a loaf of bread for a seal. You are a founding member.

choices.text: Help them without joining

effects.log: You are a friend of the Small Hearth, never a member. It suits you.

events.text: You learn where the deeds are kept, and in the night you copy the ones that matter. The small gods will keep their shrines, if the deeds can be read to the right court. The right court, as it turns out, is a very sleepy judge.
events.arc: The Plain Coat at the Court Feast

choices.text: Present the copies to the judge, in your plain coat

effects.log: The judge reads them with a sigh, then smiles. The shrines are saved, and the Will is rebuked in a footnote.

choices.text: Pass the copies to the small gods

effects.log: You hand over a packet and are gone before the thanks.

events.text: You walk part of a pilgrim's road in a plain coat. {npc}, a pilgrim of forty years, walks beside you. {He} is going to a shrine of a god who, {he} says, may or may not exist. {He} prays to them anyway. {He} has not asked for a thing in all those years.

choices.text: Walk with {him} the whole way

effects.log: The road is long and mostly flat. {npc} sings under {his} breath, an old walking song.

choices.text: Ask {him} why {he} walks

effects.log: {He} thinks. To keep the road, {he} says. Someone should.

choices.text: Part ways at the next crossroads

effects.log: You wave. {He} waves back, and keeps walking.

events.text: Halfway, a rain-storm drives you into a roadside barn. {npc} tells of the shrine ahead: a small stone, no priest, no doors. {He} says the god of the stone has never answered. {He} says it is not the point.

choices.text: Say that the god hears

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. I know, {he} says. That is why I keep walking.

choices.text: Ask how {he} bears the silence

effects.log: {He} smiles. Silence is a kind of listening, {he} says. You think about that for a week.

events.text: {npc} says the road itself is the shrine. The god, {he} says, is the road; the road does not answer, and yet leads somewhere. {He} says the road leads gently, if you let it.

choices.text: Accept the thought quietly

effects.log: You walk on in silence. The road leads on, and you let it.

choices.text: Argue the point cheerfully

effects.log: {He} argues back with relish. By the end, no one has won, and the road is shorter.

events.text: At the stone shrine, {npc} kneels, in the rain, and says a short prayer of thanks for another year of walking. You stand behind {him} in your plain coat. And you, the god of the place, are moved so deeply you cannot answer. You lay a hand on the stone. It is warm.

choices.text: Answer, finally, in the warmth of the stone

effects.log: {npc} feels it, a hand on the stone from the other side. {He} bows, and weeps, and is not surprised.

choices.text: Stay unknown, and let the stone be warm

effects.log: {npc} puts a hand on the warm stone and smiles. You walk back down the road together, unspoken.

events.text: The road ends at a plain stone, and {npc} sits down and eats a heel of bread and a pear. You share it. {He} says, with a mouthful, the road was good this year. That is all the shrine asks.

choices.text: Offer to build a roof for the stone

effects.log: {He} laughs. No, no. Leave it. A roof would be an answer. You nod.

choices.text: Eat the pear and be silent

effects.log: The pear is perfect. The silence is full.

events.text: Above the door of an ordinary shrine, in the stone, is a name that has been chiselled out. The gap is the exact width of a god's name. The shrine-keeper says it was done before their time, and is not to be discussed. Pilgrims touch the gap as they go in.
events.arc: The Missing Name on the Lintel

choices.text: Touch the gap yourself

effects.log: The stone is smooth and warm. You feel, faintly, a laugh.

choices.text: Ask the oldest pilgrim what they know

effects.log: The pilgrim says the god was loved, and then not talked about. That is all.

choices.text: Admire the carving around the gap

effects.log: The pattern of vines and wheat frames the gap perfectly. Someone loved this god.

events.text: Under a loose floor tile in the shrine you find a copper plate, scratched with the god's name in a small hurried hand. You read it. You say it aloud. The air in the shrine changes: warmer, as if someone had come in from the cold.
events.arc: The Missing Name on the Lintel

choices.text: Re-carve the name in the stone

effects.log: It takes three days. When it is done, pilgrims weep. The keeper, shaken, says: I always knew.

choices.text: Keep the copper plate and the name to yourself

effects.log: You hold it in your pocket. It warms. The shrine keeps its gap.

events.text: The pilgrim leads you to a house in the hills where an ancient weaver keeps a loom, who was the god's last priest. You are told how the god died: not a fall, not a war, but a disagreement with the high court, and a quiet request to be forgotten, so that the court could forget its shame.
events.arc: The Missing Name on the Lintel

choices.text: Promise to remember the god

effects.log: A nod, and a hand takes yours. It is dry and warm.

choices.text: Ask for the god's name

effects.log: It is whispered to you. It is a good name. You will not tell it, but you will not forget.

events.text: The name, once carved, draws the court's attention. A herald arrives with a rolled decree: the name was struck by order of a high court, and may not be restored. The keeper looks at you in terror. The herald looks at you in anger.
events.arc: The Missing Name on the Lintel

choices.text: Argue the order was long past its term

ok.log: You cite the lapse of the order, an old clause. The herald sputters, checks, and retreats.

fail.log: The herald produces a fresh seal. The name is struck again, by force, in front of the pilgrims.

choices.text: Back down and take the keeper away

effects.log: You leave the shrine. It will keep the gap. It will keep the memory.

events.text: The name stands, and the shrine, after an age, has its god. Pilgrims come from three domains. The keeper bows to you daily. And one night, in the hush of the shrine, the god, faintly, laughs: a warm sound, as of a meal shared. You are thanked.
events.arc: The Missing Name on the Lintel

choices.text: Sit in the shrine and listen to the laugh

effects.log: You sit till dawn. It is a laugh worth an age of waiting.

choices.text: Leave quietly, a guest who did a small thing

effects.log: You go with a full heart and no credit. The god, you suspect, knows.

events.text: The name is struck again, but the pilgrims have seen it and cannot unsee. They begin to scratch it into their doorposts and into the dust of the road. The court cannot strike a name from ten thousand doors. The god, in the end, is remembered.
events.arc: The Missing Name on the Lintel

choices.text: Add the name to a doorpost of your own

effects.log: You carve it small, at the foot of your door. It is a quiet act of defiance.

choices.text: Let the pilgrims do the work

effects.log: They do. By spring the name is on a thousand lintels.

events.text: The ferryman who crosses the river of your domain has not looked up from the oar in years. In a plain coat you pay the fare, and the ferryman says, without looking: the god of this river is a lazy one. You agree, to be polite.

choices.text: Ask what the god should do

effects.log: The answer: nothing, mostly. Just be seen once a year. A wave would do.

choices.text: Wave from the ferry, at the river

effects.log: You wave. The river sparkles. The ferryman looks up for the first time, frowns, and looks down again.

events.text: In a tavern of a far domain a minstrel is singing a song about you. It is a bad song, and the details are wrong, and the chorus is a pun. The crowd joins in on the chorus. You are in a plain coat, at the back, wearing a smile you cannot suppress.

choices.text: Join the chorus, loudly

effects.log: You are the loudest voice in the room. The minstrel gives you a nod, a free drink, and a new verse.

choices.text: Correct one detail to the minstrel afterwards

effects.log: The minstrel is amazed that anyone cares. The detail is fixed, and the pun stays.

events.text: A child at a roadside shrine is explaining to a clay figure of you why you are wrong about the weather. You stand behind in a plain coat. The child turns and, without surprise, asks you to agree.

choices.text: Agree with the child, solemnly

effects.log: The child nods and goes back to the figure. A good argument is a form of prayer.

choices.text: Disagree, politely

effects.log: A thirty-minute debate follows. The child wins. You are proud.

events.text: On a walk in a plain coat you find a small shrine of yours that nobody has told you about, in a corner of a field, tended by a single old person. They do not know who you are. They tell you the god of this shrine is very busy and very kind.

choices.text: Help them clear the weeds

effects.log: You weed the whole shrine. They give you bread and a nod. It is an honest afternoon.

choices.text: Leave a quiet blessing on the field

effects.log: The field yields double next season. The old one thanks the god, and you, a little.

events.text: At a harvest festival in another god's domain, the stranger in the plain coat is pulled into the dance. A partner spins you hard, laughing, and does not ask your name. It is the best dance you have had in years.

choices.text: Dance until the lamps burn low

effects.log: You dance until your feet ache. The hamlet sees you off with garlands.

choices.text: Slip away before the last dance

effects.log: You go, the music following you down the road.

events.text: On a bridge a beggar asks you for a coin. They look like every beggar in every story. You have no coin, being a god in a plain coat. You have a loaf of bread, and a bad feeling that this is a test.

choices.text: Share the bread and talk

effects.log: The beggar is only hungry. You eat together. It is no test at all, and that is the point.

choices.text: Give the bread and hurry on

effects.log: You walk on, a little ashamed of the haste.

events.text: In a roadside inn you overhear a heretic arguing that the gods are only very old people. The inn argues back. You, in a plain coat, find you agree with both sides.

choices.text: Say: perhaps both

effects.log: The inn goes quiet, then laughs. A truce over soup.

choices.text: Buy the heretic a drink and say nothing

effects.log: The heretic raises a glass. They are in better spirits afterwards.

events.text: You stop at a shrine to rest, and offer a prayer, and realise belatedly that you have prayed at the shrine of your rival. They have, in your absence, laid a flower on your own. You have not decided what to do with this knowledge.

choices.text: Leave a flower of your own, in kind

effects.log: Both shrines now have each other's flowers. Neither god will ever mention it.

choices.text: Say nothing and walk on

effects.log: You carry the knowledge lightly. It warms you, a little.

events.text: A farmer curses the god of the valley for the rain, loudly, with colour and detail. You, in your plain coat, nod along. The farmer sees you nodding, and curses you also, in the name of consistency.

choices.text: Take the curse with grace

effects.log: You bow. The farmer, appeased by your humility, invites you to supper.

choices.text: Offer to help bring in the hay

effects.log: You haul hay in the rain. The farmer revises the curse into a grudging thanks.

events.text: A pilgrim presses a small carved bird into your hand at a crossroads. It is for luck, they say; for the road. They are walking to a shrine of yours. They do not recognise you, and you are not sure you should tell them.

choices.text: Keep the bird, and say thank you

effects.log: It sits on your shelf for ages. It is a very poor carving. You love it.

choices.text: Tell them, softly, who you are

effects.log: They stare, then laugh, then cry, then ask if you would like to carry the bird the rest of the way.

events.text: Chalk marks have begun to appear on the doors of shrines across your domain: a small circle, a line, a dot. Shrine-keepers find them in the morning. The marks are tidy and friendly. No one knows who is making them.

choices.text: Sit up a night to watch

effects.log: You see a small figure in a patched coat, chalk in hand, going from door to door. They turn and wave, then vanish.

choices.text: Add a mark of your own

effects.log: The next morning, a chalk reply: a second dot. It is, you realise, a conversation.

events.text: A line of footprints crosses the dust of an empty temple floor: bare, small, running. They start at the centre of the room, from nowhere, and end at the altar. Nothing is on the altar. The dust is not disturbed around them.

choices.text: Put your foot in one print

effects.log: It fits, almost. A faint warmth runs up your leg, and the print fills in with dust.

choices.text: Sweep the floor and leave the altar bare

effects.log: Some mysteries are only mysteries because they are tidy. You respect this.

events.text: An unsigned psalm has appeared in the songbooks of your shrines, one verse at a time, over a year. It is addressed to a god nobody names, and it is beautiful. The shrine-keepers sing it, and none know who wrote it.

choices.text: Write the next verse yourself

effects.log: You write it in a hurry. The verse appears in the books a week later, slightly improved by the unknown poet.

choices.text: Wait to see the final verse

effects.log: It arrives on the first of spring. It is for you. It is signed, at last, with a single initial.

events.text: A bell is ringing at the bottom of a well in the middle of a hamlet. The hamlet folk have been lowering lanterns and hearing the bell ring under their lanterns. They ask you, the passing stranger, whether it is a bad omen.

choices.text: Lower a lantern yourself and listen

effects.log: The bell rings in a rhythm you almost know. It is a slow lullaby. You tell them it is a good omen.

choices.text: Ask the hamlet folk to leave it in peace

effects.log: They agree. The bell rings on. The well becomes a place of quiet pilgrimage.

events.text: Three gifts have been left on your shrine steps on three consecutive mornings: a pear, a pebble and a small bell. No one saw who left them. A fourth morning dawns, and the step is bare. You feel an obscure disappointment.

choices.text: Leave a gift of your own on the step

effects.log: The next morning it is gone. There is a note: thank you. It is in an unfamiliar hand.

choices.text: Keep the pear, the pebble and the bell on your shelf

effects.log: They sit together, an odd little family. You grow fond of them.

events.text: A door stands in the side of a hill in your domain. It has no handle and no lock. On a quiet morning you press a hand to it and hear, from inside, someone knocking back. A friendly knock, as to a neighbour.

choices.text: Knock again, in the same rhythm

effects.log: The knocking resumes, delighted. A conversation without words, lasting an hour.

choices.text: Sit by the door with a flask of tea

effects.log: You sit. After a time a second flask is set down on the other side. You can hear it clink.

events.text: A lighthouse on the Sea domain's coast burns, every night, with a light no one has lit. The keeper's cottage is empty and tidy. A cup is on the table, still warm. A ship-captain asks you, trembling, to tell them it is a god.

choices.text: Tell the captain it is a kindness

effects.log: The captain exhales, grateful. The lighthouse brightens, as if overhearing.

choices.text: Wait for the keeper in the cottage

effects.log: You wait till dawn. A cat comes in, sits on the cup's saucer, and looks pleased. It was the cat.

events.text: A cat sits on a sealed heaven's wall at dusk and sings the wall a lullaby, flat and heartfelt. The wardens say it has done this every night since before the war. The wall, they add, has never once woken.

choices.text: Sing a verse along with the cat

effects.log: The cat shifts to make room. The wall hums, content.

choices.text: Leave a saucer of cream

effects.log: The cat accepts it as a due.

events.text: A blue lamp hangs over a sealed gate and has burned for ages on one drop of oil. The wardens refill it with a thimble each year and swear the level never changes. Today, curious, you look into the lamp.

choices.text: Look closely

effects.log: The oil is a thin mirror, and in it a small hand lifts, waves, and withdraws.

choices.text: Add a thimble of your own oil

effects.log: The flame leaps, gold, and settles blue again.

events.text: Children of a nearby hamlet have drawn on the wall of a sealed heaven in coloured chalk: suns, boats, a lot of dogs. The wardens let them. The next morning a few new drawings have appeared, from the inside, and they are rather good.

choices.text: Add a boat of your own

effects.log: Overnight the boat sails out of your chalk and onto the next stone, with a small flag.

choices.text: Leave the drawings to the wall

effects.log: Wall and children are better at this than you. You nod.

events.text: A warden has set up a table at a sealed heaven and is selling tickets to look at the wall. The prices are written in chalk: one for adults, one for children, one for gods who ought to know better. You are, apparently, the third.

choices.text: Pay the ticket, with good grace

effects.log: The warden gives you a handful of sweets. The wall, you swear, looks smug.

choices.text: Argue it down by half

effects.log: Argument is the warden's only joy. You both come away satisfied.

events.text: A fisher of the Sea domain cuts open a fish and finds in it a brass key stamped with the seal of a sealed heaven. They bring it to you, shaking, because it is not the sort of thing one keeps.

choices.text: Take the key and promise to return it

effects.log: You carry it to the wardens. They look at it for a long time and tell you to keep it.

choices.text: Tell the fisher to throw it back

effects.log: The fisher does. The fish swims off, shrugging its fins.

events.text: A ring of white mushrooms has sprung up in the ash of a burned shrine, perfectly round. Small animals avoid it. A lantern-moth hovers over the ring, undecided whether to land.

choices.text: Step into the ring and sit

effects.log: The ground is warm. For an hour you feel the shrine as it was, full of voices.

choices.text: Leave the ring and the moth in peace

effects.log: The moth lands, finally. A good sign.

events.text: Someone has left a pot of tea and a single cup in the ash of a burned shrine. The tea is hot, and the cup has been used. A sign propped against the pot reads, in a neat hand: for whoever.

choices.text: Drink the tea

effects.log: It is jasmine, and a little too strong. It warms you to the toes.

choices.text: Pour a cup for the ash

effects.log: The ash drinks it. A quiet breath goes by, thankful.

events.text: A scarecrow stands in the field behind a burned shrine, dressed in the shrine's old vestments. Crows treat it with unusual respect. When you pass, the scarecrow tips its hat. You are almost certain it was the wind.

choices.text: Tip your hat back

effects.log: The scarecrow seems pleased. The crows croak politely.

choices.text: Straighten its vestments

effects.log: You mend a button. A feather falls from the sky and lands in your hand.

events.text: A stair of a burned shrine leads up to a doorway and a drop. Whatever the upper floor was, it is gone. A bird has built a nest on the top step and is not eager to share.

choices.text: Climb carefully and look out

effects.log: From the doorway the valley is gold in the dusk. You see further than you have in years.

choices.text: Leave the nest undisturbed

effects.log: The bird chirps a grudging thanks.

events.text: In the cellar of a burned shrine, a chest of sandalwood has survived. Inside lie small bundles of cloth, each tied with a ribbon, each marked with the name of a child. The shrine, you see, was also a nursery.

choices.text: Seek out one of the children, now grown

effects.log: You find a baker in a coastal town. They take the bundle with trembling hands: a first blanket, never given.

choices.text: Rebury the chest, and leave a lamp

effects.log: The lamp burns for a year. The chest, and the children, are remembered.

events.text: A glass globe on a shelf in a fallen god's vault holds a tiny snowy hamlet. When shaken, the snow falls, and for a breath you hear bells. A tag says: do not wake the hamlet. The hamlet is, in fact, awake, and waving.

choices.text: Wave back

effects.log: The tiny figures cheer. Snow swirls up in a spiral of joy.

choices.text: Set the globe down gently

effects.log: The hamlet settles. It will try again another year.

events.text: An apprentice of a fallen god of locks sits in the vault, still practising on the same lock after three thousand years. It has not occurred to them that the master is gone. They look up, hopeful, to ask if you are the inspector.

choices.text: Say yes, and pass them

effects.log: You inspect the lock with great gravity. It is perfect. The apprentice weeps with relief.

choices.text: Tell them gently about the master

effects.log: They sit down heavily. After a time they ask for a cup of tea and a place to start again.

events.text: In the vault of a god of small insects, a ledger is kept in the wings of a thousand butterflies. They flutter in formation to spell a line of text. Today the line reads: welcome, visitor; we have been practising.

choices.text: Applaud the butterflies

effects.log: They scatter in joy and reform into a bow.

choices.text: Ask for tomorrow's line

effects.log: They spell: more tea. You supply it.

events.text: A cold forge stands in a fallen smith-god's vault, anvil gleaming. Hung on its wall are tongs, hammer and a leather apron in your size. A note on the apron says: when you are ready. The note is blank on the back.

choices.text: Put on the apron and strike once

effects.log: The anvil rings, a clear, patient note that carries through the vault. Something old and metal nods.

choices.text: Hang the apron back on its nail

effects.log: It will wait. Forges are patient.

events.text: A cup in a fallen god's vault holds a measure of moonlight, poured long ago. It has not spilled or dimmed. A card says the god drank a cup each night to remember the sea. The cup is half full.

choices.text: Drink a sip

effects.log: It tastes of cool salt and distance. You see the sea, as a pilgrim might, from far away.

choices.text: Top up the cup from tonight's moon

effects.log: The cup brightens. A small, restful light fills the vault.

events.text: The loom-room keeps a garden of knotted threads, each growing from a clay pot, each a life that tied itself in a knot and could not undo it. A gardener god waters them gently and asks you to help unpick one.

choices.text: Unpick a small knot

effects.log: It takes patience and a pin. The thread, freed, rises like a vine and blooms.

choices.text: Water the pots and listen

effects.log: The threads hum thank-yous as you pass.

events.text: The Weaver's tea-hour in the loom-room is a quiet affair of cups and spools. A junior weaver spills their tea across a skein and a stranger's luck turns over: a coin falls from a pocket far away, and a child finds it.

choices.text: Help mop up

effects.log: You mop the skein with a cloth. The luck settles, mostly the same.

choices.text: Tell the junior it is a fine accident

effects.log: They look at you in gratitude. The child, far away, buys a kite.

events.text: A stair of silver coral runs down a drop-off on the sea-floor, each step a different pitch when trodden. A school of angel-fish plays tunes on it, tiny and exact. They invite you to join the next piece.

choices.text: Step on a low note

effects.log: You make a deep tone. The fish incorporate it into the tune, solemn as a choir.

choices.text: Listen from the rail

effects.log: The tune is simple, sweet, and ends mid-phrase in the manner of a good joke.

events.text: Hermit crabs of the Sea domain hold a court in a great conch, with robes of weed and a judge in a barnacle wig. A dispute is raised: who owns the shell on the beach. They invite you to settle it, on grounds of impartiality.

choices.text: Rule that the shell belongs to whoever lives in it

effects.log: The court nods. The conch rings. The crab in question grins.

choices.text: Rule that it is a shared shell

effects.log: The court is aghast, then delighted. Three crabs move in together.

events.text: A ghost ship drifts through the Sea domain at dusk, lanterns lit, with a crew of tide-spirits at the oars. They are late for a harbour that has not existed for a thousand years. They ask the way.

choices.text: Point them to the nearest port

effects.log: They bow, row on, and vanish into the evening. You hope they find the right quay.

choices.text: Tell them gently the harbour is gone

effects.log: They are quiet for a moment, then row in a slow circle and fade, one by one, at peace.

events.text: An old net-mender sits on a rock at the sea-floor shore, mending nets for fishers who no longer exist. The nets are exquisite. They offer you one, free, and ask only that you hang it somewhere it will be used.

choices.text: Hang it in a coastal shrine

effects.log: Fishers use it, and wonder at the weave. The mender, far below, smiles.

choices.text: Sit and learn the knots

effects.log: You learn three. They hold forever.

events.text: A clock of shells and sea-glass on the sea-floor tells the tide to two decimal places and is never correct. A tide-priest says the clock is not meant to be right, only to be consulted, and that the sea likes to be asked.

choices.text: Consult the clock

effects.log: It gives a precise, wrong answer. The tide arrives at exactly the opposite time, and everyone is pleased.

choices.text: Adjust a gear with your thumb

effects.log: The clock stops, indignant, and then starts again.

events.text: In Mongsa's paths a house stands in tall silver grass, door ajar. Inside are four chairs and a long table set for tea. A note: we are at the other end of the path; start without us. The tea is hot.

choices.text: Drink the tea and wait

effects.log: No one comes. The tea is perfect. You drink the second cup for them.

choices.text: Walk on to the other end

effects.log: You find a lake and four friendly ghosts of cats. They greet you as an old friend.

events.text: In a dream-path a stand of umbrellas, each a different colour, waits at a bus stop of silver light. A sign says: take one; it will rain, but only where you stand. The umbrellas rustle, eager.

choices.text: Take the yellow one

effects.log: It rains on you, gently, for the rest of the dream. You feel wonderfully protected.

choices.text: Leave them for someone sadder

effects.log: You step back. A sad-looking dream-figure takes the grey one and walks into the rain, smiling.

events.text: In a dream you meet a voice without a speaker. It asks you to say its name. You do not know it. It tries a few: Tuesday, Salt, Marigold. None are right. It is very polite about it.

choices.text: Offer a name of your own for it

effects.log: You name it Echo, which it likes, because it is almost correct and not at all.

choices.text: Sit with the voice until dawn

effects.log: It tells you the names of forgotten things. You wake with a few of them.

events.text: Mongsa's sleeping attendants keep a row of candles, each marking a sleeper in the waking world. One candle is nearly out. The attendant asks if you would be so kind as to carry a message to the sleeper, who is very old.

choices.text: Carry the message

effects.log: It is a single sentence: you may go when you are ready. You deliver it. The candle flares and settles, peaceful.

choices.text: Relight the candle with a spill of your own

effects.log: The sleeper gets another year. You are told, politely, not to make a habit of it.

events.text: The dream-path has a stream that flows with paper boats, each carrying a small wish. They float past in the thousands. A dream-attendant fishes them out with a net and reads them to the sleeping. Tonight they ask you to read.

choices.text: Read the wishes aloud

effects.log: They are small, human, funny and sad. You read until the stream clears.

choices.text: Fold a boat of your own

effects.log: You set a wish afloat. It does not come back, which is the way of wishes.

events.text: A fine green dust lies over a stretch of primal ground, so old it has become soft. Where you step, a shoot springs up and then stands there, awkward, like a guest who has arrived too early.

choices.text: Tend the shoots

effects.log: You water them with a cupped hand. They grow slowly, into a tiny, bright wood.

choices.text: Walk on without treading on them

effects.log: It takes some skill. At the end the dust has forgotten you.

events.text: A skin drum of enormous size stands on a plain in the primal places, beaten only by the wind. The sound arrives in slow pulses: one, two, a pause, one. The wind, you realise, is in no hurry.

choices.text: Add a beat of your own by hand

effects.log: The wind, surprised, goes quiet. Then answers, a half-beat behind, like a child imitating.

choices.text: Lie down and listen

effects.log: The drum is as deep as the earth. You sleep, and wake without a worry.

events.text: A river of the primal places runs backwards uphill over smooth stones carved with a single mark each. Gods take a stone to remember a day. A stone is warm in your palm, and you do not know what it will remember.

choices.text: Keep the stone

effects.log: Years later, you understand what it remembered: this day, exactly as it was.

choices.text: Return it to the river

effects.log: The river carries it home, humming. Nothing is lost.

events.text: A tree in the primal places grows horns instead of branches, and on each horn hangs a leaf with a note of a song. When the wind blows, the tree plays a canon of unimaginable age. A crane is listening with its head on one side.

choices.text: Listen beside the crane

effects.log: You stand shoulder to shoulder. At the end the crane bows to you, and you to it.

choices.text: Write down the song

effects.log: You jot a few bars. They look nothing like the tune, but you carry them gladly.

events.text: In the dim of a primal cavern hangs a nest of enormous silk, and a warm breath comes from it. Something large and slow turns over in its sleep. A pile of moon-lit eggs lies at the bottom. The mother is away.

choices.text: Back out quietly

effects.log: You leave without a sound. The nest sighs, unalarmed.

choices.text: Leave a gift of honey by the entrance

effects.log: In the morning it is gone. A single scale of silver is left in its place.

events.text: A hunting party of the Green Assembly wears stag-masks to confuse the quarry, and the quarry, a stag, has worn a hunter-mask to confuse them. They meet in a clearing and stare. All sit down and share a flask.

choices.text: Join the picnic

effects.log: Nobody hunts anything that afternoon. The best hunt in years.

choices.text: Take the stag's mask as a trophy

effects.log: The stag looks wounded. You give it back with a bow.

events.text: A heron stands in the shallows of your domain with the patience of a god, and a fisher-god stands beside it with the patience of a heron. Both have been there since dawn. Neither has caught a thing.

choices.text: Stand with them for an hour

effects.log: You catch nothing, either. It is the most restful hour of your year.

choices.text: Toss a pebble to startle the fish

effects.log: The fish leap into the heron's beak and the fisher-god's basket both. They glare at you, then laugh.

events.text: A nest of thunder-sparrows has been built on a lightning-rod of the Storm Throne, and the Throne will not remove it. Each time the sparrows chirp a tiny bolt jumps from beak to beak. The Throne says, rumbling, that the nest brings luck.

choices.text: Bring the sparrows seed

effects.log: They eat from your hand, crackling. Your hair stands up for a day.

choices.text: Leave them to the Throne

effects.log: The Throne approves with a low rumble.

events.text: The Wild Lord's autumn feast is held with a roast boar that was never hunted but volunteered. The boar is in good spirits and sits at the high table in a paper crown, telling stories. It will be roast tomorrow, it says, cheerfully.

choices.text: Toast the boar's courage

effects.log: The boar bows. The hall roars. It is a strange, warm, ridiculous feast.

choices.text: Ask the boar if it is quite sure

effects.log: It is sure. It has had an excellent life, and is ready, and there are plums for stuffing.

events.text: A fire-hawk of the Will of Heaven is learning to hunt. It dives at a field-mouse and sets the field alight, and flaps in dismay. A sky-warden hands you a bucket and asks if you would mind.

choices.text: Put out the fire

effects.log: You do. The hawk looks mortified. You pat its head, and it sparks.

choices.text: Comfort the hawk first

effects.log: You calm it. The fire burns itself out in a quiet circle, harming nothing.

events.text: You answer a notice on a shrine door: apprentice wanted, no experience. In a plain coat you spend a week sweeping, trimming wicks and ringing the dawn bell. The old keeper says you will do. They do not recognise you.

choices.text: Keep working for a month

effects.log: You learn a hundred small things about being a shrine. You emerge humbler and better at your job.

choices.text: Reveal yourself at the end of the week

effects.log: The keeper looks at you for a long while. Then: you still missed a spot. A friendship begins.

events.text: In a plain coat you help a child look for a lost dog across three hamlets and a marsh. You find it, finally, asleep in the sun on the doorstep of your own shrine. The child thanks you gravely and carries it home.

choices.text: Walk them home

effects.log: The walk is long, and the child tells you everything. You are a trusted adult for an evening.

choices.text: Wave from the shrine step

effects.log: The child waves back, dog in arms. A quiet, enormous contentment.

events.text: A wedding in another god's domain is short of a witness at the last moment. They grab you from the road in your plain coat and sit you in the front row. You sign the book in a false name. You cry, quietly, throughout.

choices.text: Sign with your true name, in a hidden corner

effects.log: It is a small act of faith. The couple will be lucky for fifty years.

choices.text: Dance at the reception

effects.log: You dance with the bride's grandmother. The grandmother says you step on feet. This is true.

events.text: Staying at an inn in another pantheon's domain, you discover that your rival is at the next table, in a plain coat of their own. Each of you pretends not to notice. The soup arrives. The silence is excellent.

choices.text: Send over a pot of good tea with no note

effects.log: A pot of tea returns, no note. You drink it. It is rather good.

choices.text: Leave before dessert

effects.log: You leave a coin on the table. They watch you go, politely blind.

events.text: At a lantern festival you light a lantern in a plain coat and set it on a river, with a wish you do not say aloud. A little girl beside you sets a lantern down with great ceremony, and says it is for the god of this place. Yours drifts beside it.

choices.text: Follow the two lanterns downstream

effects.log: They drift together under a bridge, and out into the open water, where a whole sky of lanterns glides.

choices.text: Kneel and pray beside the girl

effects.log: You pray together. It is a prayer to you, from you, in the voice of someone listening for the first time.

events.text: A whistling begins at dusk across your domain, a tune of seven notes, repeated. Everyone can hear it; no one can find its source. Dogs perk their ears. Herons answer it. It does not seem menacing, only lonely.

choices.text: Whistle the eighth note

effects.log: The tune pauses. Then it plays your note back, the first time it has ever been answered.

choices.text: Follow the sound to the cliffs

effects.log: It is a reed in a crack of rock, played by wind. Still, it sounds like someone calling you by name.

events.text: A trail of salt crosses a wheat field in your domain, a thin white line from nowhere to nowhere. Beside it every stalk of wheat has bowed. The farmer says it happened in a single night, and asks if it is a blessing or a blight.

choices.text: Taste the salt

effects.log: It is just salt, sea-salt, and a little sweet. The wheat grows better there for a decade.

choices.text: Follow the trail to its end

effects.log: It ends at a shrine of the Sea domain, three days inland. A tide-priest says: oh, that was us. We were saying hello.

events.text: The signpost at a crossroads has been turned overnight to point in the wrong directions. A traveller took the left road and arrived at a spring. A second took the right and found a lost brother. The post seems to know best.

choices.text: Leave the post as it is

effects.log: More travellers find what they need. The post, you suspect, enjoys it.

choices.text: Set it straight and watch

effects.log: It turns itself back by evening, sulking. The travellers grumble. You turn it once more, and it stays.

events.text: The terrace-keepers report a boar as grey as a salt-lick. Every new moon it comes down and licks the offering stones white, and where it licks, nothing grows for a season. It eats no grain. It has done this for nine moons, and the keepers are tired of being brave about it.

choices.text: Watch it from the terrace wall

effects.log: You lie along the wall with a blanket and a flask of tea and watch the dark slope.

choices.text: Leave a heap of fine grain on the stones

effects.log: You heap the best grain on the highest stone and step back into the shadow.

choices.text: Ask the keepers what they have noticed

effects.log: The keepers talk for an hour. Nobody has noticed anything useful, but they feel better for being asked.

events.text: You learn its habits. It arrives when the bell-flowers close, walks a round of seven stones, and always stops at the sixth to scratch its brow on the corner. It never touches the seventh. It leaves by the dry stream, and it stops once, halfway, to look back at the terraces.

choices.text: Dig beneath the sixth stone while it is away

effects.log: You wait for the next dawn and put a spade under the corner it scratches.

choices.text: Set a snare of warded rope at the seventh stone

effects.log: Whatever it avoids, you reason, it fears. You lay the rope in a loose ring.

events.text: The boar ignores the grain. It licks its seven stones, sits down in the dust and looks straight at you with an eye like a tired lamp. It is not hiding. It has known you were there since sunset.

choices.text: Speak to it, gently, as to a guest

effects.log: You tell it your name and your domain. It listens with one ear, then turns its flank toward the dry stream and waits.

choices.text: Throw a loop of braided straw over its neck

effects.log: The loop settles. The boar sighs, as at a rude but expected joke, and does not move.

events.text: Under the sixth stone lies a clay jar, cracked, packed with sea salt and sealed with the mark of a shrine no one remembers. The salt has been leaking into the terraces for a century. The boar has been licking the stones to keep it from spreading, and it was never eating anything.

choices.text: Carry the jar down to the Sea domain

effects.log: You wrap the jar in your coat and walk it to the tide-line with the boar trotting behind, like a clerk behind a ledger.

choices.text: Reseal the jar and set it deeper

effects.log: You mend the cracks with wax and clay and bury it deeper. The boar watches until the last handful goes in.

events.text: The ring of rope holds. The boar comes into it at the next new moon, as if keeping an appointment, and stands quietly in the loop. Torches gather on the wall. The keepers want an end to nine months of white stones, and they want it by morning.
