choices.text: Lead it to the byre and bind it with warding thread

effects.log: The thread glows faintly. The boar lies down in clean straw and the keepers go home, relieved and a little ashamed.

choices.text: End it with the arrow of dawn, cleanly

effects.log: The boar lies down on the slope as a hill settles. The terraces cheer, then fall quiet at what they have done.

choices.text: Slip the rope and let it walk

effects.log: You loosen the ring. The boar looks at you once and goes by the dry stream, and the keepers mutter all night.

events.text: The Sea domain accepts the jar. A tide-priest tips the salt out in one grey spill and the water takes it. The boar wades in to its knees, drinks, and for the first time looks young. The terraces green again that spring, and the keepers name a stone for you.

choices.text: Let the boar choose where to live

effects.log: It chooses the seventh stone, the one it never touched. By autumn it is the keeper of the terraces, and a small fat one.

choices.text: Return to your own shrine with the keepers thanks

effects.log: You leave the boar in peace and the terraces in bloom.

events.text: The sealed jar holds for a long time, and the boar goes on licking the stones of the seven, but now only twice a year, like an old man tending a grave. The keepers leave it a bowl of grain. It never touches the grain, but it never stops coming.

choices.text: Tell the keepers it is a guard, not a pest

effects.log: The keepers put up a sign at the terrace gate. It takes years for the children to stop being afraid of it.

choices.text: Leave a note of thanks at the sixth stone

effects.log: You scratch two words into the lintel. The boar scratches its brow against them the next new moon.

events.text: The boar sleeps in the byre and wakes each new moon to find the door barred. It stops eating. The keepers bring it grain, then salt, then flowers. A young keeper opens the door at last on a night with no moon, and the boar walks out and does not come back.

choices.text: Do not pursue it

effects.log: Some bindings are meant to fail. You let the matter close, and the white stones return in winter, like a quiet reproach.

choices.text: Ask the young keeper to learn the boar habits

effects.log: The young keeper keeps a notebook for forty years. It becomes the best account of the terraces ever written.

events.text: The slain boar is buried under the seventh stone with a handful of salt. The terraces do not green. The keepers say the soil is waiting for something, and they do not look at you when they say it, and no new boar comes.

choices.text: Plant a seed of kindness over the grave

effects.log: A pale shoot comes up, small, in the second spring. It is not much, but it is something.

choices.text: Accept the weight of it, and move on

effects.log: You carry it forward. A god who never regrets is a god who never learned.

events.text: Once in a century the Will of Heaven holds the Quarry Night: a god takes the shape of a white hind and runs from dusk to dawn, and the whole court hunts them. Nobody takes the part twice. This year the lot has passed from hand to hand, and it has reached yours. Refusing costs nothing but face.

choices.text: Take the lot, and become the hind

effects.log: The cord of the lot burns your palm. You wake on four legs in a clean meadow, small, quick and strangely happy.

choices.text: Hand it back with thanks

effects.log: You return the lot with a short bow. The court murmurs, and the lot is passed on.

events.text: The horns begin at the edge of the valley. As a hind you can hear every hoof in the court: Mujin on the grey horse, the young gods on their ponies, the heralds on foot. They do not sound cruel. They sound delighted. You have never in your life been this alive.

choices.text: Run for the river, to break the scent

effects.log: The cold water takes your scent and your breath together. The horns circle, lost, and the night opens like a hand.

choices.text: Run for the old cedars and hide among their roots

effects.log: You fold yourself into the dark between two roots and hold still, breathing through your whole body.

choices.text: Turn and face the first rider, head high

effects.log: The first rider reins in, startled, and then bows from the saddle. The hunt remembers that the hind is a god too.

events.text: The river runs black and singing. Halfway across you find a bank of stars caught in the reeds, and you stand in the water among them, listening to the hunt pass overhead like thunder far away. A fish touches your leg, curious, and goes on.

choices.text: Rest in the reeds until dawn

effects.log: You rest. When the horns stop you come out wet and shining and the court applauds your cleverness.

choices.text: Cross, and run the far hills

effects.log: The far hills are hard and bright with frost. You run until the moon sets, and no one catches you.

events.text: Under the cedars you meet another quarry: a wild stag who has been hunted all its life, and has no lot to hand back. It watches you with a flat dark eye. It does not ask you to stay. It only asks, without words, whether you understood any of it.

choices.text: Sit with the stag till the horns pass

effects.log: You lie side by side in the leaf-mould. At dawn you rise first and walk out where the court can see you, a hind with a stag at its shoulder.

choices.text: Run on alone, ashamed to be only a guest

effects.log: You run on until the dawn. The shame is real. It is also useful.

events.text: The first rider is young Seonhui of the Banners, who lowers the spear point, dismounts, and kneels in the grass. The rest of the hunt breaks and closes round in a respectful ring. Nobody has ever done what you did, and the court does not know whether to cheer or write a rule.

choices.text: Bow your head and let them end the hunt

effects.log: The horns sound the long note. The court takes your courage as the point of the whole rite, and the rule is written afterward.

choices.text: Slip through the ring and vanish into the dark

effects.log: The ring is open on one side, and you take it. The court laughs and cheers, and the long chase begins again.

events.text: At dawn you wake in your own shape on your own cloak, with a stag-hair tangled in your sleeve. A letter from the Will of Heaven names you Quarry of the Age. The court will keep a cup in your name. And the stag, you find, has left a gift on your shrine steps: a single antler, shed whole.

choices.text: Hang the antler over your shrine door

effects.log: Visitors ask what it is. You tell them, and the telling is a prayer of its own.

choices.text: Return the antler to the wood where you met

effects.log: You walk it back to the cedars, and leave it at the root where you hid.

events.text: Every dawn on your shrine step there is a pile of offerings: a fish, three pinecones, a stone worn smooth, and once a whole honeycomb. The keeper swears no one leaves them. Then you see the giver: an enormous bear, green with moss along its back, kneeling in the rain with its forehead on the stone.

choices.text: Sit on the step and let it finish

effects.log: It finishes slowly, without hurry. When it rises it bows twice more and shambles off, deeply satisfied.

choices.text: Speak to it

effects.log: The bear freezes, and then bows so low its nose touches the floor.

choices.text: Watch from the window for a month

effects.log: You learn that it comes in every weather, and never on the day of the new moon.

events.text: The bear brings a new gift each dawn, and the gifts grow stranger: a hawk feather, a child toy, a broken bell. The keeper whispers that these are lost things, collected from the whole mountain. The bear is trying to restore what it believes the god has lost.

choices.text: Accept the broken bell with ceremony

effects.log: You hang it by the door. The bear weeps, moss and all, and you find out that bears can weep very quietly.

choices.text: Ask it to bring no more lost things

effects.log: The bear listens with both ears. The next dawn the step is bare, and that is worse.

events.text: The bear understands your words but not your meaning. It brings you a mate: a smaller, shy bear who immediately hides behind the first and peers round it. Together they kneel at your step, and the keeper remembers that you were warned about shrines that grow.

choices.text: Bless the pair with a long season

effects.log: The two bears spend that winter in a den under your wall. By spring there are cubs.

choices.text: Thank them, and send them back to the forest

effects.log: They go slowly, looking back at every bend.

events.text: A hunting party of gods arrives in the valley, looking for the great mossy bear whose pelt would hang beautifully in a hall. They find your shrine, and the bear kneeling on its step. The party leader laughs and levels a bow. The bear does not turn its head. It has not noticed. It is praying.

choices.text: Stand between the bow and the bear

effects.log: You stand in the rain with your plain coat showing. The party leader lowers the bow, red-faced, and goes away muttering.

choices.text: Make the bow-string snap with a hard word

ok.log: The string snaps with a crack like a branch. The party takes the hint, and the valley is quiet again.

fail.log: The string holds, and the bow is raised again. The bear finally looks up, and the party, startled, goes.

events.text: The bear is old now, and slow. One dawn there is no gift, and no bear. You find it in the lee of your wall, lying on its side, breathing slowly. It looks up at you. It has brought you its last gift, a smooth white stone, and it presses it into your palm.

choices.text: Stay with it until the end

effects.log: You sit on the wet moss with the great head across your knees. It does not last long. It dies at peace, hearing a god say its name.

choices.text: Set it a shrine under the wall, and call it by name

effects.log: The new shrine is small, and the bear-god within it is very sleepy and very kind.

events.text: The cubs grow up and take over their parent duty. Every dawn there are two bears on the step now, one tall, one small, and a heap of gifts that has to be sorted by a committee. The keeper writes a rule: no more than one honeycomb a week.

choices.text: Adopt the family as the shrine guardians

effects.log: They guard the gate for forty years. Pilgrims call the shrine Bear Gate, and the rest is history.

choices.text: Let the bears set their own rules

effects.log: They invent a rota. It lasts seventy years and is the fairest in the valley.

events.text: Behind the seal marked with a candle-flame lies a small heaven, walled off by gods who forgot why. A door opens on a pale-yellow city of wick-folk: tall, slender people with flames for hair, who wear shades of tallow and speak in whispers so as not to blow each other out. {npc} meets you at the gate with a shaded hand.

choices.text: Ask to be taken before their council

effects.log: {npc} bows to you and bows again, a little stiff. {He} says the council is not sitting. It is, in fact, about to fall.

choices.text: Ask {him} to show you the city

effects.log: {npc} walks you through streets of amber glass. {He} points out every house and names every family, and sighs at each.

choices.text: Bow and withdraw, unsure you are welcome

effects.log: You leave the seal ajar. For a century afterward the candle on the seal burns a little brighter.

events.text: The wick-folk are split in two. The Tallow faction wants the heaven kept sealed forever, for safety. The Beeswax faction wants the door open and a trade with the gods. Both sides are very polite and have not spoken in thirty years. {npc} belongs to neither and is tired of both.

choices.text: Offer to speak for the Tallow, who fear the gods

effects.log: You speak at the Tallow gathering. They hear you out in a murmur like a draught under a door.

choices.text: Offer to speak for the Beeswax, who want the door

effects.log: The Beeswax gathering is warmer and less careful. They ask you to carry a petition to the gods.

events.text: The tour ends at an old furnace-house where the wick-folk are made. Here {npc} confides that the heaven is running out of light: the furnace was lit by a god who walled it in, and the wick-folk have burned lower with each generation. The politics, {he} says, are about who gets the last of the oil.

choices.text: Offer a spark of your own domain to the furnace

effects.log: The furnace roars. The wick-folk fall silent, then flare in a long gold cheer. You find your qi less after, and your faith more.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to bring their case to the gods

effects.log: {npc} nods, solemn. {He} says the Beeswax will do it, and that you have made {him} braver.

events.text: The Tallow vote to keep the seal. They do not mean it unkindly: they remember the gods who built the walls, and they remember why. They ask only that you promise never to tell the other gods where the door is. {npc} watches you, flame low, waiting for your word.

choices.text: Promise, and keep it

effects.log: You swear in the old form. The Tallow thank you in a long soft chord, and {npc} looks relieved and a little sad.

choices.text: Promise nothing, but come back to visit

effects.log: The Tallow murmur disapproval. {npc} walks you to the door and says, privately, that the visits would be welcome.

events.text: At the Hall of Courts you present the Beeswax petition. The courts are in an uproar: a sealed heaven is a scandal, and the wick-folk are, apparently, a fire hazard. Mujin demands a garrison. The Silent Hall asks quietly whether anyone has thought to ask the wick-folk what they want.

choices.text: Speak for the wick-folk, plainly

effects.log: You say what you saw. The court hears you in silence, and a small embassy is voted, and not a garrison.

choices.text: Quietly arrange for oil to be sent through the seal

effects.log: A cart of lamp-oil goes through a back door, unmarked. The wick-folk do not ask where it comes from.

events.text: Years later the Lantern Heaven is a trading partner: a stall of tallow-glass in every great market, a seat at the lesser courts. {npc} is its first envoy, and {his} flame burns steady and tall. {He} sends you a lantern each year at the turning, and every year it burns without oil.

choices.text: Hang the lantern at your shrine door

effects.log: Pilgrims say it is the warmest light in the valley. You do not argue.

choices.text: Send {npc} a thank-you of fresh oil

effects.log: It is not needed, and {he} accepts it as it is meant.

events.text: The Tallow keep the seal, and the heaven burns on, low and quiet. Every few decades {npc} slips out to see you at the door, flame cupped, to ask what the gods are saying now. Each time it is a little more, and a little less. You are, you realise, a small window in a very long wall.

choices.text: Tell {him} everything, and trust the walls

effects.log: You talk until dawn. {He} listens as if each word were oil.

choices.text: Bring a book of the gods songs for the library

effects.log: The library of the Lantern Heaven is one volume the richer. The Tallow shelve it at the front.

events.text: In the vault of a fallen war god hangs a bridle of braided red cord. A tag, in a clerks hand, reads: Whoever wears this may ride any beast to the end of its strength. Seven debts apply. The vault-keeper, a very old shade, will not say what they are. It will say that nobody has returned it.

choices.text: Take the bridle

effects.log: The cord is warm and slightly damp. You feel faintly ill, as though you had been signed for.

choices.text: Ask the shade what the debts are

effects.log: The shade says that is for the rider to discover. It adds, kindly, that most riders find the first quickly.

choices.text: Read the tag twice and leave it hanging

effects.log: Some bargains improve with a night to think. The bridle sways gently in the draught as you go.

events.text: The bridle works. A lame river-horse that would not leave its stall carries you across a mountain in a morning, and does not tire. You dismount trembling, and the horse is grey with exhaustion. The first debt falls due: you must carry the beast for the next stretch of road.

choices.text: Carry the horse over the pass

effects.log: It weighs more than it should. You carry it for an hour in a hot silence, and it forgives you in a snort.

choices.text: Put the bridle away and walk

effects.log: You lay the bridle in your coat. The horse walks beside you, slowly, bearing no weight at all.

events.text: The shade, grudging, names four of the seven: a debt of breath, a debt of road, a debt of shade, and a debt of the name. The other three the shade says it was never told, only that the last is paid by someone else.

choices.text: Take the bridle anyway, knowing

effects.log: You tie the cord around your wrist. Knowing does not make it lighter, but it makes it yours.

choices.text: Leave it, and tell no one the price

effects.log: You walk out into the light. The shade bows to you, a little sooner than is usual.

events.text: The second debt is the road: a long hard walk you did not plan, and a pain in the shoulder that is not yours. The third is the shade: for a day you cast no shadow, and a stranger on a bridge takes you for a ghost. You begin to see how the bridle collects.

choices.text: Pay on, and ride to the end of the road

effects.log: You pay, one by one, in small coin of discomfort. The beast under you never falters.

choices.text: Hang the bridle on a shrine peg and walk away

effects.log: The peg takes the weight with a creak. You leave a single coin of faith beside it, as if to say sorry.

events.text: You return the bridle to its peg. The shade takes it, and weighs it, and nods. The vault is quiet. On the way out, a small red cord is tied round your wrist, thin as thread. You cannot untie it. It does not hurt. It merely reminds you that you are known.

choices.text: Wear it as a small price for a fair walk

effects.log: The cord is a mark among the vault-keepers: this one returned what they took.

choices.text: Ask the shade what the cord means

effects.log: It means you paid nothing, and that the vault is, in a small way, grateful.

events.text: The last three debts fall due in a single night, the night of the new moon, and they are the heavy ones. The debt of the name takes your name from the lips of everyone you meet for a day. The debt of the lamp takes your light. The last, as the shade promised, is paid by someone else: a stranger you will never meet, who will be a little luckier, and a little poorer, for your ride.

choices.text: Accept it, and let the names fall

effects.log: For a day you are a plain traveller, and nobody remembers you. It is restful, and a little lonely.

choices.text: Offer a prayer for the stranger who pays

effects.log: You light a lamp for them. It is not much. It is the only coin the bridle did not ask for.

events.text: The bridle hangs on a shrine peg, and pilgrims touch it for luck. It does not seem to mind. Over the years you notice that the cord has darkened, as though something is slowly drawing a debt from the ones who touch it, and nobody seems the worse.

choices.text: Take it down and bury it deep

effects.log: You bury it in a corner of the yard with a small stone. The yard feels lighter.

choices.text: Let the pilgrims touch it, and say nothing

effects.log: You let the habit stand. A shrine needs a few mysteries, and this one is mild.

events.text: You cross into the Throne of Storms domain in a plain coat, a hat pulled low, unknown. The valley rumbles under a grey sky. Noegong of the Nine Drums is beloved here, and the drum-houses ring all day. {npc}, a ferryman at a river crossing, takes your coin without looking up and asks where you are headed.
events.arc: A Plain Coat in the Thunder Domain

choices.text: Say you are a traveller, bound nowhere

effects.log: {npc} grunts. {He} says that is the best sort, and offers you the seat by the stove.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the people here think of the Drummer

effects.log: {npc} considers for a long time. {He} says they love the Drummer and also fear the Drummer on the long days, and that this is probably the right balance.

choices.text: Pay the fare and cross in silence

effects.log: The ferry is old, and the river is brown. You reach the far bank without a word, and without regret.

events.text: In the drum-house a boy plays the great drum badly, to a hall that cheers anyway. {npc} is there too, at the back. The drum is the god heartbeat, {he} says, and the boy is learning to be a heart. The roof leaks; the stove smokes; nobody leaves.
events.arc: A Plain Coat in the Thunder Domain

choices.text: Sit and listen to the whole piece

effects.log: It is dreadful, and it is lovely. At the end you find your hand has been keeping time without being asked.

choices.text: Offer the boy a quiet lesson in rhythm

effects.log: You show the boy how to breathe between the strokes. The roof, as if impressed, stops dripping for a moment.

events.text: {npc} tells you of the Storm Throne grievance: when the harvest god Pungnyeon wanted a wetter spring, the Throne gave it, and the valley flooded. The people forgave. The Throne did not forgive itself, {he} says, and the drums have been quieter since.
events.arc: A Plain Coat in the Thunder Domain

choices.text: Say nothing, and remember

effects.log: You carry the story back to the court of the Storms in your own heart, unspoken. It changes the next thing you say there.

choices.text: Tell {him} the gods can be sorry too

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long moment under the stove-light. {He} does not ask who you are. {He} nods slowly, as one who has been answered.

events.text: A storm gathers, the first in a year, over the drum-house. The boy goes to the great drum and strikes it, once, just right, and the thunder answers from the hills. {npc} turns to you with wet eyes and says, softly, that {he} had never heard the old god forgive anyone before.
events.arc: A Plain Coat in the Thunder Domain

choices.text: Reveal yourself to {npc}, lightly

effects.log: You take off your hat. {npc} looks at your face, laughs once and bows low enough to hit the stove. The drums, somewhere, go quiet and then loud.

choices.text: Stay masked, and slip out in the thunder

effects.log: The thunder covers your steps. In the morning you are gone, and the boy plays better.

events.text: You come back to the valley after the winter, in the same plain coat. The boy is a young man now, and the drum is rebuilt. {npc} keeps the ferry as ever. {He} says the thunder has been kinder, and that a stranger once told {him} that gods can be sorry. {He} pays you no fare.
events.arc: A Plain Coat in the Thunder Domain

choices.text: Leave a coin of faith in the ferry-bell

effects.log: You hang the coin on the bell-cord. It rings every time the river wind blows, sweet and small.

choices.text: Ride the ferry across without a word, again

effects.log: The river is still brown. You find you have missed it.

events.text: The shrine at Duskwater has stood cold for the first time in four hundred years: the hearth ash is wet, and the ember that never goes out is gone. {npc}, the old keeper, sits on the step in the cold with a blanket round {his} shoulders. {He} says, quietly, that {he} did not do it, and that {he} cannot prove it.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell you the whole night

effects.log: {npc} tells it from dusk to dawn: the bell, the wind, the knock at the third hour. {He} remembers a smell of wet pine and wet iron.

choices.text: Examine the hearth yourself

effects.log: The ash is wet all through. The hearth stones have been scrubbed. Someone took a great deal of care.

choices.text: Light a fire in the cold hearth from your own domain

effects.log: The fire takes, small and uncertain. The keeper weeps. It is a start.

events.text: Three people had the means to do it. The apprentice, a boy afraid of the dark who sleeps at the far end of the hall. The ferryman, who has carried the keeper post for thirty years. And a guest god of the neighbouring Green Assembly, who arrived the same night and left before the bell. Each has a story. Each story has a hole.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Question the ferryman

effects.log: The ferryman is steady, proud and sad. He says he took pine to the shrine that night for the winter store, and wet iron is what he always smells of.

choices.text: Question the apprentice

effects.log: The boy is frightened and honest. He says he woke at the third hour, saw a pale light, and hid under his blanket until morning.

choices.text: Question the guest of the Assembly

effects.log: The guest is gracious and slippery. They say they left before the bell and heard nothing, and that the wind was loud.

events.text: The hearth stones have been scrubbed. Under the scrubbing, in the grout, there is a faint smell of resin: a fire-preserver, sold only to shrines, that keeps an ember asleep and safe. Whoever scrubbed the hearth was not putting the fire out. They were putting it to bed.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Follow the trail of resin out the back door

effects.log: The resin leads to the wood-store, then to a fresh-turned plot behind the shrine. Something warm is buried there.

choices.text: Ask the keeper who knows how to use such a thing

effects.log: The keeper turns pale, and then names a name {he} has not said in forty years.

events.text: You accuse the ferryman. The valley gasps; he stands very still, and then asks, very gently, whether you have looked behind the shrine. You have not. When you do, you find a buried clay pot, warm to the touch, and inside it the ember, safe, asleep, and wrapped in a ferryman cloak. He had hidden it to keep it safe from the guest.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Apologise to the ferryman before the whole valley

effects.log: He accepts with great dignity and some irritation. The valley thinks better of you for it.

choices.text: Quietly return the ember to the hearth, and say nothing

effects.log: The ember is relit. The ferryman nods once and does not meet your eye. Someone will have to ask forgiveness properly later.

events.text: You question the guest of the Assembly, and they are cornered, and furious, and clearly innocent: they left at the bell and spent the night three valleys away. The valley is furious with you. The keeper looks at the floor. Time has been lost, and the real trail is going cold.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Apologise, and go back to the hearth

effects.log: The guest accepts coolly, and the Assembly will not forget it. You return to the grout and the resin smell.

choices.text: Hold your ground, and press the question

effects.log: The guest stiffens. A letter of complaint will be on the court table by the next noon.

events.text: The pot behind the shrine holds the ember, wrapped in the keepers old coat. The apprentice, white as milk, confesses at last: he saw the ember dying in the storm, and buried it to save it, and then was too ashamed to say, because he had been afraid of the dark and slept. The valley erupts in relief.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Return the ember to the hearth in a public rite

effects.log: The ember is carried through the valley in a bowl of clean ash. The apprentice walks first, blushing to the ears.

choices.text: Tell the boy he saved a shrine, and let the valley hear it

effects.log: The boy stands taller than he has ever stood, and the keeper clasps his shoulder.

events.text: Whoever put the ember to bed was not a thief, or a vandal, or a saboteur. The valley slowly pieces it together: an old keeper, in the grip of a long fear, hid it out of fear. {npc} stands in front of the hearth and, with a shaking hand, takes the ember from its pot. {He} says only: I could not carry it any longer.
events.arc: Who Put Out the Hearth at Duskwater

choices.text: Take the ember, and keep the shrine with {him}

effects.log: You sit with {npc} through the long winter. The ember burns, small and steady, between you.

choices.text: Find the old keeper a younger partner

effects.log: In spring the boy comes to the shrine as an apprentice. The ember does not go out again.

events.text: A stag crosses the high pass at dusk with no shadow, and the dogs of three shrines will not follow its track. Shepherds say it appears on the longest night, drinks at the black tarn, and stands for a count of nine in the moonlight before it goes. It leaves hoofprints that are warm for an hour.

choices.text: Wait at the tarn on the longest night

effects.log: You wait through the dark, and the cold. At the far edge of the water, something lifts its head.

choices.text: Track the prints back along the pass

effects.log: The prints lead to a cairn of grey stones at the end of a ledge. The warmth in the ground is stronger there.

choices.text: Ask the shepherds what they have lost

effects.log: Each has lost a small thing: a bell, a dog, a name. They never connected them.

events.text: It drinks. It does not startle. The stag is the colour of old ivory, and where its shadow should lie the snow is bright and unmarked. It stands for a count of nine, as the shepherds said, and in the ninth count it looks at you and does not look away.

choices.text: Speak to it

effects.log: The stag lowers its antlers and your own shadow stirs on the snow, stretches, and walks a step toward it.

choices.text: Cast a net of moonlight over it

effects.log: The net falls in silver. The stag does not move, as if it had always been caught.

events.text: The cairn is a grave marker of one: a hunter who followed the stag for a hundred years and stopped, at last, under these stones. The hunter shadow lies across the cairn, long and patient, and it is the only shadow in the pass. The stag has been looking after it.

choices.text: Say a word over the cairn

effects.log: The shadow lifts a little. The stag appears on the ledge and bows its head, and lets you pass.

choices.text: Take the hunters spear from the stones

effects.log: The spear is light and bright. The stag watches with its flat dark eye, and does not stop you.

events.text: It tells you in the only way it can: with a look, and a turn of the head. Its shadow was taken long ago by a god who wanted a hunter that could never be seen. It has been walking since then in search of any place where the sun is kind. It asks for nothing. It is only tired.

choices.text: Offer to carry its shadow back from the god who took it

effects.log: You make a vow to the stag in the moonlight. It lowers its antlers, and a faint dark line unrolls a hand-length from its hoof.

choices.text: Lay your own cloak where its shadow would fall

effects.log: You spread the cloak. For a moment, in the lamplight, the stag has a shadow, and it weeps.

events.text: The net holds the stag in a pale glow, and it makes no struggle, which troubles you. The shepherds arrive with ropes and a fire, and some of them want to pen it, and some to be rid of it. The stag stands between your net and their torches, an old thing, a long thing.

choices.text: Bind it in the shepherds pen, with warding

effects.log: The pen holds. The stag pines slowly, and by spring it has stopped eating.

choices.text: Slay it, and spare the valley

effects.log: The stag lies down. The shepherds sing, and weep, and come to feel it was a mercy and a murder. No more tracks appear in the snow.

choices.text: Cut the net, and let it go

effects.log: The net parts under your hand. The stag leaves the way it came, without hurry, and without thanks.

events.text: The god who took the shadow lives in a hall of lanterns on the edge of the Dreams domain, and keeps a hundred shadows on pegs like cloaks. The god is not there; only the steward is, who says the god is away. Beside the pegs, on a hook of its own, hangs a long antlered shadow, patient as a harness.

choices.text: Take it down, and leave a coin of faith in its place

effects.log: The steward looks away. The shadow weighs nothing, and fits in your coat.

choices.text: Leave a message that you have called

effects.log: You leave a polite card. The god will find it, in a century or two, and be mildly alarmed.

events.text: In spring the stag crosses the high pass at noon, in full sun, on a bright wet slope. Its shadow trails behind it, short and sharp. The shepherds stop, and take off their hats, and the stag goes on to the tarn and drinks, and does not look up.

choices.text: Leave it alone

effects.log: You watch from a rock. It is the simplest thing you have seen all year.

choices.text: Send word to the shrines that the stag is free

effects.log: The dogs of three shrines are called off. They are very relieved.

events.text: Every longest night after, the stag does not come. The tarn is black, and the valley is quiet. The shepherds say it was a good beast, in its way. The pen stands empty. Something, you feel, was taken from the pass that no one can name, and you were the one who took it.

choices.text: Plant a shrine at the tarn for it

effects.log: A small stone for a small god of the longest night. The first year there are nine offerings, one for each count.

choices.text: Accept it, and learn from it

effects.log: You will think of the stag every longest night. It is a quiet kind of penance.

events.text: The seal is carved with a tortoise, and the door opens on a plain of flat grey stones under a still sky. A great council of very old creatures sits in a ring: tortoises as large as huts, moss on their shells. They are debating whether to open the door. They have been debating for nine hundred years. They are, apparently, close to a vote.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Patient Ones

choices.text: Sit with them, and listen

effects.log: You sit among the stones. A tortoise begins a sentence. You are fairly sure it will end before the next age.

choices.text: Ask what the question is

effects.log: The oldest tortoise lifts its head, a movement that takes some time, and says that the question is whether the question is a good one.

choices.text: Close the door gently and go

effects.log: You leave without disturbing them. A faint rumble follows you out, and may be approval.

events.text: Days pass. You learn the factions: the Early, who believe a vote should be taken at once, and the Late, who believe it should be taken after the last stone is worn smooth. The Early have been losing for seven hundred years. They are very polite about it, and very tired.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Patient Ones

choices.text: Speak for the Early, and urge a vote

effects.log: The Early are delighted, in a way that takes about a week to show. The Late look at you with deep, gentle disapproval.

choices.text: Speak for the Late, and urge patience

effects.log: The Late nod, which takes a day. The Early fall silent, and are not unkind about it.

events.text: A young tortoise, barely three hundred years old, takes you aside. It is anxious. It believes the council has forgotten why it began, and wants to look in the Book of the First Day, which is kept in a stone chest nobody has opened since. It asks whether you would stand beside it while it does.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Patient Ones

choices.text: Stand beside the young one, and open the chest

effects.log: The lid is heavy, and you lift it together. The book is a single page, and on it is a drawing of a door standing open.

choices.text: Tell the young one it is brave, and to wait

effects.log: It nods, a long slow nod. It will wait, it says, for another hundred years, and the idea frightens neither of you.

events.text: The Early call the vote, and by the standards of the heaven it is a thunderclap: four tortoises raise their heads at once. The count takes a week. The door, by a margin of one, stays open. A wind blows through it, the first in nine hundred years, and the oldest tortoise sighs, and falls asleep.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Patient Ones

choices.text: Stay to see the first guests arrive

effects.log: You stay a season. Visitors come: a fox, a pilgrim, a very lost clerk. The council receives them with grave courtesy and no haste at all.

choices.text: Take the first wind home in a bottle

effects.log: The wind in the bottle smells of stone and rain. It lasts for years on your shrine shelf.

events.text: The Late prevail, as they always do, and the door stays shut, and the council drifts back to its debate with the calm of those for whom time is a friend. They give you a gift, a smooth grey stone worn by a thousand years of thought. It is warm, and heavier than it looks.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Patient Ones

choices.text: Keep the stone at your shrine

effects.log: Pilgrims say it makes them patient. It makes them, mostly, sleepy, which is nearly the same.

choices.text: Give it to the young tortoise, and wish it well

effects.log: The young one takes the stone and tucks it under its shell. It will keep it three thousand years.

events.text: The Book of the First Day shows only an open door, and a single sentence below it in an old hand: They are not shut in; they are only unhurried. The young tortoise reads it twice, and the council, hearing, takes six months to look up. Then, slowly, every head turns toward the door, and stays there.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Patient Ones

choices.text: Leave them with the book, and the open door

effects.log: You leave. For a long time afterward the door stays open, and the grey plain quietly changes.

choices.text: Stay a decade, and help them decide

effects.log: You help them decide. It takes a year just to say good morning.

events.text: A red fox sits in the middle of the mountain road and will not let travellers by until they pay. It asks for a story, a joke or a good lie; it refuses coin. Pilgrims have started to avoid the pass, and the shrine-keepers at the top say their offerings are down by half. They want it driven off.

choices.text: Go up and pay the toll in a story

effects.log: The fox hears your story with its chin on its paws. At the end it says that it has heard it, but it was well told.

choices.text: Go up with a net and a basket

effects.log: You climb the pass with a net. The fox watches you from a boulder, entirely at ease.

choices.text: Listen to the pilgrims and the keepers first

effects.log: They disagree on everything but the fox red coat.

events.text: The fox is learning. Every traveller leaves it a story, and it keeps them all: a long catalogue of lives in its head, told back in the evening to the stars. It knows the road, the weather, the bandits, the births. The keepers had not realised it was a library.

choices.text: Offer to write the fox stories down

effects.log: You sit with a brush and the fox dictates. It is a better teller than you are a scribe.

choices.text: Leave it a new story every year

effects.log: You become part of its yearly round. The fox seems to count you among its friends.

events.text: The fox slips the net with a flick, laughs in a thin bark, and sits on top of it. It says it will go if you answer a riddle. The riddle is, what does a god owe a road? The pilgrims gather on the wall to hear what you answer.

choices.text: A road is owed a safe passage, always

effects.log: The fox tips its head and says it is a fair answer, and a dull one. It moves a paw to the left, but not very far.

choices.text: A road is owed nothing; it is the road that gives

effects.log: The fox is delighted. It rolls once in the dust and leaves the road entirely, trotting up the slope to a high place with a view.

choices.text: Bind the fox quickly with a cord of warding while it gloats

ok.log: The cord slips round its middle and holds. The fox glares, and sulks, and is carried down the pass in a basket.

fail.log: The fox slips the cord, and tweaks your hat as a farewell. It does not run, but sits again, delighted.

events.text: The fox book is finished in a year and printed in a hundred copies, and sold in the lower markets at a fair price. The fox is given a small shrine at the pass, and a ruling that no traveller may be refused for lacking a story. The offerings at the top rise, and the keepers come to love the fox.

choices.text: Keep a copy at your own shrine

effects.log: Pilgrims read it by the stove. It has a way of ending every story a little earlier than you expect.

choices.text: Send the first copy to the Silent Hall

effects.log: The Silent Hall acknowledges receipt with a single line. The line is, you suspect, a compliment.

events.text: Each year you climb the pass with a new story. The fox tells you the road news and tells you which of your stories it liked. By the fortieth year it has begun to finish your sentences. By the fiftieth it has begun to correct them. It is the best audience you have ever had.

choices.text: Let it finish this one for you

effects.log: The fox ends your story better than you would have. You thank it, and mean it.

choices.text: Bring it a story you have never told anyone

effects.log: It listens in complete silence, and does not repeat it. The pass is quiet that night.

events.text: The fox goes up the slope and is not seen on the road again. The pass opens, and pilgrims return. The keepers say the road is easier without it, and the pilgrims say it was dull. You find a single red hair on your sleeve and keep it in a pocket for a long time.

choices.text: Leave a story at the high place where it went

effects.log: The next year the story is gone, and in its place is a smooth pebble. It is a good trade.

choices.text: Tell no one that the riddle was an answer

effects.log: You keep the answer to yourself, and it keeps you.

events.text: The fox is shut up in a cage at the top of the pass, with a dish of water and the pilgrims stories read to it through the bars. It does not eat the pilgrim stories. It does not, in fact, eat anything. The keepers argue about what to do. The offerings climb, then fall, then stop. Nobody tells stories at the pass now.

choices.text: Open the cage and let it out

effects.log: The fox walks out, shakes itself, and sits in the road. It says nothing. Then it asks the first pilgrim for a story.

choices.text: Argue the keepers round to freeing it

effects.log: It takes a month. In the end, they free it themselves, which is better.

events.text: On a hill in the Mountains domain stands a cairn of black stones with no name. Locals leave a pebble on it as they pass, out of habit, and none of them can say why. The stones are warm. Under the topmost, you find a thread of faith so faint it would not stir a candle.
events.arc: A Cairn for a Forgotten God

choices.text: Ask the locals what they remember

effects.log: They remember nothing, but each has a gentle word: she was kind, he was kind, it was kind. They cannot agree what it was.

choices.text: Add your own pebble and listen

effects.log: You place the pebble. The warmth moves up your arm, a little, as if testing you.

choices.text: Count the stones

effects.log: There are nine hundred and ninety-nine. A thousandth would have finished it.

events.text: The memory is in the hill itself. You sit by the cairn for three nights and on the third a dream comes: a plain hall, a plain table, a plain cup. A god of small hospitality, whose domain was the first cup of the day. Their followers were the sleepy, the sick, the newly arrived. No one remembers because no one ever needed to.
events.arc: A Cairn for a Forgotten God

choices.text: Pour out a first cup at the cairn, every dawn

effects.log: You do it for a month. The warmth grows. It is not much, but it is steady.

choices.text: Carry the story to the Silent Hall, to be written

effects.log: The Hall takes it with a nod. A name is set down, and it is, at last, a name.

events.text: The pebble was a prayer, you find: the first in a long time. The cairn takes it and returns a gift, a small clay cup, warm as a hand. Its glaze is the colour of morning. Drinking from it, you are suddenly not tired, and the world is a very kind place for exactly the length of the cup.
events.arc: A Cairn for a Forgotten God

choices.text: Take the cup home to your shrine

effects.log: It never empties, but it never quite fills. It becomes the first cup at your shrine each dawn.

choices.text: Leave the cup on the cairn for the next to find

effects.log: You set it back on the topmost stone. A traveller will find it, one tired morning.

events.text: The dead god name is written in the Hall record, in the first morning light of the year: Aejin, of the First Cup. A lamp is lit for her at every dawn shrine in the Mountains domain for a week. On the last morning the cairn is found to have a thousandth stone, small and white, set in its crown by no one.
events.arc: A Cairn for a Forgotten God

choices.text: Leave it, and let the hill finish itself

effects.log: The cairn is whole. You walk down the hill a god who has done a small thing exactly right.

choices.text: Tell the locals what they have been keeping

effects.log: They are astonished, and then not. They knew, in their way. They had only needed it said.

events.text: A cup is poured every dawn at the cairn for years, by you and then by others. The warmth in the stones rises until the hill is warm to stand on. People sleep better in the valleys nearby, so far as anyone can tell. A small hospitality god, forgotten, is being gently remembered back into being. They do not speak. They are only a little less nobody.
events.arc: A Cairn for a Forgotten God

choices.text: Install a keeper to pour the cup

effects.log: A young shrine-keeper takes the post, and in time is blessed with a gift for welcome.

choices.text: Pour it yourself, a few mornings a year

effects.log: You keep a small faithful ritual, and the hill remembers.

events.text: At the pale end of the night a hound howls in the lower pasture, and every hunter-god within a day answers. It is not a call to a kill. It is a call to a count: the hounds are checking who is still alive. They sing the names, one by one, and wait for the answers.

choices.text: Answer with your own name

effects.log: The hounds fall silent, then howl your name back. You are, apparently, now on the list.

choices.text: Sit and listen to the count

effects.log: The names go by like a river: gods, beasts, shrines. Some are very old. Some are not answered.

events.text: A gold-flecked spoor crosses the path of every hunt this season: a beast that no one has seen but that everyone is tracking. The hunters argue about its size. Someone says it is a boar, someone a hind, someone a bird. The only thing agreed is that it is going somewhere on purpose.

choices.text: Follow the spoor for a day

effects.log: You follow it through a thicket and a gully, and lose it at a stream. It is a beautiful track, and a short one.

choices.text: Leave the spoor to the hunters

effects.log: You let it be. A quiet quarry deserves a quiet pursuit.

events.text: A sealed heaven coughs. The wardens say it happens every century or so: a long dry rattle through the wall, a puff of old air smelling of a vanished spring, and a few pale feathers on the doorstep. They sweep up the feathers and file them under Weather.

choices.text: Keep one of the feathers

effects.log: It is weightless and a little warm. It will not burn, and will not blow away.

choices.text: Ask what lives inside

effects.log: The wardens do not know. They have never asked. They are a little ashamed that no one has.

events.text: A tiny door in the base of a seal swings open, and a mouse the size of a thumb steps out with a letter. The letter is addressed to the Warden of Locks and reads, in a tiny hand: please, nothing is wrong, we are only checking that you are still there. The mouse waits for a reply.

choices.text: Write back that you are still there

effects.log: The mouse takes the note, bows and goes in. The door closes with a sound like a held breath let go.

choices.text: Slip a crumb under the door as well

effects.log: The crumb vanishes at once. The next day, a second letter arrives, thanking you in very small capitals.

events.text: In the vault of a fallen god stands a throne of pale wood, with no dust on it. The vault-keepers say it is swept by no one. Anyone who sits there hears, softly, a voice reading out the names of the god followers in order. The reading takes an hour. It ends, always, with a pause.

choices.text: Sit and hear the whole reading

effects.log: You hear four thousand names. At the pause, you say your own name into the quiet, and something that was waiting is satisfied.

choices.text: Stand and stay away from the throne

effects.log: You do not sit. Some names are better not heard by a stranger.

events.text: A rust-red banner hangs from the roof of a ruined war-hall, and it still moves in a wind that is not there. Beneath it the floor is worn in a circle by marching feet. They are not ghosts. They are only an echo of a drill, tireless, that no longer has anyone to answer to.

choices.text: Stand in the circle and give the order to stop

effects.log: You say halt in the old voice. The echo stops at once, and the banner falls slack.

choices.text: March a lap with the echo

effects.log: You march one lap. It is oddly restful, and the banner flutters once in thanks.

events.text: In the ash of a burned shrine nests a wren, and it does not build with twigs but with names: tiny rolled scraps of charred scroll, each holding one worshipper. It sings only when the wind is dry. The song is, if you listen, a roll-call.

choices.text: Leave an offering of seed at the nest

effects.log: The wren hops down, takes the seed, and sings a verse for you alone.

choices.text: Read the scraps without touching them

effects.log: There are thousands of names. You read forty, and each is a little lamp.

events.text: The door of a burned shrine has been repaired by someone, with care, in the wrong wood. It is bright pine on a black frame. The hinges are oiled. The latch is new. No one in the valley admits to doing it, and every morning the door is a little more finished.

choices.text: Leave a tool for the unseen mender

effects.log: The next morning your gift is gone, and the lintel is trimmed. You have, you feel, been hired.

choices.text: Wait up to see who it is

effects.log: You wait the night. At dawn the door is done and you are asleep against the post. You were, apparently, not meant to see.

events.text: In a primal valley, before names, you hear a sound that is not a sound but the place where one would be. It is made by a stone and the wind arguing very slowly. In ten thousand years they will have invented the vowel. For now they only lean toward each other, and the lean is lovely.

choices.text: Lean in to listen

effects.log: You lean. The lean becomes a shape, and the shape a half-word. You carry it home like a coin.

choices.text: Add a soft hum of your own

effects.log: The wind and stone seem to notice. The argument becomes, for a moment, a duet.

events.text: In the places before the domains were cut there is a pool that belongs to none of them. Its water is neither sea nor dream nor storm, and its edge keeps moving as if seeking an owner. A boundary-stone floats in the middle, blank, waiting for anyone to carve.

choices.text: Carve a small mark on it, a line and a dot

effects.log: The pool settles. For a day a patch of the primal wild feels, faintly, like yours.

choices.text: Leave it unclaimed, and drink

effects.log: The water is cold and plain. You walk away thinking your own thoughts, which is its own freedom.

events.text: In the Fire domain a roadside shrine to a minor god of matches stands neglected, the offerings dry as straw. A hand-written note on the lintel reads: if you are a god, please strike a match here just once. The note is very old and has been rewritten many times.

choices.text: Strike a match and let it burn

effects.log: The match flares and the note curls and warms, and something small and bright says thank you in your head.

choices.text: Rewrite the note in a clearer hand

effects.log: Your hand is better than the last. Perhaps it will last another century.

events.text: You walk the foreshore of the Sea domain at the turn of the tide in a plain coat. A child is herding crabs along the sand with a tiny stick, and singing. When you stop, the child looks up and says: you are a god, but a quiet one, so I will tell you the secret of the crabs.

choices.text: Ask the secret

effects.log: The secret is that crabs only go sideways to be polite. The child is entirely serious. You decide to believe it.

choices.text: Say you will not tell anyone

effects.log: The child nods gravely and puts a very small shell in your hand as the seal of the pact.

events.text: You find in a hollow tree a dream that is not yours, folded like a letter. It is a bright one: a child flying over a red field. The owner has dropped it and may be looking for it. A faint thread of longing runs from the folds back toward the valley.

choices.text: Carry it to the valley and call out

effects.log: A baker steps out of a doorway, flushed and breathless. The dream returns to her like a blown leaf, and she thanks you without knowing who you are.

choices.text: Fold it a little smaller, and keep it for a while

effects.log: The dream is gentle. You borrow a flying hour, and bring it back unharmed.

events.text: A staircase in the dream-paths descends and then, without turning, ascends again. You have been on it for an hour and are no further. A small plaque on the wall reads: this stair exists because someone could not decide whether to go down. It will end when they do.

choices.text: Sit on the stair and decide for them

effects.log: You decide, calmly, to go down. The stair ends at once at a plain door, and the plaque quietly rewrites itself.

choices.text: Go back up and leave it to its dreamer

effects.log: You climb out. Somewhere a sleeper turns over and does not decide.

events.text: A star in the Sky domain has gone out, and Cheonho has hung a black ribbon on its place. Children point it out to each other. A very old shepherd tells you it was her star, the one she steered by. She asks, humbly, whether it is permitted to name a new one for her.

choices.text: Name a faint star for her, in your own authority

effects.log: You pick the faintest in the quarter and write her name on it. She weeps, and takes it as a promise.

choices.text: Take her petition to Cheonho in person

effects.log: The Star-Keeper reads it twice, and rules that the black ribbon may be hung on her door.

events.text: In a corner of the Sky domain lies an orchard of small stars in pots, tended by a keeper with a watering can. Each is a seedling god of some tiny domain: a god of a single bridge, a god of cold mornings. The keeper says they must be watered by faith or they will not ripen.

choices.text: Water a seedling with a breath of faith

effects.log: The seedling brightens at once. The keeper gives you a leaf in thanks.

choices.text: Offer to adopt a seedling at your shrine

effects.log: The keeper wraps one carefully and hands it over like a baby bird. You have, it seems, become a guardian.

events.text: A vast hush comes down on a mountain pass. Birds stop. The wind stops. Somewhere beyond the ridge, something much larger than you has turned over in its sleep. It does not wake. The hush lasts a quarter hour, and then it lifts like a lid, and all the small noises begin again.

choices.text: Stay very still until it passes

effects.log: You stay. When the sound comes back, it is the best thing you have ever heard.

choices.text: Walk on quietly, and mention it to no one

effects.log: You walk on. Some things need no witness.

events.text: You find an unspent prayer on the road, a letter folded into a paper boat. It reads only: please let her find her way home. There is no name, no place, no sign of which way home might be. The boat is damp, and a little hopeful.

choices.text: Carry it to the nearest shrine and read it aloud

effects.log: The shrine-keeper tucks it into the lamp. By the next noon, a girl walks through the gate, footsore, and asks for water.

choices.text: Float it down the stream, to see where it goes

effects.log: The boat swings out and bobs away. You hope.

events.text: On a clear day a fog bell rings in the Mountains domain, and there is no fog. The shrine-keeper says it rings when someone in the valley is lost. You look around. There is nobody in view. The bell rings again, closer, and a small voice answers from the long grass.

choices.text: Go and find the voice

effects.log: It is a lamb, no more, and nearly asleep. You carry it home in your coat and the bell falls silent.

choices.text: Ring the bell in return, once

effects.log: The voice laughs, and a child rises out of the grass with a stick and a crooked grin, and walks off home.

events.text: A thorn-stag of the Green Assembly stands at a crossroads with a bough of thorns in its antlers, and will not let anyone by without plucking one. The thorn, it says, is a tithe: the pain of a small prick for a clearer head on the road. Pilgrims line up to pay.

choices.text: Take a thorn, and feel the road clear

effects.log: The prick is small and bright. The next mile you see everything sharply.

choices.text: Refuse and walk around

effects.log: The stag lets you go with a shrug of its antlers. It does not mind.

events.text: A river otter of the Storm domain has stolen a thunderbolt and is playing with it in the shallows, tossing it like a stone. Every toss makes a small clap and a bright ring of ripples. The gods of the Throne are on the bank, arguing about who should ask for it back.

choices.text: Lure the otter with a fish and fetch the bolt

ok.log: The otter swaps the bolt for the fish with a bow, and a clap of thunder salutes you from the hills.

fail.log: The otter keeps both and gives you a splash. The bolt cracks once, harmlessly, over your head.

choices.text: Sit on the bank and enjoy the game

effects.log: The otter plays until the sun goes down. The gods of the Throne give up and join in.

events.text: You pass a sealed heaven at the hour of the evening bell and hear singing through the wall, a choir of hundreds, in a language older than any domain. It is a hymn of thanks. The wardens tell you, shyly, that the seal is their gift to the choir. They sealed it to keep the song safe, and the song has been grateful ever since.

choices.text: Stay for the whole hymn

effects.log: The hymn runs for an hour, and it is not meant for you, and that is what makes it a gift.

choices.text: Leave a coin of faith at the seal in thanks

effects.log: The coin rings against the stone, and the choir sings one note higher.

events.text: A scroll of dust lies unrolled on a fallen god table. It was once a law. The words have flaked away, but you can still read the margin notes, left by tired clerks: this is unfair, this is unworkable, and, in a later hand, this is the only fair one we ever wrote. Someone loved it.

choices.text: Rewrite the law in your own hand, from the margins

effects.log: You reconstruct it slowly from the complaints. It turns out to be a good law, if inconvenient.

choices.text: Leave the dust where it lies

effects.log: Some laws are better remembered as arguments.

events.text: In the charred remains of a burned shrine a priest of nobody sits, tending a small fire in a bowl. He says it is the fire of the shrine, and that he has kept it alive for sixty years in the hope that a god will come. You are, it seems, the first.

choices.text: Reveal yourself, and take the shrine back

effects.log: The priest weeps with relief. The shrine is yours, and so is his lifetime of care.

choices.text: Say nothing, and add a log to the fire

effects.log: He nods, saying nothing. The fire burns brighter, and it is the only reply the shrine needs.

events.text: Under the noon sun of the Sky domain no one casts a shadow, by old custom: the god of noon does not allow them. Today a boy stands in the market square with a perfectly black shadow at his feet, and a crowd gathers. He says it grew in the night. He is not afraid, only curious.

choices.text: Ask the god of noon to allow one shadow

effects.log: The god of noon is surprised, and then charmed. The boy keeps his shadow, and a small festival is held in its honour.

choices.text: Tell the boy he is a marvel and send him home

effects.log: He goes, skipping, with the shadow beside him. The crowd drifts back to its business, a little lighter.

events.text: A wind blows through the primal places, and it carries the seed of a god not yet made. It lands on a wet rock, shivers once, and begins to grow a tiny, careful shape. It is going to be a god of something small. It does not know yet what.

choices.text: Shelter it from the wind with your coat

effects.log: You hold the coat over it for an hour. The shape settles and becomes a small clear dewdrop of intention.

choices.text: Whisper a word of domain to it, softly

effects.log: The word is dew. You are, perhaps, its first suggestion.

events.text: You are summoned to a court of very old gods who sit in a room so quiet that your breathing is loud. They ask you one question, and then do not speak again: what have you made that you would be proud to see forgotten? You may take as long as you like. They have time.

choices.text: Answer plainly, with the smallest thing you can name

effects.log: You answer. The silence grows kind. When you leave, a servant tells you it was the best answer they had heard in an age.

choices.text: Answer with a question of your own

effects.log: The old gods look at each other. It is the first time any of them has smiled in a millennium.

events.text: At the end of a long day you sit on a hillside in your plain coat and find yourself falling asleep with your back to a stone. The stone is warm. Somewhere under it a bell rings once, very far down. You sleep an hour, which is a long time for a god, and wake perfectly rested.

choices.text: Thank the stone

effects.log: The stone does not reply. The warmth, however, lasts all the way down the hill.

choices.text: Mark the stone and come back again

effects.log: You set a tiny cairn. Over the years it becomes a place you visit when you want to be no one.

events.text: A grey wolf carries a live coal in its jaws and runs the ash fields at dusk. Wherever it drops the coal a hearth lights in an empty house, and wherever a hearth lights, a family returns. The Fire shrines call it a thief, because it takes the coal from their altars. It has taken nine this winter.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Follow it at a distance, and learn where it goes

effects.log: You follow through the ash for three evenings. It never looks back, and it never stops.

choices.text: Leave a coal for it on a stone, unguarded

effects.log: You set a good coal in a bowl on a flat stone, and step well away into the dark.

choices.text: Speak to the Fire shrines about their loss

effects.log: The shrine-keepers are angry and a little ashamed. Nobody has asked the wolf anything.

events.text: The wolf has a round. It lights the hearth of a shut-up house, sits by it until the smoke rises, then goes on to the next. In each house the next morning, a stranger has moved in: a family from the burned lands, brought up to the border by some quiet road. The wolf is a matchmaker of hearths.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Keep pace with it, and help carry the coals

effects.log: You take a coal in a pot of clay. The wolf allows it with a flick of the ear, and the work goes twice as fast.

choices.text: Go ahead to the next house and wait

effects.log: You find the cold hearth, and sit there. When the wolf arrives with the coal, it is not surprised.

events.text: The wolf takes the coal from the stone, and then, instead of running, sits and looks at you. It sets the coal down. It pushes the bowl back an inch with its nose. It wants the shrine to give the coal, not a god. A shrine-keeper comes up the path behind you, red-faced, and stops.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Ask the keeper to hand over a coal

effects.log: The keeper does so, trembling. The wolf takes it with great courtesy and runs, and the keeper sits down heavily in the ash.

choices.text: Bind the wolf in warding thread while it waits

effects.log: It does not struggle. It looks at you, and then at the keeper, with the same patient, disappointed look.

choices.text: Let the wolf take the coal and go

effects.log: It takes the coal, and the keeper says nothing, and you do not know which of you was more relieved.

events.text: At the last house on the round, a girl of seven stands at the door with her mother. They have walked from the burned lands. The wolf sets the coal down at the hearth and licks the mother hand once. Then it lies down across the doorway, tired to the bone, and the girl puts her face in its grey fur.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Offer the wolf a place at your own shrine

effects.log: It listens, ear to one side, and then lowers its head onto the girl lap. It has chosen. You leave the shrine door open for it anyway.

choices.text: Leave a stack of dry wood by the door

effects.log: The mother bows to you in the dusk, and does not ask who you are.

events.text: The Fire shrines hold the wolf in a cage of iron wire, and light their altars again, and are satisfied. But the empty houses stay cold, and in spring a delegation of families from the burned lands arrives at the border and finds nobody to meet them. The shrine-keepers look at their hands.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Open the cage and apologise to the wolf

effects.log: The wolf walks out, shakes the ash from its coat, and goes to take a coal from an altar. Nobody stops it.

choices.text: Slay the wolf to end the argument

effects.log: The wolf lies down in the ash like a banked fire. The families find the houses cold, and sit in them anyway.

choices.text: Take the coals to the border yourself

effects.log: It is slow, and nowhere near as clever as the wolf. But it is something.

events.text: Some years on you pass a house in the ash fields with smoke rising from its chimney. At the door there is a grey wolf-pelt hung in a frame, and beneath it a family has set a bowl of coals that never goes out. The mother says it is not a trophy. It is a memory. She asks you to bless the hearth.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Bless the hearth, and the pelt

effects.log: The coals flare briefly, a soft red. The house hums. Somewhere a wolf is howling a thank-you, you are fairly sure.

choices.text: Say nothing, and take your hat off

effects.log: You stand a moment with your hat in your hand, and go on.

events.text: On the longest night of that year, a wolf comes up the stairs of your shrine with a coal in its mouth and sets it down on your hearth. It does not ask for anything. It sits for a count of nine and goes. The coal burns on your hearth till spring.
events.arc: The Ember-Wolf of the Ash Fields

choices.text: Keep the coal burning, and tell the story

effects.log: Pilgrims come to see it. Some of them stay, and make hearths of their own.

choices.text: Let the coal burn down without a word

effects.log: It burns to a small grey ash that smells of wet stone. You keep the ash in a jar.

events.text: Each tenth year the Throne of Storms hunts a leviathan calf, a lesser one, for the great feast. The calf is not harmed; it is chased, and mastered, and decorated with garlands. The calf, however, does not know this. A small god of tidepools comes to you in the dusk and asks, very quietly, whether you could hide it.

choices.text: Agree, and ask where the calf lies

effects.log: The tide-god shows you a kelp shelf where the calf is hiding, folded in on itself, blinking.

choices.text: Ask the tide-god why it matters so much

effects.log: The tide-god says that the calf is the last of its line, and that nobody has asked it.

choices.text: Decline politely

effects.log: The tide-god nods and goes away, small and wet. It does not argue.

events.text: You swim out in a plain coat of salt. The hunt is coming: horns on the tide, a long line of boats, the heralds singing the old hunting names. The calf is the size of a house, and trembling. It looks at you with a round dark eye, and in the eye is a fear you have not felt since you were new.

choices.text: Lead it into a drowned cave

effects.log: The cave is dark, with a long mouth. The calf slips in without a sound, and the horns pass overhead.

choices.text: Draw the hunt off with a decoy of silver light

ok.log: The hunt chases the light for an hour. The calf slips away, and you float on your back, laughing at the sky.

fail.log: The light gutters and the hunt turns toward you, and you are hauled aboard a boat, soaked, and introduced as a hero.

events.text: The tide-god explains. The calf is the last of the deep-singers, whose song once held the tides together in the Sea domain. The hunt is the Throne way of keeping the old things in sight, and their garlands are a sort of love. But the calf has begun to refuse food, and no one has noticed the reason.

choices.text: Go to Haeryong, and tell the Keeper of Tides

effects.log: Haeryong listens, slow as the sea. A hush falls. The calf, you learn, will be released after the hunt.

choices.text: Go to the hunt, and watch what the calf does

effects.log: The calf sings, once, a long low line that stills the ranks of the boats. The hunt falls silent, ashamed.

events.text: The calf lies in the dark cave with you for a night and a day. On the second dusk it begins to sing, softly, the first low notes of the old song, and the cave rings. Far above, the boats hear it through the water and turn slowly home, one by one, their garlands trailing.

choices.text: Stay with the calf until the song ends

effects.log: It sings for hours. When it stops, the tides in the Sea domain have a new gentle rhythm.

choices.text: Swim back and tell the Throne it was your doing

effects.log: You surface to a furious Throne and a delighted Haeryong. It is a good argument to have.

events.text: The Throne declares you the hunt-winner for catching the calf-lure, and puts a garland on your neck, and a chain of pearls. At the great feast the calf is brought in, garlanded and glassy-eyed. It sings nothing. It looks at you once, and then at the floor. The tide-god, at the back, turns its face to the wall.

choices.text: Ask the Throne to release the calf, in front of all

effects.log: The hall goes quiet. After a long moment Noegong says gruffly that the calf may go. It is released at dawn.

choices.text: Keep the garland and say nothing

effects.log: The garland is heavy. You wear it all night and take it off alone in the dark.

events.text: The calf is freed at dawn from a shelf of black rock into the open sea, the garlands falling off one by one into the current. It dives, and does not look back. A song comes up from the deep, a single note that makes every shell on the beach hum for a minute.

choices.text: Remember the song, and teach it to the tide-priests

effects.log: The priests learn it badly and with love. Every dawn, now, the beach hums.

choices.text: Keep the song as a private thing

effects.log: You hum it sometimes at your shrine. It helps with the long afternoons.

events.text: The hunt falls silent at the calf song, and no hunter raises a spear. The Throne admits the rite was a tradition and not a law, and calls a council. The council lasts a year. It ends with the garlands being given to the tide-pools instead, hung on the stones for the children to gather.

choices.text: Help to hang the garlands

effects.log: You hang a garland on a rock and a crab promptly eats it. It is a fine day.

choices.text: Give your blessing to the new custom

effects.log: It becomes the custom of the Sea domain, and in a hundred years no one remembers it was ever different.

events.text: A hare turns up at your shrine on what it insists is your feast day. It has a ribbon round its neck, a bundle of cress, and a very small bell. It has also, you discover, got the date wrong by four months. It will not be corrected. It sits on the step and rings the bell and waits for you to celebrate.
events.arc: The Hare Who Keeps Your Calendar

choices.text: Celebrate with the hare

effects.log: You eat cress together on the shrine step. The hare is solemn and pleased, and rings the bell at every course.

choices.text: Gently tell it the real date

effects.log: The hare listens with both ears and writes the true date on a leaf. The next year it comes on the real day and also on the wrong one.

choices.text: Slip away and leave it to its feast

effects.log: It celebrates alone and is quite happy.

events.text: The hare has been keeping your calendar for years. It has recorded your feasts, your birthdays, your first words, your first miracle, and a day on which you apparently lost your temper. Some are right. Some are made up with great confidence. It presents the whole record to you in a bundle of leaves.
events.arc: The Hare Who Keeps Your Calendar

choices.text: Read it aloud, and correct the worst errors

effects.log: You read for an hour. The hare listens with trembling ears, and weeps at the wrong bits.

choices.text: Declare the calendar official as written

effects.log: The hare faints, softly, into the cress. Pilgrims now keep your feast on the wrong date, with great sincerity.

events.text: The hare goes off at the turn of the year to find the true date, and returns a season later with three other hares in tow. They have, between them, worked out a calendar nobody could dispute. They lay it before you. It is correct, and very dull. It has one feast in it, and it is yours.
events.arc: The Hare Who Keeps Your Calendar

choices.text: Adopt the true calendar, with thanks

effects.log: The hares celebrate wildly, which for hares means running in circles until sundown.

choices.text: Add the old wrong feast beside the true one

effects.log: The hare takes it as the greatest honour. Your shrine now has two feasts a year, and one is never quite on time.

events.text: A rival god, passing, hears of the hare calendar and sneers. A calendar of a god by a hare, they say, is no god calendar at all. The hare overhears, sits very straight, and begins to recite your whole record to the rival, loudly, from the first day, and does not stop for an hour.
events.arc: The Hare Who Keeps Your Calendar

choices.text: Let the hare finish

effects.log: The rival leaves with the whole record in their ears, and the faintest look of respect. The hare is hoarse for a week.

choices.text: Gently stop the hare, and thank it

effects.log: You take the hare in your arms and thank it before the rival. It melts, in the way hares melt, entirely.

events.text: The hare grows old, as hares do, in a handful of years. One feast day it comes on the correct date for the first time and sits in the sun and rings the little bell, and sleeps. It does not wake. The other hares come to the funeral with ribbons round their necks. They have kept the calendar. They always will.
events.arc: The Hare Who Keeps Your Calendar

choices.text: Bury the hare under the shrine step

effects.log: You lay it down with its bell. The other hares ring theirs, one note each, and the sound is very small and very exact.

choices.text: Keep the bell at your shrine door

effects.log: It rings in the wind, now and again, on the wrong day, and you smile.

events.text: The seal is blank, which is unusual: a plain disc of stone, as though the sealers ran out of marks. Behind it lies a plain white hall, and in it stand figures not quite made: a person with one arm, a bird with a single wing, a house with no door. {npc}, tall and unfinished at the edges, welcomes you with a bow of one shoulder.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what this place is

effects.log: {npc} says it is where the gods put things they meant to finish. {He} says it with a faint smile and a shrug that goes on a little too long.

choices.text: Ask whether anyone here wishes to be finished

effects.log: {npc} goes still. {He} says that is the whole of the politics, and invites you to sit.

choices.text: Greet them all, and keep your counsel

effects.log: You bow to each in turn. A bird with one wing inclines its head.

events.text: The Unfinished are split in two. The Finishers want the gods to be asked to complete them, however long that takes. The Leavers say being unfinished is a form of freedom, and that a made thing is a bound thing. Neither faction can agree whether {npc} should be consulted, being so nearly done.

choices.text: Speak for the Finishers, and promise to ask

effects.log: The Finishers murmur, hopeful and a little sad. {npc} looks at you with an expression that is not hope.

choices.text: Speak for the Leavers, and promise to ask nothing

effects.log: The Leavers cheer in odd, half-formed voices. {npc} nods slowly, as though a stone had moved in {his} chest.

events.text: {npc} shows you the workshop at the back of the hall: tools laid out on benches, half-carved faces, a loom with the weft hanging. The gods who made it left in the middle of a day. They did not mean to be cruel. They were called away. {He} wants to know whether any god is ever coming back.

choices.text: Say that none is, and watch {him} take it

effects.log: {npc} bows {his} head. The room dims a little. Then, slowly, {he} lifts a chisel and tries it on the edge of a bench.

choices.text: Say you will ask, and mean to

effects.log: {npc} thanks you with the half-formed grace of a hand just beginning to close.

events.text: You carry the petition to the Weaver, Unmyeong, and the Weaver reads it with a quiet face. Finishing them, the Weaver says, would be easy, and would end the heaven. It will be done if every one of them asks, one by one, face to face. The Weaver doubts they will, and calls that the finest thing about them.

choices.text: Carry the Weaver answer back to the hall

effects.log: You carry it. {npc} listens, and is silent a long time, and then laughs a clear laugh, once, and asks for a chisel.

choices.text: Keep the Weaver word to yourself for now

effects.log: The hall waits for an answer you do not give. It is a hard silence to live in.

events.text: Under the Leaver rule, the hall is full of a quiet, odd joy. Figures begin to finish themselves, a line at a time. A one-armed carter grows a second arm of rough wood and is delighted by it. The workshop hums. The Finishers, grumbling, bring their own tools. {npc} stands in the middle of it all, a half-made smile on {his} half-made face.

choices.text: Offer to make the first stroke of a door on the house

effects.log: You carve a small door frame. The house sighs and opens, and a smell of bread comes out.

choices.text: Sit and watch them make themselves

effects.log: It is the best afternoon you have ever spent.

events.text: Years later a message arrives at your shrine, written in a mixed hand, half neat and half scrawl: the hall is finished, or finishing, and the seal has a mark on it now. {npc} has signed it. {He} asks you to come, not as a god, but as a guest, to a feast in a house that has a door.

choices.text: Go to the feast

effects.log: You go, and are fed with strange, wonderful, half-cooked dishes. {npc} is almost complete now. The part that is not is the part {he} chose.
