choices.text: Send a gift of a good chisel

effects.log: The chisel arrives. {npc} writes back that it is the best tool in the hall.

events.text: A sealed heaven hums behind a door marked simply POST. Beyond it: an enormous sorting-hall, with clerks made of folded paper and tied with string, sorting through mountains of prayers that never found a god. Each clerk is faint and busy and mild. A sign says QUIET, PLEASE. THE UNDELIVERED ARE SLEEPING.

choices.text: Ask to see the Postmaster

effects.log: A clerk of folded vellum leads you through the hall on soft feet. It is a long walk, and the air smells of old ink.

choices.text: Open a drawer at random and read a prayer

effects.log: It reads: please keep my brother safe. There is no address. It is warm.

choices.text: Leave the hall to its sorting

effects.log: You back out, quietly, and close the door gently. The clerks do not look up.

events.text: The Postmaster is a tall figure of folded cloth, tired and kind. The hall is in trouble: for centuries the clerks have delivered prayers by guess to any god they could reach, and the gods, in their pride, have returned the mail marked WRONG DOMAIN. Now the clerks are deciding whether to deliver at all.

choices.text: Offer to deliver a stack yourself

effects.log: The Postmaster hands over a bundle the size of a loaf. They are all for the same unreachable god. You are asked to read them first.

choices.text: Offer to speak for the clerks at the courts

effects.log: The Postmaster bows. Their grievance, drafted, takes eleven pages and is courteous throughout.

events.text: The drawers are full of such lines, each a person in a bad hour: please let the rain come, please let her forget, please let me be forgiven. The clerks do not read them, they only sort. But one clerk whispers that sometimes, at night, a drawer glows when a prayer in it is answered by chance, and the clerk feels it as a warmth.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to show you a warm drawer

effects.log: It is a little drawer by the stair. In it are forty prayers for a good harvest, all answered by a lucky season. The clerk glows faintly.

choices.text: Close the drawer, and think about it

effects.log: You think about it all the way back to your own shrine, and then some.

events.text: You deliver the bundle to the god it was meant for, who turns out to be a god of lost things, asleep under a tree and quite forgotten. The prayers fall into their lap, and the god wakes. They read through the whole bundle, weeping, and then say they have a great deal of catching up to do.

choices.text: Stay to help them answer

effects.log: You help for a month. The god is slow and tender, and a great many lost things find their way home that season.

choices.text: Leave them to it, and return to the Post

effects.log: The Postmaster hears the news with a cloth smile. A new drawer is labelled for the god.

events.text: The courts hear the clerks grievance, and rule it a scandal. A new office is set up: the Bureau of Right Address, staffed by gods who have to read the letters. It lasts nine years. It is deeply unpopular. The Dead-Letter Heaven receives a seal of recognition and begins, cautiously, to deliver.

choices.text: Serve on the Bureau for a season

effects.log: You read letters at a long desk. It is the most useful season you have ever had.

choices.text: Send the clerks a basket of good paper

effects.log: The clerks fold themselves into a hundred small bows. The paper is used for a thousand answers.

events.text: In a collapsed vault of a god of kept promises there stands a bronze lamp with a wick that never burns down. Anyone who lights it sees, in the flame, the face of someone they once promised something to. The vault note says only: it asks for a memory in exchange. It does not say which.

choices.text: Light it

effects.log: The flame leaps, and in it you see a face you have not seen in a long time. It says nothing. It looks at you as you were.

choices.text: Read the vault note again, slowly

effects.log: You find a faint line below the first: the lamp takes the memory of the promise itself.

choices.text: Leave it where it stands

effects.log: A lamp that remembers is better left in the dark. You go out, and the flame, unlit, seems to follow you with a look.

events.text: The face tells you what you promised: a small thing, an offering, a visit. You did not do it. The flame holds the face, and holds the debt. You feel the first memory go: the sound of the promise, the day you made it. It leaves quietly. You know, afterwards, only that you owed something.

choices.text: Carry out the promise now, from the little you know

effects.log: You go to the place and make a small offering, and the flame dims, satisfied.

choices.text: Blow out the lamp before it takes more

effects.log: The flame wavers, and gutters, and goes dark. You feel the lack, like a missing tooth.

events.text: You work out what the lamp will take. It does not take the person; it takes the promise, and with it the weight. Anyone who lights it forgets a debt, the debt stays, and the one owed is left to carry it alone. The lamp is a machine for letting go, and for leaving behind.

choices.text: Light it anyway, and visit the one owed

effects.log: You light it and look at the face a long time. Then you go to them, with what you remember and with what you do not.

choices.text: Take the note out to the Hall to be filed

effects.log: The Silent Hall files it under Hazards. The lamp is put in a cabinet with a second lock.

events.text: You find the one you owed: an old shrine-keeper, long past asking for anything. They remember, perfectly, what you promised. They have been waiting for it with no bitterness at all. You do the thing you owed, in full, and they sit with you in the sun, and the debt becomes a pleasure.

choices.text: Stay a while and keep them company

effects.log: You stay the afternoon and into the evening. The lamp, in your coat, is cool and small.

choices.text: Return the lamp to its vault with thanks

effects.log: You set it back on its stand. It is an honest relic, and you did not want to be unkind to it.

events.text: Over the years you notice the gaps. A name that will not come. A road you cannot place. A kindness you have no memory of doing but whose thanks come in the post. The lamp took more than the promise, and is slow, and gentle, and hungry. You keep it dark now. The gaps do not close.

choices.text: Write down what you can recall, to anchor it

effects.log: You write a book of remembered things. It is shorter than you hoped, and truer.

choices.text: Learn to live with the gaps

effects.log: You grow used to it. Memory, you decide, is partly a kindness one pays to others.

events.text: You hire on as a plain hand in the kitchens of Hwarin of the First Hearth, in a coat that has seen better days. The head cook, {npc}, glances at your hands and then at your face and says that you will do for the pots, and not to touch anything that glows. The kitchens run ten thousand fires and not one is ever quite out.
events.arc: A Hired Hand in the Kitchens of the First Hearth

choices.text: Scrub the pots without comment

effects.log: You scrub. The work is honest and very hot, and you like it more than you expected.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the glowing things are

effects.log: {npc} snorts. {He} says they are the old gods of cooking, left to rest in the coals, and that you are not to wake them.

choices.text: Peel a hundred roots in silence

effects.log: The roots are grey and knotty. You learn a great deal about them in an afternoon.

events.text: A feast is coming and the kitchen is a roar. The head cook is short of hands, and a sauce is turning. {npc} holds out a spoon, glaring. {He} says that you have the look of someone who tastes things. You are, apparently, promoted.
events.arc: A Hired Hand in the Kitchens of the First Hearth

choices.text: Taste the sauce, and say what it needs

effects.log: It needs salt, and smoke, and a half-spoon of patience. {npc} stares at you, then at the pot, then adds all three.

choices.text: Refuse the spoon, and keep to your pots

effects.log: {npc} shrugs. The sauce is fine. It is fine, but it is not what it could be, and both of you know it.

events.text: {npc} shows you one of the glowing things: a small, patient ember in a clay cup, warm as an animal. It is the god of the first egg boiled, {he} says, and it has been boiling for eleven thousand years. It is very old and very happy. The kitchen runs on its good humour.
events.arc: A Hired Hand in the Kitchens of the First Hearth

choices.text: Add a pinch of salt to its cup, reverently

effects.log: The ember pulses, delighted. {npc} watches, and for the first time looks at you with something like respect.

choices.text: Bow to it, and go back to your pots

effects.log: You bow. It is a small, true gesture, and you feel it all the way to your toes.

events.text: The feast is served, and Hwarin tastes the sauce, and sets down the spoon. There is a pause. Then the goddess of the First Hearth rises and asks for the cook of the sauce. {npc} pulls you forward by the sleeve, grinning like a boy, and says: it is the new hand. You have been found out, or you have found yourself.
events.arc: A Hired Hand in the Kitchens of the First Hearth

choices.text: Take off your hat, and give your name

effects.log: Hwarin laughs aloud. The kitchens roar. {npc} is stricken for a moment, then crows louder than anyone.

choices.text: Bow, and say you are only a hand

effects.log: Hwarin raises a cup, and the hall drinks to the new hand. You keep your hat on.

events.text: You keep the job for a season more, and then must go. {npc} sends you off with a small pot of the sauce and a rule: you may come back to any kitchen in any domain, so long as you scrub the pots. {He} does not ask your name, and does not need to. The pot, it turns out, never quite empties.
events.arc: A Hired Hand in the Kitchens of the First Hearth

choices.text: Take the pot to your own shrine

effects.log: It becomes the ritual dish of your feast days. It is always slightly wrong, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Leave the pot at the kitchen door, as thanks

effects.log: The pot is found by a scullion, who tastes it, and weeps.

events.text: Reedmere, a valley of reed-beds and slow water, has had no rain for a season. The clouds gather over it and move on. {npc}, the reed-warden, is out of patience and out of reeds. {He} lays out the suspects: a cloud-herder in the next valley, a small god of drought newly arrived, and a heron that has taken to sitting on the weather-stone.
events.arc: Who Stole the Rain at Reedmere

choices.text: Examine the weather-stone

effects.log: The stone is cold and dry, with a rim of worn grooves. Someone has been rubbing it with a cloth.

choices.text: Question the cloud-herder in the next valley

effects.log: The cloud-herder is weather-beaten, huffy and entirely unhelpful. {npc} watches you from the road.

choices.text: Walk the valley and listen

effects.log: The reeds whisper. The water is low, and old, and very quiet.

events.text: The stone has been rubbed by someone who wanted it clean: and under the grime is a name, scratched deep, that is not the god of Reedmere. It is a name from a distant valley. The heron, meanwhile, turns out to have been sitting there to keep something warm. {npc} has gone quiet.
events.arc: Who Stole the Rain at Reedmere

choices.text: Follow the name to the distant valley

effects.log: The trail goes through two passes. At the end is a small, wet, roadless hollow where a stranger is bailing water into a ditch.

choices.text: Question the heron

effects.log: The heron looks at you and shifts. Under its wing is a clay jar, sealed, damp, and cold as deep water.

events.text: The cloud-herder swears the clouds are not theirs to hold. They accuse the god of drought, who is new and sulky. You accuse the god of drought in a public meeting. The god is humiliated, the valley is delighted, and nothing changes. The god says, pale, that it does not even like the dry.
events.arc: Who Stole the Rain at Reedmere

choices.text: Apologise to the god of drought

effects.log: The god accepts with the dignity of a child who has been in the wrong room. {npc} looks at the ground.

choices.text: Double down, and demand an answer

effects.log: The valley goes quiet. You are not enjoying yourself.

events.text: The stranger in the hollow is bailing water into a ditch because the ditch leads to a hidden field of seedlings, a nursery of rare reeds, and the stranger has been rationing the stolen rain to keep them alive. They did not know it was the whole valley rain. They thought it was a stream that no one wanted.
events.arc: Who Stole the Rain at Reedmere

choices.text: Show the stranger how to take only a share

effects.log: You mark a line in the ditch. The stranger nods, shamed, and the rain begins at once to fall on Reedmere.

choices.text: Let the stranger keep the nursery, and share the rain

effects.log: You arrange a split. The nursery survives, and so does Reedmere, with a little less.

events.text: Inside the jar is a spoonful of cold, deep rain, a seed of storm that someone has been rocking and keeping warm. The heron sat on the weather-stone to hatch it. When you break the seal the clouds roll in at once and the valley greets the rain with wet, happy cheers. {npc} laughs until {he} cries.
events.arc: Who Stole the Rain at Reedmere

choices.text: Thank the heron, and make it the valley guardian

effects.log: The heron takes the honour with a flap of one wing. Reedmere has a god of rain at last, a tall grey bird.

choices.text: Let the heron decide what to do with it

effects.log: The heron rocks the empty jar for a while, and then drops it in the water. The reeds sing.

events.text: You return to the stone, and the god of drought, who has not forgiven you, tells you in a voice like gravel that the rain was taken three nights before it came to them. {npc} stands with the stone cloth in {his} hand, a rag that belongs to {him}. {He} had been cleaning the stone to see the name. {He} wants you to go away.
events.arc: Who Stole the Rain at Reedmere

choices.text: Go, and come back once the valley has had time

effects.log: You leave. The rain falls on the third night, and it is not a stolen rain, and it is not a gift. It is simply weather.

choices.text: Stay and help {him} find the real trail

effects.log: You return to the stone and begin again, more humble.

events.text: A white crane has begun to stand in the east of a high valley, wings spread, at the moment dawn should come. When it stands there, dawn is late. By an hour on the first day, and by half a morning on the third. The farmers wake in the dark and do not know it is day. The Sky domain wants it bound, or worse.

choices.text: Go up before dawn and watch the crane

effects.log: You watch it from a ledge. It stands in the dark with its wings out, and does not blink.

choices.text: Call out to the crane from below

effects.log: The crane turns its head slowly. It does not answer, but it holds your gaze until the sky greys.

choices.text: Consult the Sky domain about the delay

effects.log: Cheonho says that the dawn is late, and is in no hurry to say why.

events.text: The crane holds dawn because it is carrying it. In its wings, folded tight, it has a small, tired sun, and the sun has been getting heavier. It is spreading its wings to let the sun breathe. Without the crane the dawn would not rise at all, and the Sky domain has not noticed that its own lamp is dying.

choices.text: Help the crane hold the sun

effects.log: You lift a wing, and the sun is heavy as a stone and gentle as a bird. You hold it for an hour. The dawn comes on time.

choices.text: Warn the Sky domain that the lamp is failing

effects.log: Cheonho listens, long and quiet. A new lamp is ordered, and an old one honoured.

events.text: The crane lets you come close, and you see what it holds. It is not frightened of you. It is relieved. It looks at you with the patience of a creature that has been asked to do something enormous and has not been thanked, and it lowers its neck, and offers you the weight.

choices.text: Take the sun from it for a morning

effects.log: You take the weight. The crane flies to a stream and drinks and drinks. When it comes back, it is a different bird.

choices.text: Bind the crane and bring it to the Sky domain

effects.log: The crane bows its head to the cord, and the Sky domain unbinds it at once, aghast.

events.text: You and the crane make an arrangement. You hold the sun on the first morning of each month, and the crane rests. The valley has dawn on time, and a long habit of waking, and a story they tell their children about a crane and a god. The arrangement lasts until the Sky domain finds a better answer.

choices.text: Keep the arrangement for a year

effects.log: It is a strange, good year. The crane grows sleek and bright.

choices.text: Hand the monthly duty to a young shrine-keeper

effects.log: The keeper does well, and in time the crane takes the keeper for a mate.

events.text: The Sky domain sends a new lamp for the high valley, a gold one hung on a pole at the eastern gate. The crane watches it being lit. Then it folds its wings, lets the old sun go up by itself, and sleeps on one leg for nine days. When it wakes it flies off east, and the valley says it has gone home.

choices.text: Leave a long white feather on the gate in thanks

effects.log: It is the best feather you own. The lamp burns brighter by it.

choices.text: Say a prayer, and let it be

effects.log: Nine days is a long time to sleep. You hope the dreams are kind.

events.text: A fissure on the north face of Daeak mountain breathes out a slow warm wind that smells of snow and stone. The shrine-keepers say nothing lives in it. They say it too quickly. At night the whole slope hums, one low note, as though something were counting the beats of a very long breath.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Climb into the fissure with a lamp

effects.log: The fissure runs down in steps like a stair, and the walls are smooth, and the hum grows louder.

choices.text: Listen at the lip of the fissure for a night

effects.log: You lie with your ear to the stone. In the long dark, you learn the rhythm: nine beats, a pause, nine beats.

choices.text: Ask Daeak about the hum

effects.log: Daeak is silent for a long time. When he answers it is to say: do not wake them.

events.text: At the foot of the stair is a vast cavern, and in it, curled in rows, the sleepers: mountain-beasts the size of hills, each with a skin of moss and a drift of snow. They are the old guardians of the range, asleep since the domains were cut. A narrow ledge crosses above them to a door.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Cross the ledge to the door

ok.log: The ledge is slick and the drop is long, but your feet find the stone. You reach the door and rest against it, trembling and thrilled.

fail.log: The ledge crumbles under your boot and you slide toward a sleeper breath, hot and slow. You catch a root, but not before you are half buried in moss.
fail.deathCause: a fall among the sleepers of the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Go back up and leave them to sleep

effects.log: You climb out in the grey light. The slope hums as you go, softly, as if in thanks.

events.text: The hum is a lullaby. The mountain sings it to its sleepers, and has done since before names, and the song has grown tired. One verse has been dropped. The sleepers are stirring in their sleep, a rumble, a shifting of moss. If the song is not finished they will wake, hungry and confused.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Sing the missing verse, as you guess it

effects.log: You sing it badly. The mountain accepts it, and the hum settles. A sleeper rolls over and sighs.

choices.text: Go to Daeak, and ask him to sing it

effects.log: Daeak, huge and slow, sings the verse in a voice like a cliff-face clearing its throat. The hum becomes whole.

events.text: Behind the door lies a small chamber, round and warm, with a single stone seat and a bowl of water on a ledge. A voice, old as the rock, says without moving: you came all this way to see me? I am only the one who holds the song. The singer. The last of the lullaby-keepers, and very tired.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Offer to learn the song, and share the keeping

effects.log: The singer teaches you the verse, slowly, a line a day. You learn all of it by midwinter. The mountain, you feel, shifts with relief.

choices.text: Sit quietly with the singer, and leave at dawn

effects.log: You sit till the light comes down the stair. The singer says nothing more, and neither do you.

events.text: The mountain is quiet now. The hum goes on, a soft, regular note that the shrine-keepers have started to call good weather. Daeak sends you a small stone from the foot of the peak, round as an egg. In it, if you hold it to your ear, you can hear nine beats, a pause, and nine beats.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Keep the stone at your shrine

effects.log: It makes the pilgrims sleep well. A few of them dream of snow.

choices.text: Return the stone to the fissure one night a year

effects.log: You make the climb, and set it down on the first step. The hum answers.

events.text: You climb out into the grey, and the hum follows you to the shoulder of the mountain. The shrine-keepers are waiting with a flask. They ask nothing. Later, one of them mentions that the old keepers used to leave a lamp at the lip of the fissure, and that nobody remembers why.
events.arc: The Sleepers Under the Unmoving Peak

choices.text: Leave a lamp at the lip, and keep it lit

effects.log: The lamp burns through the winter. The hum, you think, is a little softer.

choices.text: Tell the keepers what you saw

effects.log: They listen, pale, and decide to leave the lamp. It is the right decision.

events.text: Pungnyeon sealed the Granary Heaven in a bad year, to keep the seed-corn safe, and forgot about it. Behind a door of straw you find a republic of mice, a thousand strong, in a hall of stacked sacks. They have a constitution, a parliament and a hereditary treasurer. They call you Honoured Visitor and ask, politely, whether you have come to collect the rent.

choices.text: Ask what the rent is

effects.log: The Speaker says it is one harvest, repaid in full, on the day Pungnyeon returns. They have been saving for four hundred years.

choices.text: Ask to see the parliament

effects.log: You sit in the gallery on a stack of sacks. The debate is on whether a bean is a vegetable. It has been going for a decade.

choices.text: Admire the sacks and leave a pinch of seed

effects.log: The mice give you a small round of applause. It is a very small round.

events.text: The republic is in a crisis. The corn the mice have been guarding is almost the last. The treasurer wants to sell the seed to buy security. The Speaker wants to plant it, and risk the winter. Neither has asked Pungnyeon. Both ask you to speak at the Great Moot, on the eve of the vote.

choices.text: Speak for planting

effects.log: The hall listens, whiskers still. The vote is close, and the Speaker wins it by a single squeak.

choices.text: Speak for keeping the seed

effects.log: The treasurer is flushed with relief. The hall votes to hold, by a landslide, with sighs.

events.text: The debate on the bean, it turns out, hides a real quarrel: who owns what grows in the sacks. The Honoured Visitor, a title the mice take seriously, is asked to settle it. You settle it badly, and with great ceremony. The mice are satisfied. They have never been so honoured in their lives.

choices.text: Decree that all beans are vegetables, and all mice are guests

effects.log: The hall cheers. The decree is carved over the door, in grain, and lasts for a hundred years.

choices.text: Admit that you do not know, and ask them to keep arguing

effects.log: The mice take this as the wisest answer. The debate carries on, and it is much happier.

events.text: The mice plant the seed-corn in a corner of the hall, where Pungnyeon old light still leaks through the door. It sprouts, thin and green, and then thick. In a season the Granary Heaven has its own small golden field, and the first real bread in four centuries. The Speaker weeps. The treasurer tries the bread, and says it is acceptable.

choices.text: Send word to Pungnyeon

effects.log: The Harvest goddess comes in a plain apron, and sits among the mice, and is given the rent in full. She does not say a word for an hour.

choices.text: Eat a slice of the first bread

effects.log: It is sweet and dense and tastes of four hundred years of patience.

events.text: The seed is kept, and the republic persists, in its small and careful way. Every few decades a mouse messenger comes up to your shrine with a basket of grain and a letter that says, in tiny hand: we are still here. We are still keeping it. Please remember us. You do.

choices.text: Send back a basket of your own

effects.log: The basket goes in at the straw door. The mice cheer, and the parliament adjourns for a week.

choices.text: Write a short note, and sign it

effects.log: The note is hung over the Speaker chair. The Speaker reads it every morning.

events.text: A horn sounds across a dark valley, a long note, answered by another. It is the hunt of a god you do not know, in a domain you do not know, for a quarry nobody names. The horn is lovely. Everything in the wood stops to hear it, and then, as one, goes still, waiting to see who it is for.

choices.text: Stay still with the wood, and let the hunt pass

effects.log: The hunt goes by in the dark, a river of hooves. When it is gone, the wood breathes again. You are not the quarry.

choices.text: Blow a note of your own, softly, in reply

effects.log: The horn answers. A hunter you will never meet salutes you from a ridge, and rides on.

events.text: A pack of divine hounds sweeps through your domain at noon, noses down, tongues out, on a scent that crosses every field. They do not bark. They do not stop. At the end of the pack runs a small old hound with a limp, and a very serious expression, bringing up the rear and looking as though it knows the way.

choices.text: Fall in behind the old hound

effects.log: You follow it, and it leads you three miles to a lost lamb in a ditch. The pack was not hunting. It was rescuing.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of water at the roadside

effects.log: The old hound stops, drinks, and nods to you before it hurries on.

events.text: You come across a snare of divine cord strung between two pines, tight and expertly made. It is not for any beast. A small tag reads, in a neat hand: set by the Wardens of the Green Assembly, to keep poachers out of the old stag grove. Beneath it, in another hand: and also to make the wardens feel useful.

choices.text: Spring the snare with a stick, for the poachers

effects.log: The cord snaps with a crack that echoes. A warden shouts from the hill, and you wave, grinning.

choices.text: Leave a note of thanks beside the tag

effects.log: A warden finds it next day and treasures it.

events.text: The tracks of a very large beast run in a circle round a lone standing stone, over and over, deepening each time. The stone has a groove at the base the shape of a hoof. Whatever made the tracks has been walking this circle for years. You cannot tell if it is guarding or grieving.

choices.text: Walk the circle yourself, once, with respect

effects.log: The ground is warm. When you complete the round, a faint low sound, like a sigh, rises from the stone.

choices.text: Leave a handful of grain at the base of the stone

effects.log: In the morning the grain is gone, and the tracks run one step wider.

events.text: A seal on a sealed heaven has been mended, recently, with gold in the cracks. The wardens insist they have not touched it. Close up you can see that the gold is the cleverest thing you have ever seen: a pattern of tiny roots that holds each crack shut, and grows, very slowly, into the stone.

choices.text: Press your palm to the gold

effects.log: It is warm, and slightly alive. A faint voice inside the seal says: please, not yet.

choices.text: Leave a coin of faith in the groove

effects.log: The coin sinks into the seal and is gone. You have, it seems, paid for something.

events.text: Two wardens sit on either side of a sealed door and have been playing the same quiet game of stones for ninety years. Neither remembers which of them is winning. Neither wants to look. They ask you, a passing god, to count the stones and tell them only whether the game has ended.

choices.text: Count them, and tell them it is a draw

effects.log: They look at each other, and laugh, and shake hands across the board. The game begins again at once.

choices.text: Say it is not over yet, and leave them to it

effects.log: They look relieved. You would be too.

events.text: Through a crack in a sealed heaven comes the sound of a flute, thin and sweet, playing the same sixteen notes. Something inside has been practising for a very long time. The wardens say it is getting better. They have not told it so, for fear of ruining it.

choices.text: Whistle the notes back, one by one

effects.log: The flute pauses, then plays the notes again, slightly changed. You have begun a conversation.

choices.text: Listen at the crack until it finishes

effects.log: It plays a seventeenth note, new, and falls silent. You would swear it was proud.

events.text: Behind a door in a fallen vault is a counter, a bell and a sleeping clerk. On shelves behind him are the relics of gods who pawned them in a bad year: a crown, a net, a flute, a lock. Each has a ticket tied to it. The tickets are all dated, and all unredeemed, and the clerk is still being paid by someone.

choices.text: Redeem one ticket for a small, sad relic

effects.log: The clerk wakes, checks the date, and hands it over with a yawn. It is a little copper bell, and when you ring it, a distant god looks up.

choices.text: Leave a coin on the counter and go

effects.log: The clerk sleeps on. The coin sits there like a prayer.

events.text: Among the ruins of a banquet hall of a fallen god lies a cup that has never been empty. It is full of something grey and still. The inscription on the foot reads: drink, and be sure of one thing. It does not say which thing.

choices.text: Drink from the cup

ok.log: The grey liquid is clear and cold. You become sure, quite calmly, that you are exactly where you should be, and the feeling lasts a week.

fail.log: The liquid is thick and cold and does not agree with you. You are sure, for a week, of an unhappy thing, and the certainty lingers like damp.
fail.deathCause: a certainty from a fallen god cup

choices.text: Pour it out on the floor and keep the cup

effects.log: The floor drinks it with a hiss. The cup, light as a bowl, becomes a small plain dish at your shrine.

events.text: In a burned shrine you hear a choir, faint, rehearsing. The voices are those of worshippers long gone, singing the same hymn they sang on the last night. The hymn ends abruptly, mid-line, at the moment the fire reached the roof. Then it begins again, and they sing it right up to that line, and stop.

choices.text: Sing the next line aloud

effects.log: You sing it. The choir pauses, and then, for the first time in an age, finishes the hymn. The ash settles like a held breath let out.

choices.text: Stand in the doorway and listen

effects.log: They sing it three times. On the third, the choir seems to notice you, and sings a little louder.

events.text: A scorched tree stands in the court of a burned shrine, black to the root. On one branch a single green leaf has opened. The shrine-keeper, who is eighty, tells you it opens every year on the anniversary of the fire, and by evening has gone. He asks if a god might help it stay.

choices.text: Give the leaf a breath of life

effects.log: The leaf trembles, and holds. By spring there are three.

choices.text: Sit with the keeper, and watch the leaf together

effects.log: It lasts until sundown, as always. He thanks you for staying anyway.

events.text: You find the first river, the one the others were copied from, a narrow bright line in a bare valley, running without a source or a sea. It is all middle, with no ends. The water is cold and tastes of beginnings. You cannot tell which way it flows, and neither, you suspect, can it.

choices.text: Follow it a day downstream, or upstream

effects.log: You walk until you are tired, and look back, and you are exactly where you began. It is a gentle, lovely trick.

choices.text: Fill a flask and carry it home

effects.log: The water in the flask never warms. You use it, sparingly, to start new things.

events.text: In a primal clay-bed there are handprints in the mud, hundreds, all pointing up, as though a crowd had once reached for something and been turned to stone. The prints are small and large and some are split five ways and some two. Something wanted very much, here, to be held.

choices.text: Press your own hand into a print, gently

effects.log: The clay is warm. For a breath you feel a hundred small hands in yours.

choices.text: Leave an offering at the edge of the bed

effects.log: A little faith, a little bread. It is not much. It is, you suppose, a hand.

events.text: In Pungnyeon fields at reaping, a stranger in a plain coat is binding sheaves alongside the others. The reapers do not look twice. At noon, the stranger sits with them in the shade, shares the bread and the water, and listens to the old stories. You realise who it is, and say nothing, and tie a sheaf.

choices.text: Work beside the stranger until sunset

effects.log: The sheaves pile up. At the last, the stranger nods to you once, and you nod back, two gods in plain coats, and neither says a word.

choices.text: Leave them to their work, and go quietly

effects.log: There are some things a god should do alone. You admire the stranger and go.

events.text: In the Silent Hall domain a vigil is kept every night for the dead who have no one to keep it for them. A plain lamp, a plain chair, a pot of tea going cold. The attendant says anyone may sit. Tonight there is only one lamp lit and one chair empty. You are invited, without a word, to take it.

choices.text: Sit the vigil until dawn

effects.log: You sit. The lamp burns low and steady. At dawn the attendant bows, and you walk out with a stillness you cannot explain.

choices.text: Light a second lamp, and leave it burning

effects.log: The attendant nods, and sets your lamp beside the first. It burns well into the next day.

events.text: On a dream-path you find a pillow lying in the road, perfectly white, with a dent in it from a vanished head. It is warm. Whoever slept here got up in a hurry and left the dream behind. A faint voice from the cloth is still talking, and it is asking, very reasonably, to be woken.

choices.text: Pat the pillow and say good morning

effects.log: The pillow sighs and fades. Somewhere a sleeper wakes, rested, and does not remember why.

choices.text: Carry the pillow back to the dreamer

effects.log: You follow a thread of warmth to a small house at the edge of the path. The sleeper takes the pillow with a murmur, and sinks back in.

events.text: A moth the colour of old paper lands on your sleeve and will not leave. It is a dream-moth, and it has fed on a thousand sleepers, and it is looking for a dream to carry. It trembles on your arm, hopeful. You have not slept in a month. You are a poor host, but you are the nearest.

choices.text: Let it feed on a dream of your own

effects.log: The moth takes a small bright dream of a river, and flies away glowing. You sleep, at last, like a stone.

choices.text: Brush it gently toward a better sleeper

effects.log: The moth flutters off toward a window where someone is dreaming loudly. It will be happy there.

events.text: A comet passes through the Sky domain once in a hundred years, trailing a long white veil of dust. The astronomers argue about its name. A child at a shrine door has decided it is called Gram, for no reason, and refuses to be talked out of it. The comet, as far as anyone can tell, is not displeased.

choices.text: Write Gram into the star-registry, quietly

effects.log: The registry takes it without complaint. The child will be told when she is old.

choices.text: Wave to the comet from your shrine roof

effects.log: You wave. The tail flickers, and you decide, for a good evening, that this means hello.

events.text: A ladder of lit rungs hangs from a gap in the Sky, ending at the top of a mountain. A sign says: CLIMB IF YOU ARE SURE. Nobody has been sure yet. The rungs are warm and a little ticklish. Some pilgrims stand on the lowest and bounce, a hand-span off the ground, and come down laughing.

choices.text: Climb ten rungs and look about

ok.log: You reach the tenth rung and see the whole domain laid out under you, bright as a map. You come down with a head full of colour.

fail.log: A rung gives way under you and you drop into a snowdrift, unhurt but sorry. The ladder rings with what sounds like laughter.

choices.text: Bounce on the lowest rung with the pilgrims

effects.log: It is fun, and not at all dignified. The pilgrims love you for it.

events.text: A footprint lies at the bottom of a ravine, a hundred paces long, of a creature that was either a god or a mountain walking. Water has gathered in it, and in the water a whole small world has formed: a pond, a heron, a field of reeds. The creature has gone on. The print is now a home.

choices.text: Stand in the print and listen

effects.log: The water is still. You feel, for a breath, the whole step of whatever made it, passing like a slow tide.

choices.text: Add a few seeds to the pond for the heron

effects.log: The heron looks at the seeds, and at you, and goes on fishing.

events.text: A cat sits on the wall by the gate of a minor shrine and has done for longer than anyone can remember. It is not a god. It is not a spirit. It is, the keeper insists, only a cat. But every pilgrim who passes it comes away a little lighter, and the cat seems to know which one needs the most.

choices.text: Scratch behind its ear, and go on

effects.log: It purrs. A weight you did not know you carried slips off.

choices.text: Leave a saucer of milk by the gate

effects.log: The cat drinks, with an air of doing you a great favour. The keeper beams.

events.text: A stone bridge in the Mountains domain is older than the road it crosses. Its keystone bears a god name that has been worn nearly to nothing by hands. Travellers touch it for luck. You touch it too, and the stone says, in a small gravelly voice: oh, that is nice. Do that again.

choices.text: Touch it again, and ask its name

effects.log: The stone tells you the name, slowly, a syllable at a time. It is a lovely, simple name, and you will not forget it.

choices.text: Wipe the moss from the keystone

effects.log: The stone sighs. By dusk it has grown a little new moss, as a thanks.

events.text: A trout in a mountain stream wears a tiny bronze bell on a cord round its gill, and rings it whenever it passes a shrine. Nobody put it there. The bell is older than the shrine. Some say it is the last of a school of bell-fish that once warned of floods. It rings, now, only for the polite.

choices.text: Bow to the trout as it passes

effects.log: It rings, once, and swims on with great dignity.

choices.text: Put a flower in the water for it

effects.log: The trout rises, takes the stem in its mouth for a moment, and lets it go.

events.text: You arrive in a domain that is new to you, and the first thing you see is a signpost that is wrong. It points to the sea, and the sea is behind you. A boy sits under it eating a pear. He says he turned it himself, last night, for a joke. He asks if the god will turn it back. He has not recognised you.

choices.text: Turn it back, and give the boy a coin of faith

effects.log: The boy grins and bites his pear. He has not the faintest idea what he was given, and is quite delighted.

choices.text: Leave it pointing at the sea

effects.log: It points at the sea, a joke at the entrance of a domain. Travellers laugh as they go in.

events.text: A neighbouring god sends you a gift: a pot of pickled plums, wrapped in six layers of cloth, with a card that says "for a warm friendship". The plums are perfectly good. The card is covered in an apologetic hand-wringing, line after line: it is not much, please do not feel obliged, they may be too sour. You have never met this god.

choices.text: Send back a small gift of your own

effects.log: You send honey. The neighbour sends back apologies for the plums, and the beginning of a friendship.

choices.text: Eat a plum and write a kind note

effects.log: They are not too sour. You say so. The neighbour sends a second pot.

events.text: At the edge of the Sea domain hangs a pocket of light where it is always the middle of an afternoon. It is the remnant of the Domain of the Fine Afternoon, which a god named Gwaeil held from dawn to dusk of a single day before the court dissolved it. Nobody will say why. The pocket has been warm for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Step into the afternoon

effects.log: The light is gold and does not move. Your shadow lies exactly where it lay when you stepped in, and stays there.

choices.text: Ask the court archivists why it was dissolved

effects.log: The archivists grow suddenly busy with their sleeves. One of them points, without looking, at a shelf nobody dusts.

choices.text: Leave a cup of cool water at the edge

effects.log: You set it down in the warm light. It does not cool and it does not warm. It simply waits.

events.text: Inside, a meadow of small folk keeps a festival that has not ended: they were worshippers of Gwaeil for one day, and no day came after. They hold hands in rings, sing the one hymn they know, and look up at you with open delight. Nobody has visited since the first dusk that never came.

choices.text: Join the ring and sing the hymn

effects.log: The hymn has only three lines. You learn them in a minute, and the ring closes round you as if you had always been missing from it.

choices.text: Count them quietly, house by house

effects.log: There are three hundred and eleven. You write the number on your sleeve in ash, as a promise to someone.

events.text: The archivists admit it, in the end. Gwaeil's afternoon was so pleasant that the morning gods and the evening gods both lost worshippers by lunchtime. The court voted by acclamation, in a hurry, and sealed the minutes. A very old clerk offers to unseal them if you will carry the blame for it.

choices.text: Take the blame and ask for the minutes

effects.log: The clerk hands over a roll tied with blue cord. It is lighter than it looks.

choices.text: Let the matter lie in its shelf

effects.log: The clerk looks at once relieved and sorry. The shelf stays undusted.

events.text: At dusk of a day that never reaches dusk, the elder of the meadow takes your hand. They ask nothing for themselves. They ask whether the afternoon might, just once, be allowed to end, so that they can find out what comes after a festival. They have wondered for nine thousand years.

choices.text: Let the afternoon end, gently

effects.log: The light lowers by slow degrees. Stars come out over the meadow, and the folk gasp as at a gift. By morning there is a morning, and they are not afraid of it.

choices.text: Promise to return each year for the festival

effects.log: You promise, and the ring cheers. The afternoon stays. Every year you bring something from the evening for them to wonder at.

events.text: The minutes are short. The vote to dissolve the Fine Afternoon was carried, and under it, in Cheonho's own careful hand, is a single added line: to be revisited when the other domains have grown less jealous. It has not been revisited. Nobody has remembered to.

choices.text: Bring the line before the court, and ask for the revisit

effects.log: The court is furious and then, slowly, embarrassed. A day is set. The meadow will have its afternoon recognised, one day in every year.

choices.text: Roll the minutes up and tell no one

effects.log: You carry the roll home. It sits on your shelf, a small quiet reproach.

events.text: The count of three hundred and eleven is wrong by one. The three hundred and twelfth is an old god sitting at the edge of the meadow with a cup, who thinks the day is still going well. It is Gwaeil, who was never told he was dissolved, and who has been very happy.

choices.text: Tell Gwaeil the truth

effects.log: He listens, nods, and says that he rather suspected, because the guests never leave. He asks, politely, if he might have a visitor now and then.

choices.text: Let him keep the afternoon as it is

effects.log: You drink his tea. It tastes of something you cannot quite name and dearly want to. You leave without a word.

events.text: There is a vault under the court where the gods are filed who were born and never once prayed to. Each lies asleep on a shelf, a god of something small and particular: the third stair, the smell after a lamp goes out. {npc}, the keeper, is a god of nothing at all, and has been dusting the shelves for a long time. {He} offers you tea.

choices.text: Ask {him} how a god is born with no one to pray

effects.log: Faith, {he} explains, is something a god can be made of or made for. These were made for it, and the prayers never came.

choices.text: Ask to see the oldest shelf

effects.log: {He} leads you down a long aisle to a shelf under a window of grey glass, where the oldest sleepers lie.

choices.text: Accept the tea, and say nothing

effects.log: It is plain tea. {He} seems very glad of someone to pour it for.

events.text: {npc} confesses that {he} has a favourite: a god of the smell after rain on warm slate, asleep for six thousand years and so far unprayed to by anyone. {He} asks whether you would be the first to say the prayer. It can be done in a breath. It is the only thing anyone has asked of you here.

choices.text: Say the prayer aloud

effects.log: The sleeper stirs. A faint smell of rain on warm slate fills the aisle, and {npc} turns away to hide {his} face.

choices.text: Write the prayer, and leave it for them to read

effects.log: You leave it by the sleeper's hand, in a clear careful script, and hope it counts.

events.text: On the oldest shelf the sleepers are older than the domains. A plaque reads: gods made in the first draft, before the cutting of the twelve. They were set aside, not unmade, and filed. One of them has opened an eye.

choices.text: Speak to the one who is awake

effects.log: It looks at you for a long moment, and says only: is it time? You do not know what to answer.

choices.text: Close the shutter on the window, to let them rest

effects.log: The light softens. The eye closes. {npc} lets out a breath {he} has been holding for centuries.

events.text: A year later the sleeper of warm slate is awake. {npc} sends word, trembling: a small god now walks the stair of the archive, scenting the air after every lamp. Pilgrims have begun to come, six, then twenty, to see the first god of the smell of rain who has ever been prayed to.

choices.text: Go and see the small god, and bless the stair

effects.log: The god of the smell after rain sniffs the air, delighted, and holds out a damp hand. {npc} stands behind them, weeping and polishing a rail.

choices.text: Send an offering of warm slate from your own shrine

effects.log: The offering arrives with a note of thanks, written in a very small, wet hand.

events.text: The prayer lies by the sleeper's hand for years. {npc} reads it every dusk, because no one else will. One dusk it is gone, and in its place is a smear of rain on slate. {He} says nothing for a long time and then asks you, very softly, whether it would be wrong to write one for all of them.

choices.text: Help {him} write a prayer for every shelf

effects.log: It takes you a season. Each prayer is three lines. When you finish, the vault smells faintly of a hundred small kinds of weather.

choices.text: Tell {him} it would never be wrong

effects.log: {He} nods and begins, alone, with the nearest shelf.

events.text: The god who woke on the oldest shelf walks out of the archive and is not seen again. {npc} finds only an empty shelf and a note in a script no one can read. In the centre of it, one word has been underlined, and it is your name.

choices.text: Search the domains for the one who woke

effects.log: You do not find them. You find, in six places, a small thing that was not there before: a new kind of dawn, a new kind of quiet.

choices.text: Frame the note, and hang it in the archive

effects.log: {npc} hangs it above the oldest shelf. Visitors ask who the god was, and no one knows.

events.text: A beast is loose in the lowlands that has no body of its own. It is stitched out of a broken oath: a promise made by two gods on a hill and abandoned on the third night. Where it walks, small promises fail. Shepherds forget which gate they closed. Lovers forget what they swore. The valley's shrines have asked for a hunter.

choices.text: Track it by the trail of forgotten gates

effects.log: You follow a line of open gates across the valley, each one swinging gently, none of them yours to close.

choices.text: Find the two gods who made the oath

effects.log: You trace the oath to a hill with two cairns. One god has gone to sleep. The other is still angry.

choices.text: Close one gate, and watch what comes

effects.log: The gate stays shut. For a moment, the whole valley holds still.

events.text: You come on the oath-beast at dusk. It is shaped like a hound made of rope that is always about to come untied, and it looks at you with the same questioning patience as any hound. It cannot hurt you. It can only make you break your word, and it knows it.

choices.text: Swear a small oath and keep it in its sight

ok.log: You swear to hold a gate through the night, and hold it. The beast watches the whole watch, and lies down beside the gate at dawn.

fail.log: Your oath slips by dawn. The beast looks sorrowful and unsurprised.

choices.text: Keep your distance, and throw it a rope of cord

effects.log: It catches the cord in its jaws and worries it, almost happily.

events.text: The angry god on the hill will not unsay the oath, and the sleeping god cannot. Between them the promise hangs unfinished. You are asked to speak for the sleeper. It would mean standing on the hill, saying what you think the sleeper would say, and being wrong in front of a god.

choices.text: Speak for the sleeper, as honestly as you can

effects.log: You say what you would have wanted to say. The angry god listens. At the end, the angry god sits down on the cairn.

choices.text: Ask the angry god to finish the oath alone

effects.log: The angry god glowers. Then, grudgingly, begins to say the second half to the empty hill.

events.text: The beast's rope-body begins to come undone at the ends, thread by thread. In the evening it is a hound's shape of light, and in the morning only a loose cord lying by the gate. The shepherds find their gates remembered. A smell of woodsmoke comes across the valley, as of something kept.

choices.text: Take the cord and hang it in a shrine

effects.log: It is the length of an oath. Pilgrims touch it for luck, and the luck holds more often than not.

choices.text: Leave the cord tied to the gate

effects.log: It stays there for a hundred years. Nobody ever opens that gate by mistake.

events.text: The beast gnaws at your promise all night and by dawn the oath is a pile of loose fibre. The valley's gates swing open again, and the shepherds blame you in loud voices. A lesser god of boundaries offers to take the cord to the Hall to be mended.

choices.text: Hand over the cord

effects.log: The boundary-god carries it away in both hands. Months later the gates stay shut, and no one says why.

choices.text: Mend it yourself, one knot a night

effects.log: It takes a winter, and it holds.

events.text: The two gods finish the oath at last, one half in a whisper and the other half in a snore, and the oath-beast rises from the valley as a small cloud and goes up the hill to lie across both cairns. The shepherds find, years after, that no one in the valley can quite remember a broken promise.

choices.text: Raise a small shrine of two stones between the cairns

effects.log: Pilgrims come to swear oaths there. The shrine keeps a cloud over it all year, a dog-shaped one.

choices.text: Walk home under the cloud

effects.log: It follows you to the edge of the valley and then sits down, looking pleased.

events.text: The angry god finishes the oath alone, in a voice that cracks twice. The sleeper does not stir. But the oath-beast comes undone all the same, and a long cord of light stretches between the hill and the sleeper's cairn, humming, as of two voices after all.

choices.text: Sit by the cairn until the humming stops

effects.log: It stops at dawn. The angry god is crying quietly, and does not mind being seen.

choices.text: Leave them to it, and walk down the hill

effects.log: The humming follows you a mile, and then there is only the wind.

events.text: Before the four pantheons there was a fifth, the Cedar Throne, and it lost a war. Its gods were not unmade; they were laid down in a tomb-heaven with their weapons and their wine, and the door was shut from the outside. A boundary-god mentions, in passing, that the door has been left unlocked for a thousand years by someone's oversight.
events.arc: The Tomb-Heaven of the Cedar Throne

choices.text: Open the door a hand's breadth and listen

effects.log: You hear a banquet. Cups, a harp, low arguing. Nothing like a tomb.

choices.text: Ask the boundary-god who left it unlocked

effects.log: They look at their feet. They think it was someone kind, and quite possibly someone who regretted it.

choices.text: Leave the door as you found it

effects.log: It sways a little in the draught, and settles.

events.text: The Cedar gods are still at their feast. They have been feasting since the war ended, in a hall of cedar pillars, in the pleasant grey light of a day that does not end. They are courteous. They are very, very tired. They ask you what the war was about, because they have forgotten.
events.arc: The Tomb-Heaven of the Cedar Throne

choices.text: Tell them the little you know

effects.log: They listen with the faint polite interest of the long dead. At the end, an old goddess laughs, and the harp stops.

choices.text: Take a cup from their table, as a guest

ok.log: The cup is warm. The goddess who poured it nods, pleased, and the others raise theirs in return.

fail.log: The wine is old and strong. Your head spins, and the hall spins with it.
fail.deathCause: a cup of cedar wine from a lost pantheon

choices.text: Bow, and say you came only to see

effects.log: They bow back, with the grace of a thousand years of practice.

events.text: The one who left the door unlocked was not a boundary-god at all. It was Cheonho, years ago, after the war. He went alone and sat in the tomb-heaven for an hour and came away without a word. The boundary-god found the key in a drawer the next morning, and left it where it lay.
events.arc: The Tomb-Heaven of the Cedar Throne

choices.text: Ask Cheonho about it, quietly

effects.log: He is silent for a long while. Then he says that a god should know where his enemies lie, and that is all.

choices.text: Do not ask

effects.log: You leave the old god his hour.

events.text: The goddess asks you to take her harp out of the tomb-heaven. She does not want to leave. She wants the harp played in a place where the notes can go somewhere, and a living hand to do it. The door, she says, has been open for a thousand years, and not one god of hers has ever stepped through.
events.arc: The Tomb-Heaven of the Cedar Throne

choices.text: Carry the harp out and play it in a shrine

effects.log: The notes fill the shrine, old and sweet. Behind you, in the tomb-heaven, the feast goes quiet to listen.

choices.text: Offer to carry a message to the court instead

effects.log: The court receives you with a long, difficult silence. Then someone sends a cedar cutting to the tomb-heaven, and the door is left deliberately ajar.

events.text: The cup has left a taste of cedar in your mouth that lasts a century. In certain rooms the pillars seem to lean toward you, and the harp is audible from three domains away. You are not sure whether you have been given something or been marked. The goddess who poured it smiles in your dreams.
events.arc: The Tomb-Heaven of the Cedar Throne

choices.text: Keep the cup on your altar

effects.log: It never empties of a faint cedar smell. Pilgrims wonder at it, and at you.

choices.text: Pour it out at the tomb-heaven door

effects.log: A little cedar shoot springs from the threshold and grows, slowly, in the cracks of the stone.

events.text: The court never speaks of the Cedar Throne again, but cedar shoots appear in the corners of the divine halls, a few at first and then a green line along the foot of the walls. Nobody says who plants them. The old pantheons agree, without a word, to water them.
events.arc: The Tomb-Heaven of the Cedar Throne

choices.text: Plant a shoot of your own in your shrine

effects.log: It takes root by the third spring. It smells of a feast.

choices.text: Say nothing, and water the line on your way by

effects.log: The shoots lean a little toward you as you pass.

events.text: A candle of grey wax turns up in the vault of a god who was forgotten. Whoever lights it is prayed to by ten thousand voices from the first moment. The voices are not real. They are borrowed, from every worshipper who ever lit the candle before, and each hour of it costs the lighter one memory. The vault-keeper wants it gone, for a price.

choices.text: Take the candle, to study it

effects.log: It is surprisingly heavy. The wax has a faint pulse, like a held breath.

choices.text: Ask what the last lighter lost

effects.log: The keeper says: the name of their own mother, and a favourite song. They noticed a week late.

choices.text: Decline, and tell the keeper to bury it

effects.log: The keeper nods, uneasy. The candle stays in its jar.

events.text: You light the candle for the length of one breath. Ten thousand voices rise in a shout of belief, and you feel enormous and wanted. Then it is out, and you cannot recall the colour of the door of the first shrine you ever kept. It is a small thing. It sits in you like a stone.

choices.text: Light it again, for one breath more

effects.log: The voices rise again, warm as bath water. You lose a second small thing, and are too pleased to notice which.

choices.text: Snuff it, and write down what you remember

effects.log: You spend the night writing every memory you can find. The door, you decide, was red.

events.text: The last lighter was a priest of a small shrine, who lit the candle once a year to feel that someone, anyone, was listening. They are alive and well and have no idea who their mother was. They keep a shrine of nothing in particular, and tend it with great care, as if tending a garden they have never planted.

choices.text: Tell them what you know of their mother

effects.log: You know a little, from the vault's records. They listen with their head to one side, as to music in another room.

choices.text: Leave them be, and bring them news of the shrine's pilgrims

effects.log: They are delighted. Pilgrims, they say, are the only people who ever remember.

events.text: The candle is half spent and you have forgotten six small things, and ten thousand voices think you are wonderful. A visiting god, passing, laughs and says: you will be a wonderful god, in a while, to everyone but yourself. The candle gutters, once, as though it agreed.

choices.text: Let the candle burn out, and lose what it takes

effects.log: It burns to a clear drop of wax. You lose a decade of weather. The shrine, afterward, has twice the pilgrims.

choices.text: Smother the candle in sand

effects.log: The voices stop mid-shout. In the silence you can hear, very faintly, the sound of the door you forgot.

events.text: You write your forgotten things on slips and keep them in a box. It becomes a habit, and then a small daily rite, and then, to your surprise, a minor tradition among your worshippers: the Keeping of the Small Things. Some of them write their own slips. The candle stays in its jar, and does not ask to be lit.

choices.text: Teach the rite to your worshippers

effects.log: It spreads. A hundred shrines begin to keep boxes of small remembered things, and the faith that comes with it is warm and quiet.

choices.text: Keep the rite to yourself

effects.log: It is private, and enough.

events.text: The priest of nothing in particular asks you to come to their shrine and light the candle there, once, for them. They want ten thousand voices for one breath, in return for a mother's name. You are not sure it is a fair trade, but it is theirs to make.

choices.text: Light it for them, and tell them the name

effects.log: They weep through the whole breath, and are happy. Afterward they cannot recall the name, and ask you to say it again.

choices.text: Refuse, and sit with them instead

effects.log: You sit all evening in the shrine of nothing in particular. It becomes a place you return to.

events.text: {npc}, a god of the third gate of a pass, comes to you in a hurry and a hat. {He} has lost {his} shadow. It walked out of {him} one morning and has not been back. It has been seen, most lately, drifting through the Harvest domain, in the shape of a tall figure with a very good manner and no feet.
events.arc: The Shadow That Left Its God

choices.text: Offer to help look for it

effects.log: {npc} presses your hands in relief. {He} has not been able to ask anyone else, because nobody believes a god can be shadowless.

choices.text: Ask what the shadow was like

effects.log: {He} describes it fondly, as one might a younger sibling: restless, a little vain, much given to sleeping in other people's doorways.

choices.text: Say you will keep an eye out

effects.log: {He} thanks you and puts the hat back on, firmly.

events.text: The shadow is in the Harvest domain, at the edge of a field of barley, being very gracious to a scarecrow. It says it left because it was tired of being cast. It wants to be someone, not merely something that follows. It has taken up a post as a night-watch to a granary, and is very good at it.
events.arc: The Shadow That Left Its God

choices.text: Tell it that {npc} misses it

effects.log: It listens with its head tilted, which on a shadow looks like a long vertical stretch. It says it will think about it.

choices.text: Ask if it would work for {npc} as a partner, not a shadow

effects.log: The shadow considers this with great attention. It has never been offered the word.

events.text: {npc} has a theory: the shadow left because {he} has never once stood in the sun. {He} has kept the pass for six hundred years in a grey coat, beneath an overhang, in a perpetual dusk. The shadow had no light to be cast by, and so it went looking.
events.arc: The Shadow That Left Its God

choices.text: Take {npc} out to stand in the sun for an afternoon

effects.log: {He} squints, and weeps a little, and stands there until evening. When {he} turns, there is a faint smudge beside {him}, shy and uncertain.

choices.text: Suggest it gently, and leave the choice to {him}

effects.log: {He} says it is a thing worth thinking about. {He} looks toward the doorway for a long time.

events.text: The shadow comes home. It walks in at the pass in the first light, stretches itself along the stones, and folds back into {npc} like a coat. But now it is a little taller than before, and has opinions. {npc} finds {him}self humming, and in the evenings, to the pass's surprise, walking about in the open.
events.arc: The Shadow That Left Its God

choices.text: Raise a cup to them both

effects.log: You share a cup with a god and a shadow, and the shadow speaks first, quite well. {npc} laughs at {his} own voice from a new angle.

choices.text: Slip away quietly

effects.log: From the road you see two figures at the gate, one standing and one sitting, and neither is quite the same shape as the other.

events.text: The shadow takes the title of Partner of the Third Gate. They hold the pass together, one by day and one by night, and the pass has never been so well kept. Pilgrims find a small unexpected comfort in it: a god who has a night self. The court adds a seat at the end of the long table, and the shadow takes it, graciously.
events.arc: The Shadow That Left Its God

choices.text: Attend the court the day the seat is first used

effects.log: The shadow sits, folded, and is addressed by name for the first time. The hall is silent. Then, gradually, it applauds.

choices.text: Send a gift of a lamp to the new seat

effects.log: It is a small lamp. The shadow lets it burn beside the seat all session, and casts a little itself.

events.text: It is a thin shadow that comes back to {npc} at last, a smudge, a hesitation at the end of a heel. But it is {his}, and {he} takes it as one takes a child's hand. {He} will wear it as lightly as it will bear. Together they cross the pass at noon for the first time in six hundred years.
events.arc: The Shadow That Left Its God

choices.text: Walk with them as far as the first turn

effects.log: At the turn the shadow gives a small, dry, delighted wave back at you.

choices.text: Stay at the gate and watch them go

effects.log: The pass is quiet behind them. You hear someone humming.

events.text: A small sealed heaven stands off the road to the Death domain, with a door that is slightly warm. Behind it everything is inhaling. Every curtain bellies inward, every flame leans toward the middle, and nothing in the place has exhaled for ten thousand years. The warder, a very polite lizard, asks you to breathe carefully.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Held Breath

choices.text: Step in, and breathe in very slowly

effects.log: The air draws gently at your sleeves and then, politely, lets go. The lizard clicks its tongue approvingly.

choices.text: Ask the lizard what happens if anything exhales

effects.log: It lowers its voice. Nobody knows. It has been thinking about it, with some dread, since the first century.

choices.text: Stay on the threshold and look

effects.log: From the doorway you see the curtains lean, the flames lean, a feather hang in air. The warmth of the door is the warmth of a mouth.

events.text: In the middle of the heaven stands a small shrine to a god of Last Words. Everything in the room is leaning toward it. The god itself is asleep on the altar, with its mouth a little open, and a single word balanced on its tongue, ready to be said. The lizard begs you not to wake it.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Held Breath

choices.text: Leave the sleeper be, and look at the shrine

effects.log: The offerings are hundreds of sealed letters, none of them opened, each addressed in a different hand to someone who is not here.

choices.text: Lean over, and read the word on its tongue

ok.log: The word is a name, and it is yours. It means nothing; it means only that someone, once, intended to say it.

fail.log: The word slips, and you breathe out. For a moment, the whole heaven shivers.
fail.deathCause: a held breath let go in a sealed heaven

events.text: The lizard, after a few days, tells you the truth: it was posted here as a punishment and has stayed from affection. It has taught itself to breathe in a manner that does not disturb the heaven. It would like to teach a successor. It has taught nobody, because nobody has come who was willing to learn to breathe like that.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Held Breath

choices.text: Learn the lizard's breathing

effects.log: It takes you a season. By the end of it you can stand in the heaven for an hour without disturbing a feather.

choices.text: Wish it well and go

effects.log: The lizard watches you leave with a long, quiet look, like a window with no one at it.

events.text: You open one letter, then, at last. It says: I meant to say this to you before you went, and I did not, and now it is too late. There is nothing else in it. The letters in the shrine are all like that, unsaid things, kept in a place that cannot hear them. The leaning stops, a little, as you read.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Held Breath

choices.text: Read the letter aloud, softly, to the sleeper

effects.log: The sleeper's mouth closes, then opens. It breathes out, once, so gently that the curtains only tremble. A word is said, and the heaven lets go.

choices.text: Fold the letter back, and leave it where it lay

effects.log: You walk out of the heaven in a hush. Behind you, the curtains lean, and are still.

events.text: You say the name that was on the sleeper's tongue, aloud, once, and the heaven exhales: every curtain, every flame, ten thousand years of held air all at once, a long gentle wind that blows through the heaven and out of the door and across the road. It smells of lamps just snuffed. The sleeper opens its eyes.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Held Breath

choices.text: Sit with the awakened god, and listen to its first word

effects.log: It says, thank you. After ten thousand years, that is all it had been going to say.

choices.text: Close the door behind you, gently

effects.log: The warm door cools in your hand, and lets you go.

events.text: The lizard retires, and you take its post. It is not hard. You sit in the heaven with a kettle and breathe slowly, and visitors come: a god of crossings who has nowhere to say goodbye, a ferryman who wants to leave a letter. The sleeper breathes once a decade. You are there to hear it.
events.arc: The Heaven of the Held Breath

choices.text: Keep the post for a hundred years

effects.log: The sleeper wakes in the ninety-third and says a word. You are not sure what it was, and neither is the sleeper.

choices.text: Train a successor, and leave the post to them

effects.log: You teach a small god of crossings to breathe. They stay for an age.

events.text: In the Mountains domain there is a road that walks. It leaves a hill-hamlet at dawn, strolls over three ridges, and comes home by dusk, with its stones a little dusty. {npc}, a grey-haired road-warden, follows it at a distance with a broom, and says it is the best-behaved road {he} has ever kept. Pilgrims use it to cross three ridges in a day.

choices.text: Ask to walk the road with {him}

effects.log: {He} gives you the second broom. The road ahead of you sets out at an easy pace, as though carrying you were a pleasure.

choices.text: Ask who first built a road that could walk

effects.log: {He} does not know. {He} says it is older than the oldest pilgrim's tale, and prouder than any of them.

choices.text: Watch it leave from the hamlet gate

effects.log: At dawn the road gets up with a long grinding sound, shakes itself, and sets off, tidily.

events.text: Halfway across the second ridge the road stops, and will not go on. It has done this once before, {npc} says, when a landslide took a hamlet on the far side. It is listening. After a while it turns, with a patient groaning of stones, and begins to walk a different way, to a place that has no pilgrims.

choices.text: Follow it, and see where it goes

effects.log: It carries you across the ridge to a small dead shrine in a hollow that nobody has visited in an age. The road lies down in front of it like a dog on a doorstep.

choices.text: Sweep the road, and wait

effects.log: You sweep. The road allows it, shifting slightly under the broom, as a cat does under a hand.

events.text: An old pilgrim, passing, claims the road was built by a god of arrivals whose domain was dissolved, and who set it walking in his last year so that it could keep on arriving. It has been arriving ever since. The pilgrim kneels, and the road, unexpectedly, bows its stones.

choices.text: Seek the god of arrivals in the court records

effects.log: You find no record. But in the margin of an old register, a very faint note: ask the road.

choices.text: Sit with the pilgrim, and listen to their story

effects.log: It is a long one, and does not end well, and the pilgrim seems comforted by telling it.

events.text: At the dead shrine the road puts down a stone, a smooth round one that fits the empty socket in the altar. A faint light rises. A god of arrivals sits up on the altar, thin as smoke, and says: oh, you came back. The road shivers all along its length, and the light goes round it like a collar.

choices.text: Light a lamp and stay until the god is solid again

effects.log: It takes three nights. At the end of them the god of arrivals is a plain, tired, delighted man sitting on an altar with a road at his feet.

choices.text: Bring the pilgrims, and let them speak to the god

effects.log: A line of travellers forms down the hollow and across the ridge. Each says one word, and the god nods.

events.text: Nothing more happens that day, and the road begins to walk again at dusk. {npc} is quietly moved. {He} says the road has never stopped before without a reason, and never gone on without telling someone. You find you have been told something, and cannot say what.

choices.text: Walk the rest of the day with it, in silence

effects.log: You cross the second ridge at sunset. The road deposits you at your door with a small bow of its gravel.

choices.text: Leave a fresh broom at the warden's gate

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and says the road will be pleased.

events.text: The margin note led to a name, and the name to a lost shrine at the end of a road that did not yet exist. You build it, one slow season, as an offering: a plain stone house with a bench and a lamp, for any traveller. The road comes by once a year, and sits down outside it, like a guest.

choices.text: Keep the lamp lit for the road

effects.log: The road returns every spring, and every spring you are glad of it.

choices.text: Name the shrine after the god of arrivals

effects.log: The name is carved over the door. It is, you think, the first time in ages it has been written down.

events.text: In a corridor behind the great court there is a small court of echo-gods, who repeat the last words of every petition and fine them down into the manner of a verdict. It is a rich office. They are vain about it. A petitioner has appealed to you for redress, because the echo-court has repeated their grievance wrongly for eleven years.

choices.text: Go and hear the echo-court in session

effects.log: The echo-gods sit in a ring, each a half-beat behind the one before. What comes out at the end is neat, grand, and almost never what was said.

choices.text: Read the petitioner's grievance aloud yourself

effects.log: The corridor gives it back to you in a thin mimic voice, slightly improved.

choices.text: Offer the petitioner tea and a place to sit

effects.log: They are grateful, and a little embarrassed to be heard the first time.

events.text: The echo-gods are not malicious. They simply cannot stop improving. A small plain complaint about a missing boundary stone comes out of them as an ornate tragedy of three acts. The senior echo asks you to judge whether this counts as error. You have to admit it is very well made.

choices.text: Rule that the echo may add, but not change

effects.log: The court recites your ruling back to you, three times, each time with a little more weight. It stands.

choices.text: Ask the echo to give things back plain, once, as a courtesy

effects.log: The echo-gods murmur, shocked. The senior one tries. It comes out thin and bare and, for the first time, true.

events.text: Your own voice comes back to you down the corridor, and it is a little braver than you are. The echo-gods have been listening. A very young echo asks, with great shyness, whether you would be willing to say something plain, and let it practise saying it back exactly.

choices.text: Say a plain sentence, and listen

effects.log: The young echo repeats it, flat and exact, and then, with a small sound, bursts into tears of relief.

choices.text: Decline, and ask it what it would like to say

effects.log: It thinks for a long time, and then says: I would like to be asked.

events.text: Over the next year the echo-court begins to issue two verdicts side by side: the grand one, and a plain one underneath. The petitioners prefer the plain. The echo-gods, to their own surprise, find they prefer it too. The senior echo sends you a small bow, a letter, and a cup carved from a bell.

choices.text: Hang the bell-cup in your shrine

effects.log: It rings faintly when a true thing is said in the room. Pilgrims take to testing it, and are mostly humbled.

choices.text: Keep the letter and thank the court

effects.log: It is a short letter, and plainly written.

events.text: The ruling stands, and the echo-court grows, if anything, more ornate. Eleven years of improved grievances are filed and published as a book. The petitioner is mentioned in it as a tragic hero. They are not sure whether to be flattered. They buy forty copies and give them to friends.

choices.text: Attend the book's reading

effects.log: The echo-gods read it in a ring, each half a beat behind. By the end the hall is moved to tears, and no one is sure about what.

choices.text: Skip the reading, and send a note of thanks

effects.log: Your note comes back, improved.

events.text: The young echo takes up a post of its own, in a quiet corner of the corridor, as a plain court of one. Petitioners come to it when they want to hear what they actually said. It is never busy. It is never wrong. It sends you a note every year, in a flat exact hand, saying only: still plain.

choices.text: Visit it, now and again

effects.log: You sit in its corner and say whatever comes to mind. It gives it back, unimproved.

choices.text: Send it a plain lamp for the corner

effects.log: It writes back: thank you, a lamp. Exactly that.

events.text: At the Pale Crossing, where Baekun ferries the newly dead, a cat has taken to riding the bow. It steals the coins the dead carry, and the ferrymen suspect it of worse. Every crossing it vanishes at the far shore and reappears at the near. The Hall has asked for it to be caught and put to some use.
events.arc: The Ferry-Cat of the Pale Crossing

choices.text: Take the next crossing and watch the cat

effects.log: It sits at the bow in a ruff of white fur, washing its face, as the dead are poled across in silence.

choices.text: Ask the ferrymen what it takes

effects.log: The ferrymen shuffle. The cat takes only the coins, and gives them to somebody, and none of them know who.

choices.text: Leave a saucer at the near shore

effects.log: The saucer is empty by morning, and licked clean.

events.text: You follow the cat to the far shore. It slips between the shades with a coin in its mouth, to a small dim stall where an old ghost sits selling dried plums to the newly arrived. The cat drops the coin in the ghost's bowl. The ghost puts a plum in the paw of a frightened newcomer. The cat has been paying for their first meal.
events.arc: The Ferry-Cat of the Pale Crossing

choices.text: Buy a plum yourself, and say nothing
