effects.log: The ghost sets one in your hand without a word. It tastes of the end of summer.

choices.text: Ask the ghost why the cat does this

effects.log: The ghost says the cat was theirs, once. It crossed first, to wait. It has been waiting a long time.

events.text: The ferrymen are quiet because the Hall forbids gifts to the dead. The coins the dead carry are the Hall's fares, and a ferry-cat that redirects them is, formally, a thief. A clerk of the Hall has drafted the paperwork to catch it, and is sharpening a pen with real appetite.
events.arc: The Ferry-Cat of the Pale Crossing

choices.text: Argue the cat's case to the clerk

effects.log: The clerk sniffs, but lets you speak. It takes the afternoon. In the end the clerk puts the pen away, unwillingly.

choices.text: Warn the cat, and keep out of it

effects.log: The cat looks at you and yawns. It is not afraid of clerks.

events.text: The ghost with the stall asks a favour: that the cat be allowed to cross the river whenever it likes, and not only at the Hall's hours. They have been cutting up the same plum for ten thousand years, and they would like to see the cat sit on the other bank in the sun.
events.arc: The Ferry-Cat of the Pale Crossing

choices.text: Take the favour to Baekun

effects.log: The Pale Ferryman considers it for a count of nine. Then he lifts the cat to his shoulder, and it rides there thereafter.

choices.text: Pay the cat's fares from your own shrine

effects.log: A trickle of coins appears at the far shore. The ghost nods, and the cat does too.

events.text: The plums are good. You find yourself returning for them, a little guiltily, in the evenings. The ghost never asks who you are. The cat sits on your knee while you eat, and when you leave, it follows to the shore and sits there, watching you cross, until you are quite out of sight.
events.arc: The Ferry-Cat of the Pale Crossing

choices.text: Leave a coin for the cat on your way out

effects.log: It is gone before you turn around.

choices.text: Take the cat a plum on your next visit

effects.log: The cat accepts it with composure.

events.text: The clerk's pen is put away. But a ruling is made, quietly, that nobody is to ask the cat about its coins, and that the Hall will go on ignoring the matter. It is the kindest ruling the Hall has ever made, and it was made by nobody in particular.
events.arc: The Ferry-Cat of the Pale Crossing

choices.text: Thank the clerk in person

effects.log: The clerk is flustered. They say they have nothing to do with it. They pat their pocket, where a plum-stone is rattling.

choices.text: Say nothing of the matter, and keep the ruling quiet

effects.log: The cat sits on the bow every crossing, now, openly. Nobody mentions it.

events.text: {npc} carries letters between two pantheons that are not on speaking terms. {He} does it for a pittance, in a grey coat, on foot. The letters are courteous, and say nothing, and each contains a hidden second letter that {he} has been trained not to read. {He} reads them anyway, and has begun to feel it a weight.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the hidden letters say

effects.log: {He} looks around for listeners. They are, {he} says, very much alike. Both gods are lonely.

choices.text: Offer to carry a letter yourself, one time

effects.log: {He} gives you a plain bundle. Even closed, it feels as though it is leaning toward the far door.

choices.text: Buy {him} a hot meal at a roadside stall

effects.log: {He} eats in silence. {He} says, afterward, it is the first meal in a decade that nobody watched.

events.text: The far pantheon's god receives your letter with a stiff bow. The hidden second letter, which you did not read, makes the god sit down. A servant brings you tea and sends you back with a reply. You are given three days of rest by a fire. No one asks you a thing.

choices.text: Carry the reply back, unopened

effects.log: Your return is quiet. The first god takes the reply with trembling hands, and does not look up for a long time.

choices.text: Ask the second god what the hidden letter says

effects.log: The god is silent. Then they say: that I am sorry. I have been trying to say it for four hundred years.

events.text: The hidden letters, {npc} says, are all the same two lines. One is: forgive me. The other is: I would, if you asked. Neither god has ever sent the second line, because it would mean asking. {He} has been waiting to be asked to carry it, and never has.

choices.text: Offer to write the second line for the one who cannot

effects.log: {npc} watches you write. You send it by {his} hand. {He} walks off down the road, upright, with the letter held close.

choices.text: Tell {him} it is not {his} burden

effects.log: {He} takes this thoughtfully. {He} had been carrying it as though it were.

events.text: The two gods meet, in the end, on a bridge over a dry river, with a bench between them and a plain cup each. {npc} watches from the far bank, in the grey coat, while the two of them sit and say nothing for an hour. Then one pours the tea for the other, and the war between the pantheons, which was never declared, is over.

choices.text: Stand witness for them both

effects.log: You stand on the bank until the tea is cold. Neither god looks round. The war ends without a ceremony, which is how it began.

choices.text: Slip away so they can be alone

effects.log: You walk away upriver. Behind you the bridge is quiet.

events.text: The second god is not ready to forgive. They send a reply you do not carry. The first god waits another century. But {npc} has changed, and hires another courier to take the hidden letters on, and goes to keep a roadside stall with a bench for tired travellers. {He} gives the first meal free.

choices.text: Eat at the stall, and help with the washing up

effects.log: It is a small kindness, and {he} remembers it for ages.

choices.text: Leave a coin on the bench for the next traveller

effects.log: It is gone by the evening. Somebody ate.

events.text: The second line reaches its god. The answer comes back, by {npc}, in the same plain bundle: a single dried flower. {He} holds it out to you on the road, and asks whether you would take it, because {he} has never had anything to carry that was not a message.

choices.text: Take the flower, and keep it

effects.log: It is faded and perfect. You press it in a book, and it is a small fine ache every time you open the page.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep it

effects.log: {He} puts it in {his} sleeve and walks on, a little taller.

events.text: Once a year, for one hour, the pear trees of a Harvest valley bloom and fruit and drop in the same breath. Pilgrims line the hill to catch the pears before they hit the ground. It is the hour of Pungnyeon's old quarrel with time, and nobody is quite sure who won.

choices.text: Catch one pear, and eat it standing

effects.log: It tastes of three seasons at once. You are a little taller afterward.

choices.text: Hold up your hat for the children to fill

effects.log: Nine children fill it. They leave you the stem.

events.text: A hunter of the Green Assembly offers to sell you a net of whispers, for catching things that are afraid. It is woven of tender talk. A beast caught in it will not struggle; it will weep, and you will have to put it down yourself. The hunter shrugs. It is only a net, they say.

choices.text: Refuse the net, and say so plainly

effects.log: The hunter nods slowly, and puts it away. They seem to have hoped you would.

choices.text: Take the net, to keep it out of use

effects.log: You wrap it in cloth and bury it under your shrine. It sleeps, there, a faint murmur at night.

events.text: A stair rises from a sealed heaven's door, and no one has ever found its top. It climbs through a cloud of its own, past empty landings with doors left open. Each door has a small chair behind it. Someone has been sitting down on the way up for ten thousand years, one landing at a time.

choices.text: Climb a hundred steps and sit in the nearest chair

effects.log: From the chair you see the stair rising and, far below, your own door small as a thumbnail. You rest a while.

choices.text: Mark the hundredth step with chalk, and go back down

effects.log: You leave the mark. Someone, years later, adds a second.

events.text: A burned shrine holds a single candle stub that no ash has put out. It has burned since the fire. The last priest left it, with a note: keep this lit until someone comes who needs it. For ages no one has needed it. The flame leans, patient, toward your sleeve.

choices.text: Light your lamp from it

effects.log: The lamp takes the flame cleanly. You carry it away, and the stub burns on, no smaller.

choices.text: Sit with it for an hour, and say you do not need it yet

effects.log: The flame steadies, as if pleased by the honesty.

events.text: A pilgrim asks you the shortest way to a distant shrine. There is one, through a sealed pass, but it is not safe for the unprepared. There is also the long way, which takes a year, and which the pilgrim, plainly, does not want to take. They have already walked a good deal of it.

choices.text: Describe the long way, and give them a lamp for it

effects.log: They set off cheerfully. The lamp is still burning in the valley when you look back.

choices.text: Describe the short way, honestly, with all its dangers

effects.log: They listen carefully, and decide for themselves. You are not sure which way they went.

events.text: Someone has left a stone carved in the shape of a small boy on your altar, with a dried flower in its hands. There is no name. The shrine-keeper says it appeared in the night. When you ask the stone who it is for, a faint warmth comes up from it, as from a hand held out.

choices.text: Keep the stone on the altar, with the flower

effects.log: The shrine seems warmer. Pilgrims touch the stone's head as they pass.

choices.text: Carry the stone down to the village below, and ask

effects.log: No one claims it. A woman cries, a little, and asks to keep it.

events.text: In the great hall of the court, a god of punctuality has installed nine clocks. All nine disagree. Each is accurate for its own part of the hall, and the god insists this is correct. Petitioners arrive late or early depending on which wall they stand by, and blame each other.

choices.text: Stand in the exact middle, between all the clocks

effects.log: At the exact middle the clocks ring together, once, and a hush falls. It lasts a second.

choices.text: Add a tenth clock, and say nothing

effects.log: It is set by the sun. The god of punctuality looks at it, aghast, for a very long time.

events.text: A stall at the market of faith sells echoes in jars: the final bar of a hymn, a prayer's last syllable, a clap in a canyon. They are cheap. The seller swears each one is the real thing. When you uncork one it says, in a small hurt voice, I thought we were friends.

choices.text: Put the cork back and apologise

effects.log: The echo sighs, and settles. The seller looks at you with sudden respect.

choices.text: Buy the echo and set it free in your shrine

effects.log: It circles the rafters for a week, repeating the last word of everything said below. Pilgrims find it comforting.

events.text: In the soft earth outside your shrine there are hoofprints of no beast you know: cloven, enormous, and sunk to the depth of a god's weight. They go in a circle three times around the shrine and then walk, with perfect calm, straight up the wall. Something has been admiring your roof.

choices.text: Follow the prints up the wall, with a rope

effects.log: At the top, on the ridge-tile, is a single warm hoof-shaped hollow, full of rainwater and a very small fish.

choices.text: Leave a salt-lick on the roof, and wait

effects.log: In the morning it is licked to a smooth cup. The prints do not come again, but the fish does.

events.text: A rain falls in a primal place that has not rained since before the cutting of the domains. It falls on a plain where nothing has ever been, and where something, now, is beginning to be. Drop by drop the dust is learning to be a soil. You stand in it, soaked, and nothing minds.

choices.text: Stand and let it rain on you

effects.log: You feel the first morning of a place that has no name yet. It stays with you for a decade.

choices.text: Plant a seed in the new mud

effects.log: The seed does not grow. But it is the first thing anyone has put in that soil, and it remembers.

events.text: In a vault of a fallen god you find a lantern whose glass is etched with every name the god was ever called. As you carry it, the names glow in turn. The last one, very faint at the bottom, is a childhood nickname that no one has said in ages. It glows brighter when you say it.

choices.text: Say the nickname aloud, and leave the lantern lit

effects.log: The lantern burns clear for a night. Somewhere, a very old god smiles, and the vault is warm for a month.

choices.text: Take the lantern home to study it

effects.log: It is a good lantern. The names glow in turn on your shrine wall, and pilgrims copy them.

events.text: On a wall of a burned shrine there are char-marks: a child's height ruled in soot at every year, from a small mark to a tall one, ending at the shoulder of a grown man. Beside the last mark, in the same hand, is a single line. The sooted ruler is still tied to the wall by a bit of string.

choices.text: Add a mark at your own height, with a note

effects.log: You write only the year. It seems proper to answer, even if no one will read it.

choices.text: Copy the marks onto a scroll for the family, if they live

effects.log: You find a family in the next domain who weep, and take the scroll home.

events.text: An elder god invites you to tea in a room with eleven chairs and nine cups. It says, calmly, that the other two guests are late, and have been late for four thousand years. It would like to have a conversation with someone who has at least arrived. It asks about your day, and listens to the whole answer.

choices.text: Tell it everything, from morning to dusk

effects.log: It nods at every turn. At the end, it says only: that is a good day. It is the nicest thing anyone has said to you in ages.

choices.text: Ask about its day, in turn

effects.log: It talks for three hours. It has been rehearsing the answer for a very long time.

events.text: On a clear night you notice a gap among the stars the shape of a small door. It is not dark; it is simply unfilled, as a tooth is, with the sense that something used to stand there. Cheonho, asked, says he will fill it in due time, and has been saying so for six centuries.

choices.text: Offer to hold the place with a lamp

effects.log: You hang a small lamp in the gap. It burns, a point of warm yellow, among the cold white. Pilgrims call it your star.

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep looking at the gap

effects.log: After a while you can almost see what used to be there. It is gone again at dawn.

events.text: A rival pantheon sends you a gift: a very beautiful jar, tightly sealed, and a card that reads, with a courtesy so exact it hurts, for the one who has everything. There is something moving in it. The courier will not meet your eye, and leaves rather quickly.

choices.text: Open it in an empty room, at arm's length

effects.log: It is a sparrow. It looks about, outraged, and flies out through the window singing a tune that makes the rival pantheon sound faintly ridiculous.

choices.text: Leave it sealed on a high shelf and send a polite note

effects.log: The jar hums for a month. Then it stops, and you do not look.

events.text: At a court feast you are seated opposite an empty chair, set with a full place. The steward whispers that it is for the god who is always invited and never comes. Everyone passes the dish to the empty chair first, and then to you. It is a custom, no one remembers why.

choices.text: Serve the empty chair first, with your own hand

effects.log: You fill the empty plate. The table goes quiet, then approving. Nobody eats it, and it is not wasted.

choices.text: Ask the steward who the guest is, in a low voice

effects.log: The steward mutters a name that has not been said in this hall in a thousand years. You write it down.

events.text: A priest of your shrine rings the bell eleven times at dawn, though the old rite calls for nine. When asked, they say two of the strokes are for the people who do not know they are being prayed for. They have rung it that way for thirty years. No one ever corrected them.

choices.text: Leave the bell as they ring it

effects.log: The extra strokes carry across the valley. People pause, and do not know why.

choices.text: Ring the last stroke yourself, one dawn, as a thanks

effects.log: The valley holds still. A little dog barks, and a window opens.

events.text: It rains tea over a corner of the Harvest domain for a single afternoon, a warm, fragrant, faintly sweet rain that fills barrels and streaks the windows brown. No god takes credit. Several quarrel over it. The children of the valley stand with their mouths open and refuse to come in.

choices.text: Stand in it a while, yourself

effects.log: It is, honestly, excellent. You collect a barrel for the shrine-keeper.

choices.text: Quietly take credit, as a joke

effects.log: Three gods call you a liar to your face within the hour, and each of them smiles as they do it.

events.text: On a visit to another domain you come to a rope bridge over a gorge, and a sign in a hand you do not know: toll, one true thing. A tiny god of tolls sits at the near post with a cup. They are not stern. They have been very bored for a very long time.

choices.text: Tell them one true thing about yourself

effects.log: It is a small thing, and plainly meant. The god of tolls lowers the rope, nods, and does not say what they thought of it.

choices.text: Ask the toll-god for one true thing in return

effects.log: They think about it for an hour. The answer is a very quiet one, and you walk across the bridge in a good mood.

events.text: At a long council the minute-taker, a thin god of the second hour, stops writing in the middle of a speech and puts down their brush. They look around the table with an expression of dreamy sadness. Nobody has noticed the lull. The speech goes on. The minutes are blank for the first time in four thousand years.

choices.text: Offer to take the minutes for the rest of the session

effects.log: You write it all down, badly. The minute-taker slumps in grateful sleep, and is better afterward.

choices.text: Ask the minute-taker to step out with you for tea

effects.log: They walk out of the hall in the middle of the speech. It is, in its way, a small act of liberation.

events.text: A farmer prays for rain at your shrine, and then, a day later, comes back and prays against it, because the rain has flooded his neighbour's field. He says he prayed for the rain on behalf of his neighbour, and the neighbour prayed against it for him. They are, it seems, great friends.

choices.text: Send a mild, even drizzle on both fields

effects.log: Both farmers stand in the drizzle, laughing. It is a fine small day for a god.

choices.text: Let the weather do what it likes, and watch

effects.log: The neighbours argue, amiably, over a wall, until dusk.

events.text: In your sleep you find yourself in another god's dream, a plain dull one, of washing cups in a back room. It is perfectly peaceful. The dreamer, you realise, has chosen this over every grander thing, and is smiling in their sleep. You dry one cup, and leave.

choices.text: Wake gently, and leave the dreamer be

effects.log: You wake with a tidy feeling, as if you had done a small good chore.

choices.text: Leave a clean cup in the dream, as a gift

effects.log: The dreamer wakes, mildly bewildered, and finds a cup on their shelf.

events.text: A fallen god kept a ledger of every laugh in his domain, and it is in a vault you open by mistake. It is warm. The columns are in small neat handwriting: a laugh at the harvest-end, a laugh in a doorway, a laugh from a child who did not see the god. It is the happiest document in the realm.

choices.text: Read a page aloud in the empty vault

effects.log: The vault rings faintly with the laughs. You laugh too, a little, in the dust.

choices.text: Take the ledger to the domain it recorded

effects.log: The people there have forgotten how to laugh in the old way. They read it, and slowly, they remember.

events.text: Two gods are quarrelling at the court door over who is to go through first. Each insists that the other is the elder. They have been at it since morning. The doorkeeper, a patient and underpaid shade, sits on a stool and carves a small wooden bird. A crowd has begun to gather and trade guesses.

choices.text: Go through the door yourself, and thank them for holding it

effects.log: They both look up in horror, then fall to arguing about who should have held it.

choices.text: Offer to stand as the third, and go in last

effects.log: They solve it at once, by both going in together, and you follow.

events.text: In a place where a god was unmade, you find a handful of salt on a flat stone, and nothing else. The salt is not a relic. It is simply what was left when the rest was taken. A bird has left a feather on it, and some small hand has drawn a circle around the whole in chalk.

choices.text: Leave the salt as it is, and the circle

effects.log: You pass on, touched. When you return a year later, the chalk has been renewed.

choices.text: Add a feather of your own to the stone

effects.log: It is, you think, the only grave the god has. You stay until the light changes.

events.text: A goddess of small weavings asks you to hold the end of a thread for her, while she crosses a room with the loom. It is a long thread. It runs out of the door, down the stair, across a courtyard, and as far as you can see. She says she will only be a moment. It is some hours.

choices.text: Hold the thread patiently, and watch the court go by

effects.log: You hear a great deal of gossip, wound into the thread. By the time she returns, you know the whole of the season's politics.

choices.text: Tie your end to a pillar and go for tea

effects.log: She returns to find it tied, and smiles. She has used worse knots in her day.

events.text: In a plain coat you sit in a barber's chair in another god's domain. The barber, who has no idea, talks the whole time about their god: the stiff manner, the odd habits, the surprising kindness to cats. By the end you have heard more about that god than in a thousand years of court. You tip generously.

choices.text: Tip, and say that you will tell their god you were happy

effects.log: The barber laughs. They say, well, tell them to cut down on the incense.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the barber think you a traveller

effects.log: You walk out into the street a little more informed and a little less proud.

events.text: Beneath the loom-room of Fate there is a round stone well, and nobody on the staff will say who dug it. Threads run down into it from every loom, thousands of them, taut as harp strings. The weaver on duty, a grey fidgety god, says the well is where the finished fates go. They have never come back up.
events.arc: The Well at the Bottom of the Loom-Room

choices.text: Lean over the edge and look down

effects.log: The dark is warm. Far below there is a faint dry sound, like paper being folded, over and over.

choices.text: Pluck one of the taut threads

effects.log: It sings a long clear note, and the whole room stills. Down in the well, something sings back, a third higher.

choices.text: Ask the weaver why no one has gone down

effects.log: The weaver says: because everyone assumes someone else has.

events.text: You are lowered on a thread, in a basket, past rings of mossy stone. At the bottom there is no water. There is a quiet room with a long table, and at the table sit the finished fates, each a small folded figure of paper, patiently waiting to be read. A sign says, in careful script: please do not hurry them.
events.arc: The Well at the Bottom of the Loom-Room

choices.text: Read one fate aloud, softly

effects.log: It is the story of a ferryman who lived and died in the one cottage. It is very short and very full. You find you are moved.

choices.text: Sit at the table and keep them company

effects.log: They do not speak. Their paper rustles slightly as if in comfort, and for an hour you feel, absurdly, like a guest.

events.text: The note the second voice sang was no echo. A hidden weaver, old and half-blind, lives on a ledge a hundred feet down, and mends frayed fates from beneath. They have not been to the loom-room for a thousand years, and they ask, very civilly, for a pair of shears, as their own are blunt.
events.arc: The Well at the Bottom of the Loom-Room

choices.text: Bring them a pair of good shears

effects.log: They take them in both hands as one takes a bird. The first snip is so clean that the well hums.

choices.text: Say you will ask the loom-room, and go

effects.log: The old weaver nods without bitterness. They have been told that before.

events.text: A fate on the table lies a little apart from the rest, unfolded. It is your own. It is not finished. It has gaps where decisions are still to be made, and a number of lines that have been written in and scratched out, and written in again. Someone has been adding a small mark of kindness in the margin for years.
events.arc: The Well at the Bottom of the Loom-Room

choices.text: Add your own mark in the margin, a small one

effects.log: You write one line. It is not wise or grand. It is, however, yours, and the paper seems warmer afterward.

choices.text: Leave it exactly as it is, and fold it with care

effects.log: You fold it back along its creases and set it down. The quiet room accepts this, and the rustle softens.

events.text: The fates at the table begin to stir, one by one, and rise, paper-light, and drift up the shaft on a warm breath. You are, apparently, the first visitor to have sat with them. They go to their weavers, to the looms, to the dreams of those they were about. The well is empty and clean. The room is quiet in a new way.
events.arc: The Well at the Bottom of the Loom-Room

choices.text: Ride up the shaft with them, in your basket

effects.log: The fates swirl around you, a fine paper snow. At the top the weaver on duty weeps, and says nobody has done that in a long age.

choices.text: Stay below a while, and watch them go

effects.log: The room is bare when the last one leaves. You sit until the lamp gives out.

events.text: The hidden weaver mends a fate that has been frayed for ages: yours, as it happens, though you do not learn this until a day when you are suddenly, inexplicably, lucky. They send up the shears, wrapped in a cloth, with a note: thank you. Cut as you must. Mend where you can.
events.arc: The Well at the Bottom of the Loom-Room

choices.text: Keep the shears on your shrine

effects.log: They never dull. Pilgrims with worn luck sometimes ask to touch the handles.

choices.text: Send the shears back to the ledge, with a loaf

effects.log: They come back empty, the cloth folded, in a week.

events.text: Before any god was a god, someone said a prayer. It was not to anyone. It went up out of the dark, small and ragged, and a beast was set to keep it from being used up. The beast lies across the mouth of a cave in the primal places, as large as a hill, patient as one. Its fur is the colour of the first dawn.
events.arc: The Beast That Guards the First Prayer

choices.text: Approach it with empty hands

effects.log: The beast lifts one eyelid. Its eye is the size of a lake and entirely without malice.

choices.text: Watch from a ridge for a night and a day

effects.log: It does not move, except to breathe. When the sun rises it sighs, very softly, as at a thing remembered.

choices.text: Leave a small offering at a respectful distance

effects.log: You set down a fruit. By morning the fruit is gone, and in its place is a smooth grey stone.

events.text: The beast lets you come close and rests its chin by your feet. It does not speak, but it hums, and the hum is a tune of seven notes, simple and old. Behind it, in the cave mouth, you can hear a thin, ragged voice, very faint. It is saying a prayer. It has been saying it ever since.
events.arc: The Beast That Guards the First Prayer

choices.text: Hum the seven notes back to the beast

effects.log: The beast closes its eyes. The cave voice falters, and then goes on, a little steadier.

choices.text: Slip past its shoulder to the cave mouth

ok.log: You pass under the great shoulder as a breath passes. The beast does not stir. Inside there is a faint, tender light.

fail.log: The beast shifts in its sleep, and you are pressed gently but irresistibly back out into the grass.

events.text: Two nights on the ridge teach you the beast's habits. It sleeps at noon, wakes at dusk, and every hour it breathes out in a long, warm, patient line, which carries the prayer outward over the primal plain. The prayer is not for itself. It is for whoever is coming. The beast has no idea whether anyone is.
events.arc: The Beast That Guards the First Prayer

choices.text: Wait with it until dusk, and breathe out with it

effects.log: Together you send the prayer out across the plain. Far off, something small answers.

choices.text: Mark the beast's habits in a notebook, and leave

effects.log: You write them down plainly, so no one who comes after will have to guess.

events.text: In the cave, on a small stone altar, there is nothing but the prayer: a faint voice that rises out of the dark, saying only: is anyone there. It has been asked a hundred thousand times, and has never been answered, because it has never stopped to be. You are asked, without a word, by the beast behind you, to say yes.
events.arc: The Beast That Guards the First Prayer

choices.text: Say: yes, I am here

effects.log: The voice falls silent. After a long time it says: thank you. The beast breathes out a single, enormous sigh, and the cave is full of dawn.

choices.text: Say your name, and where you keep your shrine

effects.log: The voice repeats it, wondering. The beast lowers its head. You have, it seems, made an appointment.

events.text: You are carried out of the beast's reach and set gently on the grass, as one sets down a very small guest. It looks at you, apologetic, and pushes the smooth grey stone from your offering toward you with its nose. On the stone is scratched a rough drawing of a cave, and a tiny figure standing at its mouth.
events.arc: The Beast That Guards the First Prayer

choices.text: Keep the stone, and come back when you are ready

effects.log: You return in a century, and the beast is still there, and lifts an eyelid. You go in, at last, and say yes.

choices.text: Leave the stone beside the beast

effects.log: It curls a paw around it, and sleeps.

events.text: A small answer comes out of the plain at dawn: another voice, thin as yours, saying a prayer of its own. It is a very young god, newly woken, who heard the beast's breath and followed it. They sit down next to the beast, and are not afraid. You are asked, by the beast's eye, to see them safe.
events.arc: The Beast That Guards the First Prayer

choices.text: Take the young god home to your shrine

effects.log: They are small and quick and constantly delighted. They keep the first prayer in a corner of your hall, and it is never silent.

choices.text: Stay with the young god by the beast for a season

effects.log: The young god learns the seven notes. They are, by the end, passably good at humming.

events.text: You open a sealed heaven by a hair, as a courtesy to a petition from the gods of the lower halls, and find a prisoner inside who has been there nine thousand years. {npc} is a thin, polite figure in a faded coat, who greets you at the door with a small bow, a cup of tea, and the unexpected remark that {he} would prefer not to be released.
events.arc: The Prisoner Who Asks to Stay

choices.text: Ask {him} why, and sit down

effects.log: {He} says the heaven is quiet, the tea is good, and the world outside is, {he} suspects, much changed. {He} is not sure there is anything in it for {him}.

choices.text: Ask what {he} was imprisoned for

effects.log: {He} thinks. {He} says it was a quarrel with a god whose name {he} has forgotten, over a matter of no importance.

choices.text: Say you will tell the petitioners that all is well

effects.log: {He} thanks you with a look of real relief.

events.text: The heaven is small and tidy. {npc} has made it a garden: a path, a pond, three willows, a bench where {he} sits and reads books {he} wrote on the walls. {He} says the first thousand years were the hard ones. By the second, {he} had forgiven the god. By the third, {he} had stopped wanting to leave.
events.arc: The Prisoner Who Asks to Stay

choices.text: Offer to bring {him} news of the outside, from time to time

effects.log: {He} accepts, and gives you a short list: weather, prices of tea, whether anyone remembers the willow-song.

choices.text: Ask if {he} would like company, rather than news

effects.log: {He} looks startled, and delighted. {He} says the bench is long enough for two.

events.text: The quarrel, {npc} remembers at last, was about whether a god may be forgiven by those they have not wronged. {He} had said yes, loudly, at a feast, and the god opposite had said no, louder. {He} was sealed in for disturbing the peace. The god opposite is long since gone, and the peace remains disturbed.
events.arc: The Prisoner Who Asks to Stay

choices.text: Take the matter to the court, as an appeal

effects.log: The court is slow, and embarrassed. In a year, a pardon is drawn up, and sent. {npc} reads it and sets it on the bench beside {him}.

choices.text: Say that the quarrel seems to have been decided, in the end, in {his} favour

effects.log: {He} laughs for the first time in a thousand years.

events.text: Over the years you come to the heaven by habit, with tea and news, and sit on the bench. {npc} grows no younger, but grows lighter. One evening {he} says {he} has decided to stay, officially, as the keeper of the garden, and asks if you would sign as witness. A seal on the door becomes, for the first time, a gate.
events.arc: The Prisoner Who Asks to Stay

choices.text: Sign as witness, and hang a lamp over the gate

effects.log: The lamp burns steady. The heaven is not a prison any longer, but a place with a keeper, and the keeper welcomes pilgrims.

choices.text: Sign, and promise to bring a willow cutting every spring

effects.log: A fourth willow takes root by the pond. {npc} names it for you.

events.text: The news you bring is plain, and {npc} receives it with great seriousness. {He} writes it on the wall in a small hand: rain in the east, tea dear, the willow-song forgotten. Then {he} adds something, and does not show you. In a decade the song is sung again, in three domains, from a single copied verse.
events.arc: The Prisoner Who Asks to Stay

choices.text: Ask who sang it first

effects.log: No one knows. But {npc} smiles, and puts a finger to {his} lips.

choices.text: Hum it yourself at the gate on the way out

effects.log: The willows nod along, three of them, in a still wind.

events.text: The pardon arrives, formally, in a gold box. {npc} reads it once and asks you to say nothing of it. {He} signs the reply: gratefully received, respectfully declined. The court accepts it, with a mutter. The heaven's seal is taken off, and left on the step, where {he} keeps it as a doorstop.
events.arc: The Prisoner Who Asks to Stay

choices.text: Visit on the first free morning, and share the tea

effects.log: It is the best tea you have had. The door is open, and nobody has ever walked in.

choices.text: Send a gift of a good teapot

effects.log: {He} pours with it at once, and sends back a pressed willow leaf.

events.text: Each year the pilgrims of another pantheon walk a long road to their own high shrine. You have never been invited, and you are curious. You put on a pilgrim's grey cloak and bast sandals, put your name away, and fall in at the back of the line, among a crowd of tired, cheerful strangers with sticks.

choices.text: Walk quietly at the back, and listen

effects.log: The pilgrims talk of their gods as one talks of difficult relatives: with exasperation, and no shortage of love.

choices.text: Strike up a talk with the oldest pilgrim

effects.log: She carries a gourd of water she has carried for forty years. She gives you a mouthful and asks no name.

choices.text: Carry another pilgrim's pack for a mile

effects.log: The owner is moved and suspicious by turns. You keep walking.

events.text: The pilgrims sing at night around a small fire. The songs mock their gods affectionately, and praise them in the same breath. You hear a verse about your own pantheon, which is frank, funny, and not entirely wrong. A young pilgrim catches your eye across the fire and winks, as if you were in on the joke.

choices.text: Laugh, and sing the chorus

effects.log: The fire roars. You are, for one verse, the pilgrim you pretend to be, and it is a pleasure.

choices.text: Stay silent, and take it in

effects.log: The verse turns kinder as it goes. By the end it is almost a prayer.

events.text: The old pilgrim tells you why she walks. Her husband died on this road thirty years ago, on the way to a prayer he never finished. She walks to finish it, a verse a year. She is nearly at the end. She asks whether you think the god will hear it, or whether it is merely a habit of love.

choices.text: Say you think the god will hear it

effects.log: She nods slowly. She does not ask how you know. She tucks her hand into yours for the last stretch of the hill.

choices.text: Say it does not matter whether the god hears

effects.log: She is quiet for a mile. Then she laughs, softly, and says: that is what he would have said.

events.text: At the high shrine the pilgrims kneel in the courtyard, and the god of the place, a stern figure you know well from court, comes out to bless them. They do not recognise you under your cloak. The god's eyes pass over you and pause for a moment, and then, with a tiny motion of the lips, the god keeps the secret.

choices.text: Kneel with the others, and take the blessing

effects.log: It is a good blessing. It is the first you have ever knelt for, and it goes in deeper than you expected.

choices.text: Leave your cloak at the gate as a gift to the shrine

effects.log: The shrine-keepers hang it above the door. It is there, a grey cloak, for the ages, and no one knows whose.

events.text: You stay on a day longer than the others, helping the shrine-keepers clear the courtyard. A sour old keeper asks, without looking up, whether you are a god. You say you are a pilgrim. The keeper snorts, and gives you a bowl of soup, and says in that case, you will wash it yourself.

choices.text: Wash the bowl, and thank the keeper

effects.log: The keeper nods grudgingly. It is the best bowl of soup you have eaten in an age.

choices.text: Admit it, and offer to help in whatever way a god may

effects.log: The keeper looks you up and down and says: scrub the steps, then. And do not tell the others.

events.text: The old pilgrim reaches the last verse of her prayer at the top of the hill, at sunset, and says it aloud. The god of the shrine does not appear. But the wind drops, and the sun hangs on the edge of the hill a little longer than a sun should. She says thank you to no one in particular, and you stand beside her until the light goes.

choices.text: Walk her down the hill in the dusk

effects.log: She leans on you the whole way. At the foot she lets go of your arm, says goodbye by no name, and goes to her sleep.

choices.text: Let her go alone, with respect

effects.log: You watch her small figure down the path, until she is a spot of grey.

events.text: She does not finish the prayer. She stops at the end of the third-to-last verse and says she has decided to leave it undone. A prayer finished is a prayer over, she says, and she is not ready to have her husband's road end. She hands you the gourd, and says: finish it, if you like. Or do not.

choices.text: Take the gourd, and keep walking the road

effects.log: Each year you walk a verse. It becomes a habit of love, and a habit of walking, and a small gentle penance you do not need.

choices.text: Hand the gourd back and thank her

effects.log: She fills it from the stream, and goes on, humming.

events.text: Each autumn the glass hinds come down from the high pastures to the weather-valleys, delicate things whose antlers hold a day of weather apiece. A hunter who takes an antler holds the sky of that day for a year. The domain gods have always hunted them for the sport. This year there are only nine hinds, and the herd's old leader, a hind called Seo, is lame.
events.arc: The Season of the Glass Hinds

choices.text: Join the hunt, to see the hinds

effects.log: The horns sound, the horses stamp, and the hinds, as one, turn and look at you across the valley. Their antlers catch the light like cut glass.

choices.text: Go to the high pastures and wait for the hinds

effects.log: You sit among thistle and cloud. In the dusk, the glass hinds pick their way past you, close enough to touch.

choices.text: Ask the hunters whether anyone has counted the herd

effects.log: Nobody has. A hush goes round the horses.

events.text: Seo the lame hind lags in the heather. The hunt gains. You could put an arrow in her antler and take a day of weather home: a fine blue noon, a century of fame. Or you could ride across her path, and make the hunt turn. The other hunters are watching.
events.arc: The Season of the Glass Hinds

choices.text: Ride across her path and turn the hunt

effects.log: The hunt wheels, swearing. Seo vanishes into the heather and leaves a trail of glass on the grass.

choices.text: Shoot the antler cleanly, and let her go

ok.log: The arrow takes the tip of one tine, no more. A blue noon falls into your quiver, and the hind runs on unharmed.

fail.log: The arrow flies wide, and the herd bolts. You have the sense of having been watched by all of them, kindly.

events.text: In the high pasture, Seo comes to you at dusk and puts her nose to your hand. Her left foreleg is wrapped in a rag of green cloth that somebody tied there. The herd is small because the hunts have been large. She seems to want to say something. A fawn, newly weaned, watches from the thistles with its ears up.
events.arc: The Season of the Glass Hinds

choices.text: Unwrap the rag, and look at the leg

effects.log: It is a clean sprain, healing slowly. You re-tie the rag with a better knot, and Seo bows her head.

choices.text: Offer the fawn a handful of salt

effects.log: The fawn takes a step, and a second, and licks your palm. Its antlers are the size of a spoon, and clear as water.

events.text: At year's end the court calls you to account for your hunt. You carry no antler. You tell them the herd is nine, that the leader is lame, and that there is a fawn. The hall is quiet. A great lord of the Sky says: it has been a long while since anyone counted. By spring the hunts of the glass hinds are suspended by decree.
events.arc: The Season of the Glass Hinds

choices.text: Stand witness at the decree, and read out the count

effects.log: The hall listens. At the final line a murmur runs along the benches. For one season the weather-valleys are still.

choices.text: Say nothing more, and leave the hall quietly

effects.log: In the doorway, an old lord touches your sleeve and murmurs: well done.

events.text: The blue noon sits in your quiver for a year. You ride out under it and the whole valley is bright. It is the best day of weather you have ever held. At the end of the year you let it out on a hill, and the glass hinds come down to graze beneath it, and are not afraid.
events.arc: The Season of the Glass Hinds

choices.text: Return the day to the hinds with an apology

effects.log: Seo lifts her head. The noon spills back into her antler. The herd seems, for a breath, to glow.

choices.text: Keep the blue noon for your own shrine

effects.log: On certain holidays the temple has a perfect noon, whatever the season. Pilgrims think it a miracle.

events.text: The fawn grows, over the years, into a hind with antlers like a chandelier. She returns to the thistle slope every autumn to find you. She brings a younger hind with her one year, and a stag another, until the herd stands at forty. A day of weather is borne on every antler. None of them is ever hunted.
events.arc: The Season of the Glass Hinds

choices.text: Hold a small festival for them at the slope

effects.log: Pilgrims come with shawls and lanterns. The hinds graze through it, unconcerned, in a drift of glass.

choices.text: Come alone, and sit among them as the light fades

effects.log: A hind leans against your shoulder. Weather runs through you like a long slow music.

events.text: There is a god of lost keys, a small cheerful figure with a ring of ten thousand keys on a belt, none of which open anything. {npc} looks after the keys that people drop, and is very sad when they are never reclaimed. {He} stops you on a stair to ask whether any of them look familiar. They all do, a little.

choices.text: Look through the ring with care

effects.log: Among the keys is a small brass one, bent, which you did lose, in a boyhood you scarcely remember. It fits nothing. You are glad to see it.

choices.text: Ask what the keys were for

effects.log: {He} says the god's secret is that nobody knows. The keys are for doors that have since fallen, or never been built.

choices.text: Tell {him} you have lost nothing important lately

effects.log: {He} sighs happily. It is the answer {he} likes best.

events.text: {npc} gives you the bent brass key as a keepsake, and adds a promise: if you ever find a door that fits it, {he} will come and see it opened. You carry the key for a decade and try it on every lock you pass. It never fits. But the trying becomes a habit, and the habit a small kind of faith.

choices.text: Keep trying, door after door

effects.log: Years pass. You become known in three domains as the god with the key. Strangers come to show you their strangest locks.

choices.text: Give the key to a child who is fascinated by it

effects.log: The child takes it and runs. Later the child tries it on a door in a ruin. It does not fit. They keep it all their life.

events.text: {npc} leads you to the Hall of Fallen Doors, a long gallery of doorframes standing alone in the dust, with nothing in or behind them. Each has a keyhole. {He} says each was a door that somebody once opened with something precious. {He} has been collecting the keys for the doors. It is the only thing {he} does.

choices.text: Help {him} match a key to a doorframe

effects.log: It takes the afternoon. At last a small silver key turns in a frame with a hollow click, and a faint light, as of a room long dark, falls across the floor.

choices.text: Dust the frames, and say nothing

effects.log: It is a quiet, good job. {npc} hums.

events.text: Far beyond your own shrine, in a ruin of a sealed heaven, you find a door that will take your brass key. It is a small door in a wall behind a fallen pillar. It opens onto a closet containing a hat, a chair, and a note saying: for whoever finds this. Please keep it. There is no other message. You send word to {npc}, and {he} comes at a run.

choices.text: Let {npc} be the one to turn the key

effects.log: {He} turns it with trembling hands and stands in the doorway of the closet for a long time. Then {he} puts on the hat.

choices.text: Turn it yourself, and share the hat

effects.log: You wear it for an afternoon, and {he} wears it for another. It fits neither of you quite.

events.text: The child grows into a locksmith of some renown, and in a ruined temple at last finds a door the brass key opens. They send you a letter, in careful lettering: I found it, and it was empty, and it was the best day of my life. {npc} reads the letter over your shoulder and weeps at the line.

choices.text: Write back, and thank the locksmith

effects.log: The reply comes in a month, in a fine hand. It is a long and happy letter, and ends with an invitation.

choices.text: Let {npc} write the reply, and sign it

effects.log: It is a rambling thing, and perfect.

events.text: The silver key opens the frame, and the faint light is joined, over the following year, by others. Doors open, one by one, along the gallery: not into rooms, but into small private weathers, a snow, a summer rain, a night of stars. {npc} lights a lamp in the hall for each. The Hall of Fallen Doors becomes a place pilgrims come to sit, and listen to old weather.

choices.text: Add a lamp of your own for a door you lost

effects.log: You light it. It burns a little brighter than the others, as if glad to have been asked.

choices.text: Sit on the bench at the end of the gallery for the evening

effects.log: The weathers go by, one door at a time, until the lamp gutters.

events.text: In the ash of a burned shrine there is a stone that remembers. It is a boulder of black basalt with a faint smoothness on one side, as though a hand had worn it for centuries. Pilgrims who sleep against it dream of a god who is not in any record. The shrine-keeper will not touch it, and no one will say why.
events.arc: The Stone That Remembers Being a God

choices.text: Sleep against the stone for a night

effects.log: You dream of a broad river and a woman with a ladle, saying: drink. You wake with a taste of cold iron.

choices.text: Ask the keeper why no one touches it

effects.log: The keeper says the stone is not an altar. It is a god who sat down one day to wait, and never got up.

choices.text: Sweep the ash from its base, and go

effects.log: Under the ash the stone is warm, like a hearth-flag.

events.text: In the dream the river-god's ladle gives you water that tastes of every spring you have ever known. She says her name is lost, but not her work: she kept the wells of a hundred hills, and when the shrines burned she sat to guard the last one, and was petrified by the sitting. She asks you to carry a cup to the well.
events.arc: The Stone That Remembers Being a God

choices.text: Agree to carry the cup

effects.log: She puts it in your hand in the dream. You wake holding a cup of plain clay, with a damp ring at the bottom.

choices.text: Ask her what the well is guarding

effects.log: She says: a name. Mine. I put it at the bottom for safekeeping.

events.text: The keeper explains. A god who sits to wait has made a choice, and a god who has made a choice cannot be moved by another's hand. The stone is her answer to the fire. The keeper's own mother was a pilgrim who slept against it, and woke with a cup in her hand and a kind of peace. The keeper has never dared to try.
events.arc: The Stone That Remembers Being a God

choices.text: Offer to sleep there on the keeper's behalf

effects.log: You sleep. The dream is the same. In the morning you tell the keeper, quietly, what the ladle said. The keeper has to sit down.

choices.text: Leave the keeper to decide for themselves

effects.log: The keeper looks at the stone for a long while, and then at their hands, and does not touch it.

events.text: The well is a mile from the shrine, in a gully gone to bramble. At the bottom, in a bed of dry silt, you find a bronze ring with a name engraved in it. You say it aloud, once. Rain begins to fall on the dry gully, and the well, slowly, begins to fill. From the shrine, a mile away, comes a sound like a long out-breath.
events.arc: The Stone That Remembers Being a God

choices.text: Carry the cup of water back to the stone

effects.log: You set it against the basalt. The stone is warm, and then, softly, wet. A hand's width of it has gone to the colour of skin.

choices.text: Leave the cup at the well, and the ring in it

effects.log: The well keeps the cup. By morning the gully is green, and a woman with a ladle is sitting on the rim.

events.text: The name is her own. You bring it back to the stone and speak it, and the stone is quiet for a long time. Then a crack runs down it, from top to bottom, with a sound like a breath after a century of holding. She steps out of it, wet, stiff, and a little confused, with a ladle in one hand and a look of acute interest.
events.arc: The Stone That Remembers Being a God

choices.text: Offer her your coat, and a hearth to sit at

effects.log: She sits at your hearth for a week and says very little. Then, one morning, she asks which wells have gone dry.

choices.text: Let her walk off alone into the hills

effects.log: She goes at a steady pace, ladle in hand. In a year the springs of the hills begin to run.

events.text: The keeper touches the stone at last, one dusk, and finds it warm, and unexpectedly kind. The dream they have is brief. They never tell what was said. But the next morning the keeper clears the bramble from the well in the gully, and lays the first stone of a new shrine, a plain small one, for a god without a record.
events.arc: The Stone That Remembers Being a God

choices.text: Help lay the stones

effects.log: You work through a summer. The shrine is unadorned and perfect. A cold spring rises in its floor.

choices.text: Bless it from a distance, and let the keeper have their own

effects.log: The keeper keeps the shrine for sixty years. It is theirs, entirely.

events.text: A folding altar of grey wood, no bigger than a trunk, wanders from domain to domain on the back of a mule. {npc}, its priest, sets it up at crossroads and in marketplaces, and anyone who wishes may pray at it, to any god, in any form. Nobody quite knows who it is dedicated to. The priest does not seem to mind.

choices.text: Pray at it, quietly, to no one in particular

effects.log: The altar smells faintly of cedar. For a moment the whole crossroads is attentive.

choices.text: Ask {npc} who it is dedicated to

effects.log: {He} says: whoever is not yet dedicated. {He} says it with the calm of one who has said it ten thousand times.

choices.text: Buy the mule a bag of oats

effects.log: The mule accepts with dignity. {npc} looks at you for a long moment.

events.text: {npc} asks if you would mind sitting by the altar while {he} goes to find water. The mule snorts. The altar, left alone, begins to fill with prayers. A woman asks for a safe road. A child asks for a lost kitten. A man asks to be forgiven for something small. You have no domain here. You find yourself listening anyway.

choices.text: Answer the prayers you can, in secret

effects.log: You nudge a wind, a kitten, a mood. It is quiet work, and entirely anonymous.

choices.text: Simply listen to each, and let them be

effects.log: It is enough. The prayers go in and settle in the grey wood.

events.text: {npc} confesses that the altar has no god of its own because {he} cannot choose. Each domain asks {him} to dedicate it, and each time, the altar goes quiet, and the prayers stop. It works only because it belongs to no one. The gods of the road, tired of this, have begun to leave a hand-written offer on it: dedicate it to us.

choices.text: Advise {him} to stay undedicated

effects.log: {He} nods slowly. {He} had hoped someone would say it. The altar creaks, a little, as if relieved.

choices.text: Offer to dedicate it to your own shrine, as a gift

effects.log: {He} regards the offer for a long time, and refuses with courtesy. The altar, {he} says, is a thing for everyone.

events.text: Years later {npc} arrives at your shrine with the altar on the mule, and sets it up in the courtyard without comment. It fills at once, with prayers for everything. {He} says: I wanted to see what it did in a place with a god. It does the same. The pilgrims pray on, mixed in with the others, and the altar thrives.

choices.text: Let the altar stay a season

effects.log: The pilgrims love it. In the morning the courtyard smells of cedar. You are, you find, a better god for having a stranger's altar in your yard.

choices.text: Walk with {npc} to the next crossroads, and see it set up

effects.log: At the next crossroads a stranger kneels, and weeps, and rises with a lighter face.

events.text: A prayer is left at the altar addressed to you by name, though you did not do anything to earn it. It is only: thank you for listening. You do not know who left it. {npc} says it is the ninth of its kind, from nine different people. The altar, {he} says, keeps a kind of ledger. {He} lets you read it.

choices.text: Keep the prayer, folded in your sleeve

effects.log: It is a small light weight. You carry it a very long time.

choices.text: Put the prayer back, and leave it to the altar

effects.log: The altar, you feel, has been trusted with it, and takes the job with all seriousness.

events.text: The gods of the road keep leaving offers, and {npc} keeps declining, and the altar goes on. One day the offers stop. In their place a plain note appears: we will pray at it, then, in our own right. A line of road-gods stands before it, each kneeling, all uncertain. {npc} watches in astonishment. The mule, as ever, eats.

choices.text: Kneel at the altar beside them

effects.log: No god rises above the others. The altar is a level place. The mule looks up and sighs.

choices.text: Watch from the back, and smile

effects.log: It is the best sight you have seen in a thousand years.

events.text: On a clear night, over one valley in the Sky domain, every star goes out. The sky above the valley is plain black. The sky above the hills on either side is spangled as ever. The valley folk stand in their fields with lanterns, and the shrine-bell rings, and no god has an explanation. Cheonho sends word that it is not his doing.
events.arc: The Night the Stars Went Out in One Valley

choices.text: Go to the valley and see

effects.log: At the valley's edge the stars begin like a wall: a bright rim, and inside it, a deep clean dark.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho what it could mean

effects.log: He is silent a long while. Then he says that stars do not go out. They are put away. And that somebody, he suspects, has been asked to.

choices.text: Send a lamp down to the valley's shrine

effects.log: The shrine-keeper receives it with relief and sets it burning in the window.

events.text: In the middle of the valley you find a child of nine, asleep on a rock, with a bag of stars at her side. She has been picking them from the sky since evening, one by one, into a sack, because her grandmother is ill, and told her once that a bag of stars would make anyone well. The stars are flickering inside the sack like fireflies.
events.arc: The Night the Stars Went Out in One Valley

choices.text: Wake her gently, and tell her what she has done

effects.log: She weeps, and says she did not know. The sack is heavy, and she is so tired. She asks if she is in trouble.

choices.text: Carry the sack to the grandmother's bed yourself

effects.log: You take it up the track to a small house. The grandmother looks at you, and the sack, and says: ah. I was only telling a story.

events.text: Cheonho and you stand at the valley's rim at midnight. He explains: the stars can be borrowed, by anyone with a clean enough wish, and returned. A borrowing of this size has not been made since the first age. He is more impressed than angry. He asks you to find the borrower and see that the stars go back before dawn.
events.arc: The Night the Stars Went Out in One Valley

choices.text: Go down into the valley to search for the borrower

effects.log: You walk the dark fields with a hooded lamp. At the far end, a pale light flickers by a stream.

choices.text: Offer to stand watch on the rim until sunrise

effects.log: Cheonho nods. The two of you stand and watch the valley sleep.

events.text: You put the stars back with the child, one by one, in the order she took them, saying each name softly. It takes until the grey hour. The grandmother, who has crept out in her blanket, sits on the rock and watches, and says she has not seen the sky so well-ordered since she was a girl. The child falls asleep on her knee.
events.arc: The Night the Stars Went Out in One Valley

choices.text: Tell the grandmother to rest, and promise a star of her own

effects.log: You choose a small bright one over the hill, and name it for her. She laughs and says it will do very well.

choices.text: Help carry the sleeping child home

effects.log: She does not wake. Her small hand holds a last star, which she forgets to give back, and no one minds.

events.text: The grandmother makes tea for the three of you. The stars in the sack hang in the little room like a lit ceiling, and the old woman sits under them and says it is the loveliest she has ever been. By dawn she is well, as if the telling of the story had been the cure. You put the stars back in the morning, in good order.
events.arc: The Night the Stars Went Out in One Valley

choices.text: Return the stars at sunrise, with the child

effects.log: She hands each one up, carefully. By full day, the sky over the valley is the same as the sky over the hills.

choices.text: Leave the sack in the house for one more night

effects.log: The grandmother sleeps well. In the morning the sack is empty, and the sky is full again.

events.text: Cheonho takes a star from the sack and holds it up. He says that it is a child's wish, clean as water, and that he would not have it any other way. He tells you to let the child keep one. The bag is returned and the sky restored, save for a single small light, at the valley's edge, which twinkles, you notice, rather more cheerfully than its neighbours.
events.arc: The Night the Stars Went Out in One Valley

choices.text: Thank Cheonho, and name the star

effects.log: You name it after the grandmother. In the morning she waves at it from her door.

choices.text: Say nothing, and look up for a while

effects.log: It is a good sky. It is a very good sky.

events.text: A war was sealed into a heaven long ago, with its armies, its banners and its hounds. The seal is thinning. One hound has got out, a huge grey war-hound with a cracked collar, still on the scent of an enemy nobody remembers. It trots through the domains at a steady pace, and wherever it passes, old grudges wake.
events.arc: The Last Hound of a Sealed War

choices.text: Track the hound by the grudges it wakes

effects.log: You follow a trail of quarrels: a feud reopened, a gate slammed, a name hissed. At each stop the hound has long gone.

choices.text: Go to the sealed heaven and look at the seal

effects.log: The seal is a wall of grey stone with a hole at hound's height. Beyond the hole it is dark, and the smell is of old iron.

choices.text: Hang a lamp on your door against grudges

effects.log: The lamp burns steadily. The night is quiet.

events.text: You catch up with the hound at a river crossing. It stands on the bank, stiff, with the cracked collar glinting. It does not growl. It looks at you with the weary, trusting look of an old dog who has not been told the war has ended, and who does not quite want to be.
events.arc: The Last Hound of a Sealed War

choices.text: Approach it slowly, with a hand out

ok.log: It sniffs your hand for a long moment, and then, with a sigh, lays its great head against your knee.

fail.log: It bristles, and its hackles rise, and you have to back off, shaken.

choices.text: Wait at the crossing with food on a flat stone

effects.log: It eats, warily, while watching you. When it has finished it sits, and looks across the river, waiting.

events.text: Inside the hole at hound height, by your lamp, you find the old kennel. A row of collars hangs on pegs. One is empty and one is cracked. A message is scratched into the wall: to whoever finds the last of us. He is only doing what he was taught. He does not know it is over. Tell him.
events.arc: The Last Hound of a Sealed War

choices.text: Take a collar from the pegs to gentle the hound

effects.log: It is a good collar, soft with age. It smells of oil and dog.

choices.text: Close the hole with a stone, and leave the war inside

effects.log: The stone fits. The seal holds. It is tidy, and it is not the whole of the matter.

events.text: You tell the hound, as plainly as you can, that the war is over, and that the one it is hunting is gone. It listens with one ear up. Then it lies down on the bank with a long groan, and puts its chin on its paws. Its eyes close. It is not dead. It is, at last, off duty.
events.arc: The Last Hound of a Sealed War

choices.text: Sit by it until it sleeps, and cover it with your coat

effects.log: It sleeps for a week. When it wakes, it follows you, and lies by your hearth, and flinches at any raised voice.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of water, and let it rest where it lies

effects.log: The river sings past. The hound sleeps for a month, and no grudge wakes.

events.text: The hound runs, and you let it. In its wake, quarrels spark in three domains over a pair of cattle, a missing hat, a long-dead word. A god of boundaries is forced to arbitrate a dispute about a stream that was settled a thousand years ago. It takes a year. The grudges pass. The hound is never seen again, but never stops being talked of.
events.arc: The Last Hound of a Sealed War

choices.text: Help the god of boundaries settle the old quarrels

effects.log: You spend a winter with them. By spring you have a list of forty, all gently put to rest.

choices.text: Leave a lamp at each crossing the hound passed

effects.log: A string of lamps runs along the road for a hundred years, and each one is lit by someone.

events.text: You put the collar on the hound in the end, gently, and it lets you. It stands up, wags once, and trots back into the old kennel, and lies down in the dark. You close the door behind it. The seal glows. The war is now sealed with something that wants to be there, and no grudge has woken since.
events.arc: The Last Hound of a Sealed War

choices.text: Leave the lamp burning at the hole

effects.log: A small warm light sits in the dark. You return, once a year, with water and a bone.

choices.text: Walk away, and do not look back

effects.log: Behind you, the hound's tail thumps twice on stone.

events.text: In a primal place a single standing stone hums a note so low you feel it in your teeth. The note has not changed since before the cutting of the domains. If you listen long enough, the plain around it settles into an order, as iron filings do around a magnet.

choices.text: Hum the note back for a quarter-hour

effects.log: The stone brightens. When you stop, the plain keeps humming.

choices.text: Sit with your back to the stone and listen

effects.log: The note passes through you without hurry. You come away steadier than you went.

events.text: In a burned shrine a book has survived, its pages fused into a single black brick. On the cover, scorched but legible, there is a prayer for rain. Beneath it, in a small cramped hand, someone has added a second prayer: and for the one who reads this, if the first was not enough.

choices.text: Say both prayers aloud over the brick

effects.log: A little cold rain begins on the roof. It lasts a minute. It is enough.

choices.text: Carry the brick to your shrine, and set it on the altar

effects.log: Pilgrims touch the cover and ask for rain. They get it, more often than not.

events.text: A sealed heaven has a door of mirror, and on the other side, in the mirror, a second you is trying to open it from within. You push, and your reflection pushes, and the door does not move. You step back, and your reflection steps back, and sits down. It looks as patient as you feel.

choices.text: Sit down too, and wait together

effects.log: You wait an hour. Your reflection yawns first. Neither of you pushes again.

choices.text: Knock three times, softly, and listen

effects.log: The reflection knocks three times in return. A thin line of light runs round the frame, and fades.

events.text: On a white plain a single fox leaves a line of prints that stops dead, as though it had been lifted off the ground. At the stopping place the snow is melted in a perfect circle the size of a table. In the circle, green grass has grown. Something has taken the fox, and it has left a small spring behind.

choices.text: Kneel at the circle and touch the green

effects.log: The grass is warm and smells of summer. In the centre a tiny flower is just opening.

choices.text: Plant a stick at the edge as a marker, and move on

effects.log: When you come back in spring the stick has leafed.

events.text: Every morning at your shrine you find an offering you do not recognise: a dried fish, a blue bead, a child's tooth in a twist of paper. You cannot find who leaves them. One day you stay hidden to see. It is a very small, very old goat, who has been bringing them from a neighbouring shrine, as a tithe.

choices.text: Thank the goat, and leave it a sack of oats

effects.log: It accepts the oats gravely. The next morning it brings a feather.

choices.text: Ask the goat which shrine sent it

effects.log: It looks at you with a long yellow eye, and does not say. But it leads you there the next day.

events.text: In the Sea domain at low tide, a stair of white salt appears, going down from a rock into the sand. It is perfectly dry, and perfectly cold. At the bottom, you are told, is a door, and behind the door a hall of drowned sailors who are very pleased to be remembered. The tide will be back within the hour.

choices.text: Go down quickly, and give them your name

effects.log: They say it back to you in a murmur, like waves. You climb out as the first water touches your heels.

choices.text: Stay on the rock and call down a greeting

effects.log: A faint cheer comes up the stairs. The tide takes the stair at its usual hour, kindly.

events.text: In a corner of Mongsa's dream-paths there is a library whose books are all asleep. Each volume breathes gently on the shelf. If you open one, it yawns, and its pages fill with the dream of the last reader. You open one, and see yourself, small, in a courtyard, being told something kind. You cannot hear what.

choices.text: Close it gently, and let it go back to sleep

effects.log: The book sighs and settles. The whole shelf rustles in approval.

choices.text: Read the dream through, though you cannot hear it

effects.log: You watch your small self nod. When you wake you feel as though you were told, and are still working out what.

events.text: At a feast a god offers you salt from a small silver dish, and says it is the last of a sea that has gone. You have heard of such a sea. You do not know if it is true. The salt tastes of a long way out, and of an afternoon on a deck. Everyone is watching to see how you take it.

choices.text: Take a pinch, and say it is the finest you have tasted

effects.log: The god glows. It is, in its way, true.

choices.text: Ask the god about the sea it came from

effects.log: The god talks for the rest of the course, and the other guests lean in, and the meal is quite changed.

events.text: A petition arrives at the court written in chalk on the side of a goat. It reads: please look at my field. The goat has been walking the court's corridors for three days. It is thin, determined, and bears a faint odour of thyme. The clerks have been trying not to look at it.

choices.text: Take the goat's petition up to the god of fields

effects.log: The god reads the side of the goat, nods, and sends a rain that same afternoon.

choices.text: Feed the goat, and ask where its field is

effects.log: It leads you out of the court at a brisk trot. At the field's edge an old woman is weeping with relief.

events.text: In the great hall a lamp burns that has never been refilled. Its keepers say it burns on gratitude, and that when the gratitude runs short it will go out. Nobody has ever checked the level. This morning it is, you notice, a little low. A line of keepers stands in front of it, looking at their feet.

choices.text: Say a sincere thanks to something, aloud, in front of the lamp

effects.log: The flame brightens at once. One of the keepers wipes an eye.

choices.text: Ask the keepers when they last said thanks themselves

effects.log: There is a long, embarrassed silence. By evening the hall is full of murmuring.

events.text: One of your worshippers has never asked for a thing. She comes each dawn, sweeps the step, polishes the bell, and goes. You have tried to reward her with luck, a mild harvest, a lost coin found. She declines each in the same plain way, by quietly putting the thing back. She says she is happy to be useful.

choices.text: Leave her a clean broom, with no message

effects.log: She uses it for thirty years. She mentions it once, to the bell.

choices.text: Sit on the step one dawn and watch her sweep

effects.log: She does not look up. At the end she says good morning, and you realise she has known you were there for years.

events.text: From the rim of the Sky domain at dawn you see the edge of the world below, a line of gold laid along the sea. A god of small things stands at the rail, quietly crying, because it is so very beautiful, and because there is no one to tell. They have not noticed you. You stand at the other end of the rail.

choices.text: Move down the rail, and stand beside them

effects.log: Neither of you speaks. The gold climbs, and widens, and is day.

choices.text: Stay where you are, and let them have it

effects.log: When the sun is up they wipe their face and go. You stay another hour.

events.text: A new god arrives at the court doors, shivering, with a satchel and an enormous hat. They have been given a domain, a small one, the Domain of the Quarter-Hour, and have come to be introduced. No one is waiting for them. The doorkeeper is on a break. The god looks about with the pale hope of the newly appointed.

choices.text: Introduce them to three gods, and the doorkeeper

effects.log: By the end of the afternoon they have a seat, two enemies, and a friend. It is a good start.

choices.text: Offer them a cup of tea, and a plain word of advice

effects.log: You tell them: the first century is the hardest. They nod. They write it on their hat.

events.text: At the market of faith a stall sells hats stitched from other people's prayers. Each one rustles faintly as you pass. The seller swears the fit is perfect for any head. You try one. It says, in a muffled whisper, please let her get home safe, over and over. You take it off, and the whole stall grows quiet.

choices.text: Return the hat to its stall, and say a prayer of your own for the person

effects.log: The seller lowers their eyes. The hat, on its stand, rustles softly in thanks.

choices.text: Buy the hat, and hang it in your shrine

effects.log: It hangs there, murmuring. Pilgrims come to listen, and leave quieter.

events.text: On the head of your statue at the shrine a bird has built a nest. The priests are scandalised. The bird is delighted. It is a small plain brown thing with a loud voice. Each morning it sings from the top of your stone brow, with absolute confidence, as if the statue were its own idea.

choices.text: Leave the nest, and let the priests sulk

effects.log: In spring there are four chicks. The pilgrims love them and leave seed.

choices.text: Speak to the bird in the dawn, as a god might

effects.log: It stops mid-note, stares at you, and resumes, louder. You feel gently outranked.

events.text: Your oracle gives a prophecy that is clearly wrong. It says a river will run backward at noon. By noon nothing has happened, and the oracle, a trembling old god, is nearly in tears. At that moment a landslide upriver dams the water, and for exactly one breath, the river does run backward.

choices.text: Pat the oracle on the shoulder, and say well done

effects.log: They glow with an odd embarrassed joy. They go on to be right a great deal.

choices.text: Tell the oracle gently that they were nearly right

effects.log: They nod, slowly. It's a more useful answer than praise.

events.text: At a festival of lanterns the children race paper boats down a stream, each carrying a candle. The boats mostly sink or snag. The winner is a boat that has gone round a bend and run into a patch of reeds, and is declared by acclamation the champion for the sheer courage of its failure.

choices.text: Fish the champion out, and dry it by the fire

effects.log: The child who made it gets to keep it. They are very serious about it all evening.

choices.text: Float a boat of your own, and let it sink

effects.log: It sinks nobly. The children cheer, and award you a very small trophy.

events.text: In a hunt that is entirely a ceremony, the hunters ride out, blow horns, shout, and ride back, and no quarry is ever sought. A very old hunter admits, over cider, that the quarry was lost in the third age, and the hunt was kept going out of a sense of manners. The cider is rather good.

choices.text: Ask if they would like to hunt something real

effects.log: The old hunter's eyes brighten. They ask which beast. You suggest, after thought, a fine lazy hare.

choices.text: Join the next hunt, and enjoy the ride

effects.log: It is a splendid morning. Nothing is caught. Everyone is pleased.

events.text: On the primal plain you find a lamp made of a single stone, hollowed and set with a wick of grass. It is not lit. Beside it is a flint with a groove worn by a thumb. Whoever made the lamp lit it once, to see, and left it as a gift for the next. The groove fits your thumb exactly.

choices.text: Light the lamp, and leave it burning

effects.log: The light is small and steady. Far away on the plain, something small looks up.

choices.text: Light it, and carry it with you a day

effects.log: In its light the plain is all different, as though the dark had been waiting for a reason to move.

events.text: An elder god takes you aside at a council recess and apologises, with great stiffness, for something said to you four hundred years ago at a feast. You do not remember it. They do. They have been waiting for the right moment, and the right moment, it seems, is now.

choices.text: Accept the apology with grace, though you do not remember

effects.log: They are visibly lighter. They tell you at length about the rest of their conscience.

choices.text: Tell them you had forgotten, and thank them for remembering

effects.log: They laugh, relieved, and offer you a seat at their table the next feast.

events.text: In a vault of a fallen god you find a shelf of crowns made of tin and cheap glass, each labelled with the name of a child. The god was a patron of make-believe, and gave a crown to every child who asked. The tin is tarnished. The labels are in a neat hand. You read all of them, and then you cry a little.

choices.text: Polish one crown and set it where a child can find it

effects.log: A child will find it, sooner or later. The vault is warm for a day.

choices.text: Take the names, and write each child a short thanks

effects.log: You send forty letters across the domains. Some are returned, with the happy puzzlement of the very old.

events.text: Wearing a plain coat, you take a public ferry across the Sea domain. The ferryman sings constantly, off key. The passengers wear the weary smiles of the long-suffering. A girl asks if you are a god. You say no. She says, relieved, good, because the gods are so tiring, and goes back to her sandwich.

choices.text: Agree with her, and share a sandwich

effects.log: She tells you at length what she would change about the Sea domain. It is all quite sensible.

choices.text: Hum along with the ferryman, off key

effects.log: The ferryman beams. For the length of a crossing, the whole boat is in a bad but cheerful tune.

events.text: A single pale moth the size of a dinner plate lands on your lamp and stays there all night. It does not burn. It sips the light slowly, as from a cup. In the morning the lamp is nearly dark, and the moth is glowing faintly all over, like the moon in a mist, and sits on your shoulder until noon.

choices.text: Let it sit, and carry on with the day

effects.log: It leaves at noon, in a spiral. A pilgrim at the gate says it blessed her.

choices.text: Refill the lamp for the next one

effects.log: A second moth arrives at dusk. They have, it seems, been told.
